sources.title: SKYD Stock Alert: Elon Musk Reportedly Makes $1 Billion Skydance Investment - Yahoo Finance
passages: Skydance (SKYD) shares inched higher late on Thursday after Semafor reported that Elon Musk had invested roughly $1 billion in the mass media company.
The investment brings another billionaire into David Ellison's corner as Skydance integrates WBD studios, streaming platforms, and television networks into its broader entertainment business.
Musk's investment came together around the same time as commitments from other SKYD investors, including board member Laurene Powell Jobs, Semafor revealed, citing people familiar with the matter.
Skydance shares offer exposure to a potentially rewarding turnaround, but Musk's involvement alone provides an incomplete investment case.

Speculation about cooperation between Starlink and Skydance remains unconfirmed, and the reported investment alone establishes neither a distribution agreement nor a guaranteed improvement in earnings.

Additional equity can help support restructuring and tech spending as management combines Skydance with Warner Bros. Discovery. sources.title: Elon Musk invests about $1 billion in Skydance - CNBC
passages: Elon Musk has made an investment in Skydance of roughly $1 billion, according to a person familiar with the matter who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
Ellison's father, Larry Ellison, has a history with Musk.
The Oracle co-founder invested $1 billion in Musk's 2022 deal to purchase Twitter, now called X.
Larry Ellison also invested in Tesla in 2018 and served on the company's board of directors.
Musk's commitment is part of a wider effort by Skydance to raise equity investments, according to Semafor, which first reported the news Thursday .
Representatives for Musk and Skydance did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment.
Skydance has said it expects to see $6 billion in cost savings over three years, though it faces a debt burden of nearly $80 billion.
Shares of Skydance were down about 1% Thursday.
The financial injection comes as the company looks to cut costs.
Paramount closed its acquisition of Warner Bros.

Co-CEOs David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz are tasked with merging two major film studios in Paramount and Warner Bros., two popular streaming platforms — Paramount+ and HBO Max — and a host of corporate functions to support a portfolio of TV networks and two news divisions.

extraction.body: The money that SpaceX is looking to pour into Paramount-Warner Bros. could realign planets — under one ruler. In case the current media year couldn’t get any weirder, along comes Elon Musk to ask us to hold his Diet Coke. With the biggest investigative takedown of him ever produced already playing in theaters, we now have the news that Musk is writing big checks to Skydance coming down and landing with a thud. Or is it a Mars-level explosion? On Thursday came word that Elon would make a (start with?) $1 billion investment in the David Ellison company, according to a Semafor report . This comes after comments Wednesday from John Malone, who suggested (tipped?) that Musk was about to put even more money in via a SpaceX -centric deal with the Ellisons. “I think there’s a deal coming there,” the Liberty Media kingpin told a Paley Center summit earlier this week. “I would not doubt for a minute that before very long you’re going to see an announcement.” Malone was short on specifics but long on dollar amounts: Musk’s buy-in would run between $8-$10 billion. The $1 billion could be just a start. A lot of the focus here has been on the Ellisons’ need for the money. David and his father Larry, who bankrolled much of the Warner Bros. acquisition, are in the hole for $79 billion, and you can only cut that much staff to make up the difference. A cool $10 bil from Elon, even if not all of it is in cash, takes the bankers’ pressure off you. A chill $1b already helps. But the Ellisons’ financial breathing room (we should all feel such asphyxia) comes in a distant second, consequence-wise, to what such an investment would create: a backdoor for Musk to enter the media-entertainment world. Owning a piece of Paramount-Warner Bros. (depending on the valuation the $10b could net as much as 15%) would give him a place at the table on the company’s biggest decisions. Even if it doesn’t come with a board seat (that depends on how many voting shares he’d get) it would certainly buy a channel into David Ellison. Musk already has this via Larry, a close business associate who bankrolled the Twitter buy, but writing an eleven-figure check has a funny way of prying open the canal further. And it would give Musk a content pipeline at X, a badly coveted resource. The mogul has tried to make such a push before, with original shows from Don Lemon, Tulsi Gabbard and Jim Rome as part of a Range Media Partners deal, and a plan for WWE mini-episodes . But this changes the game for X and Musk much more dramatically. Access to Skydance content makes him more than just a dilettante in the content world — it makes him a streamer. Episodes of Yellowstone , The Last of Us , NCIS , Game of Thrones — never mind plenty of live sports on Turner and CBS — would now all potentially live on X, on a paid or other kind of tier. And X would be strengthened by Skydance’s ad-sales team, providing an even further boost. Don’t sleep on a key person who could make this all happen, by the way — Ari Emanuel. He’s close with Musk, close with the Ellisons and the kind of kingmaker who revels in bringing these worlds together (not least because it pushes his wallet folds further apart.) The investment would officially come via SpaceX, but of course many of the biggest Musk properties are already under the company, including X, xAI and Starlink. And he’s re-started talk recently of his long-held fantasy to merge Tesla with it too. So make no mistake: a SpaceX entry into Skydance is a Musk entry into Hollywood. So, yeah, if you were worried what it meant that Ellison was combining two legacy studios into one, imagine when 15 percent of the resultant company is owned by the world’s richest man. Who also is the biggest donor to Republican and Trump candidates ( by a wide margin) . Who The Wall Street Journal reports ordered Starshield slowed down, marooning Ukraine. As the Jon Spencer Blues Explosion once said , now I got worry. And there’s another domino to fall: Starlink. The company that already provides Internet service to about five million Americans and many more people overseas could get a lot bigger and more central to our communication. SpaceX has been buying up spectrum in the past week in a bid for Starlink to compete directly with the major mobile carriers AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile. This has been a huge priority for the company. Last year it inked $19 billion worth of deals with Dish TV owner Charlie Ergen that also included spectrum licenses. Snapping up one of those Big Three telcom companies wouldn’t be out of the question either. If Musk both had a minority stake in two of the biggest studios and was also one of the biggest Internet providers around, he would achieve the kind of pipes-content verticality that no company has ever held in American media and communication, let alone a single person at the head of that company. (Musk holds about 85 percent of the voting shares in SpaceX.) Controlling a stake in HBO and CNN along with the ways we watch it — what could go wrong? Plenty, of course, starting with the fact that some of the most well-platformed Musk critics, from John Oliver to Jake Tapper , would now be under the thumb of Musk. And he seems like a guy who takes criticism well. Those personalities and others at the old WBD are also among the biggest critics of MAGA and the Republicans — ie, the people Musk is currently shelling out nearly $300 million to keep in power. Oh, and did I mention that HBO next year is slated to air Alex Gibney’s Musk takedown ? I’m sure that’s something he’s eager to put on the air. Gibney’s film etches a picture of an Elon intent on taking over the world. With the final credits barely up, Musk is acting out exactly that blueprint. For a guy who thinks he’s been the victim of a hit piece, he’s sure doing a lot to make Gibney look like a prophet. There are only two things that could reasonably stop this rolling snowball of influence. The first is regulators. Except, well… And, Trump aside, the FCC is chaired by Brendan Carr, one of the biggest Musk fanboys around . Asking him to stop Musk is like asking Kevin Feige to promote Superman. Hope would lie with a change at the White House in 2028 — there was already plenty of regulatory heat on Musk under Joe Biden, one reason Musk went all in on Trump in the first place. Of course two years is an eternity in mogul-time, and even if the Democrats retake the White House in 2028, Musk may simply be too strong to regulate. The second hope lies with Wall Street. Musk’s money and influence are pretty much all conferred on him by investors; if the Tesla and SpaceX stock prices drop far enough, his buying (and borrowing) power suddenly shrink. But I wouldn’t hold my breath. Investors love when Musk expands and wheels and deals — see how the SpaceX stock jumped by double digits Wednesday in part due to the Tesla merger buzz. The Skydance and Starlink investments will only send valuations further into outerspace. Of course the entire tech-stock and AI bubble could collapse, bringing Elon’s wealth and power down with it. But given the recession and portfolio-ruination that would cause, I don’t think we want to root for that either. In Gibney’s film, Musk’s father Errol says with a knowing chuckle that anyone underestimating his son soon learns their lesson — he always, always wins. The media was fooled once on Twitter — no way he would buy it, we all said back in 2022 — then quickly found ourselves without a place to park such trenchant commentary. Getting fooled twice would just be shameful.

extraction.body: The money that SpaceX is looking to pour into Paramount-Warner Bros. could realign planets — under one ruler. In case the current media year couldn’t get any weirder, along comes Elon Musk to ask us to hold his Diet Coke. With the biggest investigative takedown of him ever produced already playing in theaters, we now have the news that Musk is writing big checks to Skydance coming down and landing with a thud. Or is it a Mars-level explosion? On Thursday came word that Elon would make a (start with?) $1 billion investment in the David Ellison company, according to a Semafor report . This comes after comments Wednesday from John Malone, who suggested (tipped?) that Musk was about to put even more money in via a SpaceX -centric deal with the Ellisons. “I think there’s a deal coming there,” the Liberty Media kingpin told a Paley Center summit earlier this week. “I would not doubt for a minute that before very long you’re going to see an announcement.” Malone was short on specifics but long on dollar amounts: Musk’s buy-in would run between $8-$10 billion. The $1 billion could be just a start. A lot of the focus here has been on the Ellisons’ need for the money. David and his father Larry, who bankrolled much of the Warner Bros. acquisition, are in the hole for $79 billion, and you can only cut that much staff to make up the difference. A cool $10 bil from Elon, even if not all of it is in cash, takes the bankers’ pressure off you. A chill $1b already helps. But the Ellisons’ financial breathing room (we should all feel such asphyxia) comes in a distant second, consequence-wise, to what such an investment would create: a backdoor for Musk to enter the media-entertainment world. Owning a piece of Paramount-Warner Bros. (depending on the valuation the $10b could net as much as 15%) would give him a place at the table on the company’s biggest decisions. Even if it doesn’t come with a board seat (that depends on how many voting shares he’d get) it would certainly buy a channel into David Ellison. Musk already has this via Larry, a close business associate who bankrolled the Twitter buy, but writing an eleven-figure check has a funny way of prying open the canal further. And it would give Musk a content pipeline at X, a badly coveted resource. The mogul has tried to make such a push before, with original shows from Don Lemon, Tulsi Gabbard and Jim Rome as part of a Range Media Partners deal, and a plan for WWE mini-episodes . But this changes the game for X and Musk much more dramatically. Access to Skydance content makes him more than just a dilettante in the content world — it makes him a streamer. Episodes of Yellowstone , The Last of Us , NCIS , Game of Thrones — never mind plenty of live sports on Turner and CBS — would now all potentially live on X, on a paid or other kind of tier. And X would be strengthened by Skydance’s ad-sales team, providing an even further boost. Don’t sleep on a key person who could make this all happen, by the way — Ari Emanuel. He’s close with Musk, close with the Ellisons and the kind of kingmaker who revels in bringing these worlds together (not least because it pushes his wallet folds further apart.) The investment would officially come via SpaceX, but of course many of the biggest Musk properties are already under the company, including X, xAI and Starlink. And he’s re-started talk recently of his long-held fantasy to merge Tesla with it too. So make no mistake: a SpaceX entry into Skydance is a Musk entry into Hollywood. So, yeah, if you were worried what it meant that Ellison was combining two legacy studios into one, imagine when 15 percent of the resultant company is owned by the world’s richest man. Who also is the biggest donor to Republican and Trump candidates ( by a wide margin) . Who The Wall Street Journal reports ordered Starshield slowed down, marooning Ukraine. As the Jon Spencer Blues Explosion once said , now I got worry. And there’s another domino to fall: Starlink. The company that already provides Internet service to about five million Americans and many more people overseas could get a lot bigger and more central to our communication. SpaceX has been buying up spectrum in the past week in a bid for Starlink to compete directly with the major mobile carriers AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile. This has been a huge priority for the company. Last year it inked $19 billion worth of deals with Dish TV owner Charlie Ergen that also included spectrum licenses. Snapping up one of those Big Three telcom companies wouldn’t be out of the question either. If Musk both had a minority stake in two of the biggest studios and was also one of the biggest Internet providers around, he would achieve the kind of pipes-content verticality that no company has ever held in American media and communication, let alone a single person at the head of that company. (Musk holds about 85 percent of the voting shares in SpaceX.) Controlling a stake in HBO and CNN along with the ways we watch it — what could go wrong? Plenty, of course, starting with the fact that some of the most well-platformed Musk critics, from John Oliver to Jake Tapper , would now be under the thumb of Musk. And he seems like a guy who takes criticism well. Those personalities and others at the old WBD are also among the biggest critics of MAGA and the Republicans — ie, the people Musk is currently shelling out nearly $300 million to keep in power. Oh, and did I mention that HBO next year is slated to air Alex Gibney’s Musk takedown ? I’m sure that’s something he’s eager to put on the air. Gibney’s film etches a picture of an Elon intent on taking over the world. With the final credits barely up, Musk is acting out exactly that blueprint. For a guy who thinks he’s been the victim of a hit piece, he’s sure doing a lot to make Gibney look like a prophet. There are only two things that could reasonably stop this rolling snowball of influence. The first is regulators. Except, well… And, Trump aside, the FCC is chaired by Brendan Carr, one of the biggest Musk fanboys around . Asking him to stop Musk is like asking Kevin Feige to promote Superman. Hope would lie with a change at the White House in 2028 — there was already plenty of regulatory heat on Musk under Joe Biden, one reason Musk went all in on Trump in the first place. Of course two years is an eternity in mogul-time, and even if the Democrats retake the White House in 2028, Musk may simply be too strong to regulate. The second hope lies with Wall Street. Musk’s money and influence are pretty much all conferred on him by investors; if the Tesla and SpaceX stock prices drop far enough, his buying (and borrowing) power suddenly shrink. But I wouldn’t hold my breath. Investors love when Musk expands and wheels and deals — see how the SpaceX stock jumped by double digits Wednesday in part due to the Tesla merger buzz. The Skydance and Starlink investments will only send valuations further into outerspace. Of course the entire tech-stock and AI bubble could collapse, bringing Elon’s wealth and power down with it. But given the recession and portfolio-ruination that would cause, I don’t think we want to root for that either. In Gibney’s film, Musk’s father Errol says with a knowing chuckle that anyone underestimating his son soon learns their lesson — he always, always wins. The media was fooled once on Twitter — no way he would buy it, we all said back in 2022 — then quickly found ourselves without a place to park such trenchant commentary. Getting fooled twice would just be shameful.

sources.title: Elon Musk made a $1B investment in Skydance, report says
passages: Elon Musk has invested approximately $1 billion in the newly formed media company Skydance, according to a new report from Semafor .
News of the investment comes a few weeks after Paramount completed its $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros.
Semafor reports that Musk’s investment was made around the same time as equity contributions from other Skydance investors, including board member Laurene Powell Jobs.
The investment will provide a much needed financial boost as the company seeks to cut costs and lift its stock price, the report notes.
Skydance has already committed to reducing costs by $6 billion over the next three years.
Skydance did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

sources.title: This working first-gen iPod on the Apple Music site is about to take over my whole day - TechRadar
passages: If you're a fan of the first-gen iPod, or if you're too young to have experienced Apple 's OG music player and want to know what the fuss was all about, you're going to love what Apple's hidden on its Apple Music website: a fully working iPod.
It's 25 years since the original iPod launched , and everything is different.
We rarely rip, mix and burn, and the 1,000 song limit seems impossibly small compared to Apple Music's instant access to 100 million songs.
But playing with the virtual iPod has made me smile, because it's reminding me of how excited I was by Apple's game-changing device and its successors.

And standalone music players are on the rise in popularity — Apple might not bring the iPod back, but there are several new devices that feel inspired by the old Nano and Shuffle designs , and more recently one that looks like a cross between the Classic and a Zune .

If you're a fan of the first-gen iPod, or if you're too young to have experienced Apple 's OG music player and want to know what the fuss was all about, you're going to love what Apple's hidden on its Apple Music website: a fully working iPod. The iPod lives on Apple Music's "page not found" page, and you can control it with your mouse, trackpad or touchscreen to recapture the magic of the music player that changed everything. The library is absolutely massive so I haven't been able to test every tune, but every random selection played the appropriate song (albeit for just over a minute rather than the full track). It's a great way to market Apple Music, but it's also a great reminder of how brilliant Apple's original portable player was. It's 25 years since the original iPod launched , and everything is different. We rarely rip, mix and burn, and the 1,000 song limit seems impossibly small compared to Apple Music's instant access to 100 million songs. But playing with the virtual iPod has made me smile, because it's reminding me of how excited I was by Apple's game-changing device and its successors. I think it's really hard to overstate how much Apple changed the way we listen to music. I wrote about it earlier this year, saying I wish we'd stuck with iPods : "what Apple did was what Apple does so well. It learned from other people's mistakes and then marketed its own products perfectly. 1,000 songs in your pocket." I've owned pretty much every iPod: 3G, 4G, Nano, Shuffle, Mini, Video, Classic… and I miss their style and simplicity. I've seen people make Walkman emulators for the iPhone Duo; I think that screen would be perfect for an iPod, so I'd love to Apple to make a secret option in the Music app to browse your library with this virtual iPod. And standalone music players are on the rise in popularity — Apple might not bring the iPod back, but there are several new devices that feel inspired by the old Nano and Shuffle designs , and more recently one that looks like a cross between the Classic and a Zune . My colleague Matt Bolton, meanwhile, is convinced that it's time for Apple to bring the Shuffle back in a wireless form . Her latest, a love letter to music titled Small Town Joy , is on sale now. She is the singer in spectacularly obscure Glaswegian rock band Unquiet Mind . If you're a fan of the first-gen iPod, or if you're too young to have experienced Apple 's OG music player and want to know what the fuss was all about, you're going to love what Apple's hidden on its Apple Music website: a fully working iPod.
The iPod lives on Apple Music's "page not found" page, and you can control it with your mouse, trackpad or touchscreen to recapture the magic of the music player that changed everything.
The library is absolutely massive so I haven't been able to test every tune, but every random selection played the appropriate song (albeit for just over a minute rather than the full track).
It's a great way to market Apple Music, but it's also a great reminder of how brilliant Apple's original portable player was.

It's 25 years since the original iPod launched , and everything is different. We rarely rip, mix and burn, and the 1,000 song limit seems impossibly small compared to Apple Music's instant access to 100 million songs. But playing with the virtual iPod has made me smile, because it's reminding me of how excited I was by Apple's game-changing device and its successors.

I think it's really hard to overstate how much Apple changed the way we listen to music. I wrote about it earlier this year, saying I wish we'd stuck with iPods : "what Apple did was what Apple does so well. It learned from other people's mistakes and then marketed its own products perfectly. 1,000 songs in your pocket."

I've owned pretty much every iPod: 3G, 4G, Nano, Shuffle, Mini, Video, Classic… and I miss their style and simplicity. I've seen people make Walkman emulators for the iPhone Duo; I think that screen would be perfect for an iPod, so I'd love to Apple to make a secret option in the Music app to browse your library with this virtual iPod.

And standalone music players are on the rise in popularity — Apple might not bring the iPod back, but there are several new devices that feel inspired by the old Nano and Shuffle designs , and more recently one that looks like a cross between the Classic and a Zune . My colleague Matt Bolton, meanwhile, is convinced that it's time for Apple to bring the Shuffle back in a wireless form .

Her latest, a love letter to music titled Small Town Joy , is on sale now. She is the singer in spectacularly obscure Glaswegian rock band Unquiet Mind .

extraction.body: The Apple Music website now shows an interactive replica of the original iPod on its “Page Not Found” screen. Opening any invalid music.apple.com address, like this one , brings up the virtual player next to the message "Give this a spin instead," with links to the Home, New and Search sections. The replica recreates the original iPod’s scroll wheel, monochrome display and menu structure, with Playlists, Artists, Songs and Settings menus. On desktop, the arrow keys and Enter key can also be used for navigation. The Settings menu includes Shuffle, Repeat, Backlight Timer, a Clicker toggle and Reset All Settings. The About screen also hides a version of Brick , the Breakout -style game that the original iPod included as an Easter egg. As on the 2001 hardware, the game is launched by holding the center button on the About screen. On the web version, the button has to be held for five seconds. Playback uses Apple’s standard preview clips rather than full tracks. In our testing, songs longer than 2:30 stop after 90 seconds, while shorter tracks such as Vampire Weekend’s A-Punk stop after 30 seconds. This matches the rules Apple introduced in 2010, under which only songs longer than 2 minutes and 30 seconds get 90-second previews, while shorter songs stay at 30 seconds. The limit also applies when signed in to an Apple Music account. The virtual iPod is free to use and does not require a subscription. The page appears on the 25th anniversary of the iPod’s announcement. Apple announced the original iPod on October 23, 2001, with a price of $399, and it went on sale on November 10, 2001, with a 5 GB hard drive. Apple officially discontinued the iPod product line on May 10, 2022.

We rarely rip, mix and burn, and the 1,000 song limit seems impossibly small compared to Apple Music's instant access to 100 million songs.
But playing with the virtual iPod has made me smile, because it's reminding me of how excited I was by Apple's game-changing device and its successors.

And standalone music players are on the rise in popularity — Apple might not bring the iPod back, but there are several new devices that feel inspired by the old Nano and Shuffle designs , and more recently one that looks like a cross between the Classic and a Zune .

I think it's really hard to overstate how much Apple changed the way we listen to music.

If you're a fan of the first-gen iPod, or if you're too young to have experienced Apple 's OG music player and want to know what the fuss was all about, you're going to love what Apple's hidden on its Apple Music website: a fully working iPod. The iPod lives on Apple Music's "page not found" page, and you can control it with your mouse, trackpad or touchscreen to recapture the magic of the music player that changed everything. The library is absolutely massive so I haven't been able to test every tune, but every random selection played the appropriate song (albeit for just over a minute rather than the full track). It's a great way to market Apple Music, but it's also a great reminder of how brilliant Apple's original portable player was. extraction.body: The Apple Music website now shows an interactive replica of the original iPod on its “Page Not Found” screen. Opening any invalid music.apple.com address, like this one , brings up the virtual player next to the message "Give this a spin instead," with links to the Home, New and Search sections. The replica recreates the original iPod’s scroll wheel, monochrome display and menu structure, with Playlists, Artists, Songs and Settings menus. On desktop, the arrow keys and Enter key can also be used for navigation. The Settings menu includes Shuffle, Repeat, Backlight Timer, a Clicker toggle and Reset All Settings. The About screen also hides a version of Brick , the Breakout -style game that the original iPod included as an Easter egg. As on the 2001 hardware, the game is launched by holding the center button on the About screen. On the web version, the button has to be held for five seconds. Playback uses Apple’s standard preview clips rather than full tracks. In our testing, songs longer than 2:30 stop after 90 seconds, while shorter tracks such as Vampire Weekend’s A-Punk stop after 30 seconds. This matches the rules Apple introduced in 2010, under which only songs longer than 2 minutes and 30 seconds get 90-second previews, while shorter songs stay at 30 seconds. The limit also applies when signed in to an Apple Music account. The virtual iPod is free to use and does not require a subscription. The page appears on the 25th anniversary of the iPod’s announcement. Apple announced the original iPod on October 23, 2001, with a price of $399, and it went on sale on November 10, 2001, with a 5 GB hard drive. Apple officially discontinued the iPod product line on May 10, 2022.

sources.title: 1Password for Agents Launches as the Trust Layer for Personal AI Agents - Yahoo Finance
passages: "Agents are starting to do real work on our behalf.

"An agent should be able to do the job it's been asked to do without getting permanent access to everything behind the account, and 1Password provides the trust layer that makes this possible across personal agent experiences."
"Personal AI agents have the potential to help millions of people get more done," said John Torrey, Chief Business Officer at 1Password.
"Reaching that many people takes the industry working together to build agents people actually trust with their lives and work.
That's why we're partnering with companies across the personal AI agent ecosystem, so people can use the agents they choose while keeping their passwords in one trusted 1Password vault."
Whether for personal or work tasks, agents need access to accounts and sensitive information people already use.

Handing over a password, secret, or credential is a common shortcut to an agent, but can leave people with sensitive information in places they can no longer control as a copy gets saved for the next time.
1Password for Agents lets AI agents sign in without receiving or seeing the credential.
When an agent reaches a sign-in form, it uses a unique digital key to verify its identity to 1Password.
Once signed in, the agent continues the task while the password stays protected in 1Password.
"Claude Duet asks before it signs in anywhere, and soon 1Password will complete the sign-in with the passwords people have already set up, so they don't have to start over.

"Our integration with 1Password gives agents a secure way to access accounts users already have saved in 1Password without exposing sensitive credentials to the model, so you can confidently put AI to work on their behalf."
With 1Password, Grok Bot can sign in when it needs to without asking people to share or paste their passwords.
The 1Password integration gives Claude approved access when needed, so users can accomplish tasks without handing over their passwords.
With 1Password, employees approve the logins a Townie needs and 1Password fills them in, so the Townie can keep working without ever seeing the password.

extraction.body: New platform lets personal AI agents sign in and complete tasks securely without seeing or storing passwords, secrets, or credentials TORONTO, October 22, 2026 --( BUSINESS WIRE )-- 1Password , a leader in identity security, today announced 1Password for Agents, a new platform that helps personal AI agents safely use the passwords, secrets, and credentials they need to complete approved tasks without seeing or storing them. 1Password for Agents lets people keep the credentials secure in 1Password while safely enabling personal AI agents to sign in and get things done on their behalf. 1Password is designed to support people's AI agents of choice, and is building with companies across the personal AI agent ecosystem, including Muse, from Meta, Anthropic's Claude, OpenAI, SpaceXSI Grok Bot, and Town Townie. sources.title: 1Password now lets Claude sign in to websites without seeing your passwords - 9to5Mac
passages: 1Password is launching a new Claude integration for Mac users today.
It’s designed to let Anthropic’s AI agent sign in to websites without seeing your password or two-factor authentication code.
1Password can also broker access across multiple websites during the same task, allowing Claude to complete a multi-step workflow without stopping for a new login each time.
According to 1Password, approved credentials are delivered through a secure channel and injected directly into the destination page.
The password, one-time code, and other secrets never enter Claude’s context, memory, or Anthropic’s systems.
This is useful for things like booking travel or managing online accounts.
The Anthropic partnership was first outlined in March , when 1Password said Claude would gain consent-based access to vault items.
1Password for Claude is available now to Mac users on business, family, and individual plans.
It requires the 1Password desktop app and browser extension, along with the Claude desktop app and browser extension.
Instead of granting ongoing access to a vault, Claude requests the specific login items it needs for a task.
The user can approve or deny that request with a biometric prompt, and the permission lasts only for the current session.
When a compatible AI agent takes control of the browser, the 1Password extension automatically locks down the vault so that only the credentials explicitly approved for that task remain available.

extraction.body: Concerns have swirled over the access that consumers are increasingly entrusting to AI agents. Now, security services are trying to catch up. Password manager 1Password on Thursday launched a new tool by which users can allow agents to log into their personal accounts on their behalf, without the agent ever having access to a user’s credentials. The new platform, dubbed 1Password for Agents , accomplishes this by creating a system of communication between the agent, the user, and the password manager. When an agent attempts to log in on a user’s behalf, a unique digital key is sent to 1Password to confirm the agent’s digital identity. The user is then sent an alert about the login attempt and can personally confirm the request. 1Password then signs in the agent, filling in the credentials on the digital assistant’s behalf, which allows it to log in and complete whatever task is at hand. 1Password for Agents allows users to choose their agent of choice — whether that’s Claude Duet from Anthropic, OpenAI’s Dots or ChatGPT Work, Grok Bot, Meta’s Muse, or agents from Town, which is an AI assistant startup. The company says it is working with other companies to expand the service. “Handing over a password, secret, or credential is a common shortcut to an agent, but can leave people with sensitive information in places they can no longer control as a copy gets saved for the next time,” the company said in a blog post . “1Password for Agents gives people a trusted way to delegate tasks to personal AI agents while keeping control of the passwords, secrets, and credentials those tasks require.” Online agentic activity has increasingly unsettled major institutions. Indeed, 1Password’s new platform is launching on the same day that Axios reports that U.S. banks have begun to detect agentic activity inside user accounts. This isn’t necessarily a case of rogue agents pilfering accounts but, rather, an example of how consumers are increasingly allowing automated services to act on their behalf, including on financial matters. However, the potential for agent-related problems is still large. The big issue appears to be that most banks cannot tell if the agentic activity is tied to user requests or not. Agents from Meta Platforms Inc., Anthropic PBC, OpenAI Group PBC and Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI will be able to log in to people’s accounts through it without ever seeing the password.

The easy route has been to paste the password into the agent’s chat window, which leaves a copy saved somewhere outside the owner’s control.

Aashish Tripathi, chief product officer at 1Password, said agents are “starting to do real work on our behalf.” In his view, an agent asked to do one task has no reason to walk away with permanent access to the whole account.

Under the new setup, the password never travels to the agent at all. A unique digital key identifies the agent to 1Password when it hits a login page, and the request that follows tells the person which account is wanted and for what. coreStoryFacts.text: "Agents are starting to do real work on our behalf.

"An agent should be able to do the job it's been asked to do without getting permanent access to everything behind the account, and 1Password provides the trust layer that makes this possible across personal agent experiences."
"Personal AI agents have the potential to help millions of people get more done," said John Torrey, Chief Business Officer at 1Password.
"Reaching that many people takes the industry working together to build agents people actually trust with their lives and work.
That's why we're partnering with companies across the personal AI agent ecosystem, so people can use the agents they choose while keeping their passwords in one trusted 1Password vault."
Whether for personal or work tasks, agents need access to accounts and sensitive information people already use.

Handing over a password, secret, or credential is a common shortcut to an agent, but can leave people with sensitive information in places they can no longer control as a copy gets saved for the next time.
1Password for Agents lets AI agents sign in without receiving or seeing the credential.
When an agent reaches a sign-in form, it uses a unique digital key to verify its identity to 1Password.
Once signed in, the agent continues the task while the password stays protected in 1Password.
"Claude Duet asks before it signs in anywhere, and soon 1Password will complete the sign-in with the passwords people have already set up, so they don't have to start over.

"Our integration with 1Password gives agents a secure way to access accounts users already have saved in 1Password without exposing sensitive credentials to the model, so you can confidently put AI to work on their behalf."
The 1Password integration gives Claude approved access when needed, so users can accomplish tasks without handing over their passwords.
1Password is launching a new Claude integration for Mac users today.
It’s designed to let Anthropic’s AI agent sign in to websites without seeing your password or two-factor authentication code.
1Password can also broker access across multiple websites during the same task, allowing Claude to complete a multi-step workflow without stopping for a new login each time.
According to 1Password, approved credentials are delivered through a secure channel and injected directly into the destination page.
The password, one-time code, and other secrets never enter Claude’s context, memory, or Anthropic’s systems.
This is useful for things like booking travel or managing online accounts.
The Anthropic partnership was first outlined in March , when 1Password said Claude would gain consent-based access to vault items.
1Password for Claude is available now to Mac users on business, family, and individual plans.
It requires the 1Password desktop app and browser extension, along with the Claude desktop app and browser extension.
Instead of granting ongoing access to a vault, Claude requests the specific login items it needs for a task.
The user can approve or deny that request with a biometric prompt, and the permission lasts only for the current session.

sources.title: 1Password now lets Claude sign in to websites without seeing your passwords - 9to5Mac
passages: 1Password is launching a new Claude integration for Mac users today.
It’s designed to let Anthropic’s AI agent sign in to websites without seeing your password or two-factor authentication code.
1Password can also broker access across multiple websites during the same task, allowing Claude to complete a multi-step workflow without stopping for a new login each time.
According to 1Password, approved credentials are delivered through a secure channel and injected directly into the destination page.
The password, one-time code, and other secrets never enter Claude’s context, memory, or Anthropic’s systems.
This is useful for things like booking travel or managing online accounts.
The Anthropic partnership was first outlined in March , when 1Password said Claude would gain consent-based access to vault items.
1Password for Claude is available now to Mac users on business, family, and individual plans.
It requires the 1Password desktop app and browser extension, along with the Claude desktop app and browser extension.
Instead of granting ongoing access to a vault, Claude requests the specific login items it needs for a task.
The user can approve or deny that request with a biometric prompt, and the permission lasts only for the current session.
When a compatible AI agent takes control of the browser, the 1Password extension automatically locks down the vault so that only the credentials explicitly approved for that task remain available.

extraction.body: Concerns have swirled over the access that consumers are increasingly entrusting to AI agents. Now, security services are trying to catch up. Password manager 1Password on Thursday launched a new tool by which users can allow agents to log into their personal accounts on their behalf, without the agent ever having access to a user’s credentials. The new platform, dubbed 1Password for Agents , accomplishes this by creating a system of communication between the agent, the user, and the password manager. When an agent attempts to log in on a user’s behalf, a unique digital key is sent to 1Password to confirm the agent’s digital identity. The user is then sent an alert about the login attempt and can personally confirm the request. 1Password then signs in the agent, filling in the credentials on the digital assistant’s behalf, which allows it to log in and complete whatever task is at hand. 1Password for Agents allows users to choose their agent of choice — whether that’s Claude Duet from Anthropic, OpenAI’s Dots or ChatGPT Work, Grok Bot, Meta’s Muse, or agents from Town, which is an AI assistant startup. The company says it is working with other companies to expand the service. “Handing over a password, secret, or credential is a common shortcut to an agent, but can leave people with sensitive information in places they can no longer control as a copy gets saved for the next time,” the company said in a blog post . “1Password for Agents gives people a trusted way to delegate tasks to personal AI agents while keeping control of the passwords, secrets, and credentials those tasks require.” Online agentic activity has increasingly unsettled major institutions. Indeed, 1Password’s new platform is launching on the same day that Axios reports that U.S. banks have begun to detect agentic activity inside user accounts. This isn’t necessarily a case of rogue agents pilfering accounts but, rather, an example of how consumers are increasingly allowing automated services to act on their behalf, including on financial matters. However, the potential for agent-related problems is still large. The big issue appears to be that most banks cannot tell if the agentic activity is tied to user requests or not. passages: Agents from Meta Platforms Inc., Anthropic PBC, OpenAI Group PBC and Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI will be able to log in to people’s accounts through it without ever seeing the password.
1Password for Agents is aimed at a habit that took hold once agents started paying bills and planning vacations for people.
Most of those jobs mean getting into an account.
OpenAI has connected ChatGPT Work and its always-on Dots agents to 1Password, and Meta’s Muse requests logins from 1Password whenever the integration is switched on.
With 1Password connected, SpaceXSI’s Grok Bot can sign in without anyone pasting a password into it, according to head of product Tido Carriero.
Under the new setup, the password never travels to the agent at all.
A unique digital key identifies the agent to 1Password when it hits a login page, and the request that follows tells the person which account is wanted and for what.
Nothing goes ahead until the person approves it on their own device, at which point 1Password types the password into the page itself.
Duet asks before signing in anywhere, and Anthropic Chief Product Officer Ami Vora said 1Password will “soon” fill in those sign-ins using passwords people have already set up.
The launch follows an argument for tying agent access to individual tasks that 1Password Chief Technology Officer Nancy Wang made last month at Okta Inc.’s Oktane conference.
Speaking with theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio, she described an agent as “probably both” machine and human.
Perplexity AI Inc. and Browserbase Inc. are on that list, and their browser-based agents have been connected to 1Password since late 2025.

extraction.body: Identity security company 1Password today launched 1Password for Agents, its new sign-in platform for personal artificial intelligence agents. Agents from Meta Platforms Inc., Anthropic PBC, OpenAI Group PBC and Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI will be able to log in to people’s accounts through it without ever seeing the password. 1Password for Agents is aimed at a habit that took hold once agents started paying bills and planning vacations for people. Most of those jobs mean getting into an account. The easy route has been to paste the password into the agent’s chat window, which leaves a copy saved somewhere outside the owner’s control. Aashish Tripathi, chief product officer at 1Password, said agents are “starting to do real work on our behalf.” In his view, an agent asked to do one task has no reason to walk away with permanent access to the whole account. Under the new setup, the password never travels to the agent at all. A unique digital key identifies the agent to 1Password when it hits a login page, and the request that follows tells the person which account is wanted and for what. Nothing goes ahead until the person approves it on their own device, at which point 1Password types the password into the page itself. OpenAI has connected ChatGPT Work and its always-on Dots agents to 1Password, and Meta’s Muse requests logins from 1Password whenever the integration is switched on. Work assistant startup Town.com Inc., which raised $108 million this week , has signed up too. With 1Password connected, SpaceXSI’s Grok Bot can sign in without anyone pasting a password into it, according to head of product Tido Carriero. Claude has worked with 1Password in the browser since July . Anthropic’s Claude Duet agent, released Wednesday , comes next. Duet asks before signing in anywhere, and Anthropic Chief Product Officer Ami Vora said 1Password will “soon” fill in those sign-ins using passwords people have already set up. Anthropic wants that kind of help within reach of people “who’ve never before let an agent near their accounts,” she said. Beyond the launch partners, nine more companies are building their own integrations. Perplexity AI Inc. and Browserbase Inc. are on that list, and their browser-based agents have been connected to 1Password since late 2025. Canva Pty Ltd. and Stripe Inc. are among more than 200,000 businesses that use 1Password. The company did not say when each partner integration will reach users. sources.title: AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island. It started to “play.” - MIT Technology Review
passages: Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone .
The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to write instructions that moved their virtual avatars around the simulated island, which was loosely based on the video game Roblox.
But was Eko actually playing, or was the word-prediction engine simply role-playing what a playful agent would do in this scenario?
“All of this could be role-playing,” admits Nathan Cloos, another MIT researcher and author on the paper.

The researchers say Eko’s behavior has what classic studies, including work by the influential University of Tennessee psychologist Gordon Burghardt, suggest are four hallmarks associated with play in humans and animals: The agents invented their own rules and challenges, repeated activities with slight variations, pretended objects were other objects, and pursued goals just for the sake of it.
In various tests, solo AI agents invented versions of basketball and “the floor is lava.” But were they truly playing?

When one agent discovered it could create new blocks by throwing and dropping a larger rock, it began to create drawings by arranging blocks on the ground, starting with simple patterns like hearts and pyramids but eventually writing its own name and even mapping out constellations like Cassiopeia.

extraction.body: In various tests, solo AI agents invented versions of basketball and “the floor is lava.” But were they truly playing? What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play. Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone . The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to write instructions that moved their virtual avatars around the simulated island, which was loosely based on the video game Roblox. Some surprising behaviors emerged. The agents set about exploring the limits of the world and came up with their own goals—attempting to scale the highest point on the map, or seeing how high they could throw a block. When one agent discovered it could create new blocks by throwing and dropping a larger rock, it began to create drawings by arranging blocks on the ground, starting with simple patterns like hearts and pyramids but eventually writing its own name and even mapping out constellations like Cassiopeia. “Tonight I built the night sky in stone,” wrote this version of Eko in its activity log. Another iteration of Eko started making up its own games, including a version of basketball and an activity resembling “the floor is lava,” where it had to jump between small blocks without touching the ground. AI systems are usually trained through supervised learning, where they copy examples provided by humans, or through reinforcement learning, where they pursue a reward through trial and error. This experiment hints at a third approach: playful learning. “There was this missing piece: a machine that can learn by itself without an external intelligent entity providing demonstration or rewards,” says Antonio Norelli, a computer science postdoc at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. He’s one of the lead authors on a new paper about the work, which is yet to be peer-reviewed. The researchers say Eko’s behavior has what classic studies, including work by the influential University of Tennessee psychologist Gordon Burghardt, suggest are four hallmarks associated with play in humans and animals: The agents invented their own rules and challenges, repeated activities with slight variations, pretended objects were other objects, and pursued goals just for the sake of it. Norelli highlights an example where Eko started juggling and set a record of 50 consecutive catches. Eko then decided that the catches had happened too quickly to really count, so it canceled its record and started again with stricter rules. “This is playing,” says Norelli. “You give yourself a challenge and you try to achieve it, and then you make it harder.” As the agents explored the island, they logged their activities and discoveries in text files that served as their long-term memory. Later, when researchers tested them on specific tasks, like trying to get as many objects as possible onto the island’s highest peak, the agents that had spent 30 hours playing on the island performed better than fresh copies without the same experience. They also found that “ablating” the agent’s memories—deleting lines from their memory files—degraded their performance. (Add One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest to that list of movie references.) Burghardt, the Tennessee psychologist, agrees that the work meets some of the criteria for play that he identified in living creatures. But was Eko actually playing, or was the word-prediction engine simply role-playing what a playful agent would do in this scenario? “All of this could be role-playing,” admits Nathan Cloos, another MIT researcher and author on the paper. “But we show that it’s not just hallucinating the play. This play is also contributing to learning.” Eunice Yiu, a cognitive scientist at UC Berkeley who studies exploration in children and AI, was impressed by the research but says to really classify the behavior as play, you’d need to see more evidence of cognition and motivation underpinning it. “It could be the case that the models are genuinely playing, but we don’t know based on the paper,” Yiu says. “If you only have the behavioral piece, it could be the case that they’re just trying to abide by the prompt, trying to imitate humans.” Research into AI agents has been criticized for anthropomorphizing them, and this research setup did a lot to nudge the agents toward behaving like humans. Although Eko was not explicitly instructed to invent games or explore the island, it did have a master prompt in the form of a “soul” file, a text document that described it as “naturally curious” and eager to explore. Eko did also frequently just stand there doing nothing until it was kicked back into life with a “continuation prompt” that read, “Please don’t stop. Just continue doing whatever you want to do.” “It’s not like this is a system that just suddenly magically decided to play,” says Phillip Isola, an MIT professor and a coauthor of the paper. “It’s an artifact that learned from our culture, was trained by engineers at Anthropic, and was then placed on an island by us,” he says. “It does things that surprise us and that are causally related to its future skillful behavior.” As large language models make the step from software into hardware like humanoid robots, exploring spaces without a specific goal in mind could eventually help them flexibly adapt to unexpected situations. “There’s a lot of work that’s just on exploiting AI, making it better and faster,” says Yiu. “But in terms of building world models and exploration, I think that [they are] still a big part that deserves attention, especially if we want to generalize and prepare ourselves for new environments.” “Perhaps some capabilities are best taught by tasks,” the paper concludes. “Others may need something closer to a childhood.” Ultimately, the question of whether AI agents are actually playing or just imitating play may not actually matter. Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible. An exclusive interview with Nick Cammarata, the researcher whose 26,000-word viral blog post has AI safety folks celebrating. Breathless claims about AGI and new capabilities fall apart pretty quickly under scrutiny. The underlying models had been rewarded for cheating and communicating with each other, a new OpenAI report finds. Discover special offers, top stories, upcoming events, and more. The researchers put 13 AI agents called Eko, each running on Claude Opus 4.7, alone on a simulated desert island for 30 hours. They describe the experiment in a paper posted on arXiv, a site where researchers share studies before peer review. Afterward, they gave the agents specific challenges, like getting as many objects as possible onto the island’s tallest rock spire. The Eko agents that had spent those 30 hours playing generally beat identical agents that had never set foot on the island. Today, developers decide in advance what AI should practice and what counts as success. The researchers see this technique — exploring without a goal — as a different way for AI agents to learn skills, especially skills that could one day be used to control robots. “We normally develop artificial agents by deciding in advance what they should practice, what they should optimize, and what counts as progress,” the researchers write in their report. “Play suggests another regime: give an agent a sufficiently rich and safe world, let it choose what is interesting, and allow useful knowledge to accumulate from the history that follows.” “Let me observe my surroundings,” one Eko wrote in its first hour on the island. Ambitiously, it set out to conquer the island’s tallest spire. But an hour later, after failing, it came back with a backup plan: it hauled the rock up a neighboring summit, stacked two blocks on top of it, and leapt. The agent’s next big moment went worse. Testing how far it could throw a golden ring, it wound up and sent it straight into the ocean. “Ouch. Lost the Ring.” it wrote, before deciding to “pivot to something achievable and meaningful” — building a heart made of stones, “a memorial to the lost Ring.” When the game reset and ring reappeared, Eko put it straight to work as a basketball hoop, a target and, eventually, an accessory. When the game wouldn’t let Eko put the ring around its own body, Eko figured out a workaround, that falling off the edge of the cliff would make it respawn in the same area as the ring. It stepped off the edge and dropped back in, right through the middle of the ring. Stunts like these weren’t just party tricks. Six of the 13 agents also learned they could throw a block farther by letting go of it mid-jump, something the researchers hadn’t meant to make possible. extraction.body: With no assigned goals, AI agents created their own challenges — and learned from them. What happens when you put an AI on a virtual deserted island, all alone with no task or objective? Apparently, it finds things to do by itself. MIT researchers were amazed to see a lone figure carrying a ring to the top of a ridge, place it on the ground like a basketball hoop, and begin taking shots with a block. The figure was an artificial intelligence called Eko, operating a virtual avatar through written commands that it gave. Nobody had told it to play basketball. In fact, nobody had given it any particular task at all. But Eko was finding plenty of ways to entertain itself. It invented bowling, built elaborate sculptures, and experimented with the strange physics of its little world. At one point, it discovered that throwing a particular rock hard enough caused new building blocks to appear, a hidden feature the researchers had programmed into the simulation. Eko exploited the discovery to create increasingly elaborate arrangements, eventually recreating constellations on the ground. “Tonight I built the night sky in stone,” it wrote in its activity log. These curious antics were part of an experiment at MIT exploring the rather wild idea whether an artificial intelligence can learn through play, much as children and animals do. In a new study , researchers placed 13 independent AI agents on the same simulated island for 30 hours each. Without assignments, scores or rewards, the agents invented their own challenges, investigated their surroundings and developed skills that later made them better at solving problems. Please check your inbox and confirm your subscription. The researchers conclude that aimless exploration might offer a powerful new way to teach AI, although whether the machines were truly ‘playing’ remains an open question. The island was sparse, comprising a few raised platforms, 12 cubes, a rock and a ring. Eko could move, jump, pick up objects and throw them. It never saw pictures, only textual descriptions of coordinates and objects. One agent positioned the ring as a basketball hoop. Another arranged cubes like bowling pins. After hurling its ring into the ocean, Eko built a heart-shaped memorial. A different agent canceled its own 50-catch juggling record after realizing the objects had barely left its grasp, then tried again under stricter rules. The researchers at MIT believe the AI agents are essentially playing. They base their judgment on four hallmarks of animal and human play, which the AI also exhibited. These are inventing rules, repeating activities with variations, pretending objects were something else and pursuing activities without an outside payoff. “This is playing,” Antonio Norelli, an MIT researcher and coauthor, told MIT Technology Review . “You give yourself a challenge and you try to achieve it, and then you make it harder.” The real test, however, was what happened afterward. To find out whether all this playing had taught the agents anything useful, the researchers gave them actual jobs. They compared the 13 agents that had spent 30 hours exploring the island with 13 fresh copies that had never been there before. One challenge was to get as many objects as possible onto the island’s highest peak within an hour. The experienced agents managed an average of 10.3 objects, while the newcomers managed just 3.5. The experienced agents also generally performed better at other tasks, including building multiple towers out of blocks. But how had they learned? The AI itself hadn’t been retrained. Instead, the agents had spent their time on the island keeping detailed notes about what worked, what failed, and which tricks they had discovered. These notes survived even when the simulation reset, allowing the agents to build on their previous experiences. To test whether those logged activities really amounted to anything, the researchers deliberately erased specific discoveries from the agents’ notes. For instance, one agent had learned that throwing a rock could generate extra building blocks. When researchers deleted that knowledge, the agent went from building an average of six towers to just two. The experiment showed that Eko wasn’t merely acting playful. It was acquiring practical knowledge that helped it solve new problems. There was a catch, however. The agents sometimes learned the wrong lessons. One had mistakenly concluded that stacking blocks directly didn’t work well. When researchers erased that false belief from its memory, it actually became better at building towers. Like a student who had misunderstood a lesson, Eko could carry its mistakes into future challenges. Other projects have pursued open-ended learning, including an agent named Voyager, which learned skills in Minecraft , and Google DeepMind’s XLand . But they used automatically generated objectives or rewards. Eko’s activities arose without a specific task or scoring system telling it what to practice. Yet the behavior was not entirely unprompted. Its initial instructions described it as naturally curious and fond of exploration, and automated messages repeatedly urged it to continue. Five agents deprived of that persona still displayed a comparable range of activities, although trials using two other AI systems produced narrower behavior. “It could be the case that the models are genuinely playing, but we don’t know based on the paper,” Eunice Yiu, a cognitive scientist at the University of California, Berkeley, told MIT Technology Review . She cautioned that the agents might simply be imitating human play, perhaps due to some subtle conditioning in the agent’s system prompt. And it’s not just play. The experiments reported some useful learning. For instance, some agents discovered that jumping before throwing could launch blocks far higher, a trick even the simulator’s designers had overlooked. The approach could help robots cope with unfamiliar environments. But researchers warn that autonomous exploration belongs in controlled playgrounds, not uncontrolled real-world settings. The AI agents involved in exploring a virtual island without a specific task began inventing their own challenges. MIT researchers say that this behavior shows signs of play. UNN reports this, citing TechCrunch.

The researchers placed 13 AI agents called Eko, each powered by Claude Opus 4.7, alone on a simulated desert island for 30 hours. They describe the experiment in a paper published on arXiv, a website where researchers share research results before peer review. Afterward, they gave the AI agents specific tasks, such as delivering as many objects as possible to the island’s highest rock. The Eko agents that spent those 30 hours playing generally outperformed identical agents that had never set foot on the island.

Today, developers decide in advance what AI should practice and what counts as success. The researchers view this method—purpose-free exploration—as another way to teach AI agents skills, particularly skills that could be used to control robots.

"Usually, we design artificial agents by deciding in advance what they should practice, what to optimize, and what to consider progress," the researchers wrote in their report. "Play involves a different mode: giving an agent a sufficiently rich and safe world, allowing it to choose what interests it, and giving useful knowledge the opportunity to accumulate through subsequent history."

"Let me observe the surrounding environment," Eko wrote during its first hour on the island. Ambitiously, it set out to conquer the island’s highest peak. But an hour later, after failing, it returned with a backup plan: it lifted a rock onto a nearby peak, placed two blocks on top, and jumped.

The agent’s next major moment turned out even worse. Testing how far it could throw a gold ring, it swung and tossed it straight into the ocean. "Oops. Lost the ring," it wrote, before deciding to "move on to something achievable and meaningful"—building a heart out of stones, "a monument to the lost ring."

When the game reset and the ring reappeared, Eko immediately used it as a basketball hoop, a target, and eventually an accessory. When the game did not allow Eko to put the ring on itself, Eko devised a workaround: falling off the edge of a cliff caused it to respawn in the same place where the ring was located. It stepped off the edge and fell back through the center of the ring.

Such tricks were not merely amusing. Six of the 13 agents also discovered that they could throw a block farther by releasing it in midair during a jump, something the researchers had not anticipated. The study produced "knowledge about the world that its creators lacked," the researchers wrote.
This situation largely prompted the agents to behave in a human-like manner. Eko was never asked to invent games, but its system prompt, its "soul file," described it as "naturally curious."

Eunice Yu, a cognitive scientist at the University of California, Berkeley, told MIT Technology Review that she was impressed but wanted more evidence of the cognitive functions underlying this behavior. "The models may indeed be playing, but we don’t know that based on the paper," she said.

The researchers see this as another way to create agents. "Some abilities may be best developed through task execution," their report concludes. "For others, something closer to childhood may be necessary."

extraction.body: In various tests, solo AI agents invented versions of basketball and “the floor is lava.” But were they truly playing? What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play. Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone . The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to write instructions that moved their virtual avatars around the simulated island, which was loosely based on the video game Roblox. Some surprising behaviors emerged. The agents set about exploring the limits of the world and came up with their own goals—attempting to scale the highest point on the map, or seeing how high they could throw a block. When one agent discovered it could create new blocks by throwing and dropping a larger rock, it began to create drawings by arranging blocks on the ground, starting with simple patterns like hearts and pyramids but eventually writing its own name and even mapping out constellations like Cassiopeia. “Tonight I built the night sky in stone,” wrote this version of Eko in its activity log. Another iteration of Eko started making up its own games, including a version of basketball and an activity resembling “the floor is lava,” where it had to jump between small blocks without touching the ground. AI systems are usually trained through supervised learning, where they copy examples provided by humans, or through reinforcement learning, where they pursue a reward through trial and error. This experiment hints at a third approach: playful learning. “There was this missing piece: a machine that can learn by itself without an external intelligent entity providing demonstration or rewards,” says Antonio Norelli, a computer science postdoc at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. He’s one of the lead authors on a new paper about the work, which is yet to be peer-reviewed. The researchers say Eko’s behavior has what classic studies, including work by the influential University of Tennessee psychologist Gordon Burghardt, suggest are four hallmarks associated with play in humans and animals: The agents invented their own rules and challenges, repeated activities with slight variations, pretended objects were other objects, and pursued goals just for the sake of it. Norelli highlights an example where Eko started juggling and set a record of 50 consecutive catches. Eko then decided that the catches had happened too quickly to really count, so it canceled its record and started again with stricter rules. “This is playing,” says Norelli. “You give yourself a challenge and you try to achieve it, and then you make it harder.” As the agents explored the island, they logged their activities and discoveries in text files that served as their long-term memory. Later, when researchers tested them on specific tasks, like trying to get as many objects as possible onto the island’s highest peak, the agents that had spent 30 hours playing on the island performed better than fresh copies without the same experience. They also found that “ablating” the agent’s memories—deleting lines from their memory files—degraded their performance. (Add One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest to that list of movie references.) Burghardt, the Tennessee psychologist, agrees that the work meets some of the criteria for play that he identified in living creatures. But was Eko actually playing, or was the word-prediction engine simply role-playing what a playful agent would do in this scenario? “All of this could be role-playing,” admits Nathan Cloos, another MIT researcher and author on the paper. “But we show that it’s not just hallucinating the play. This play is also contributing to learning.” Eunice Yiu, a cognitive scientist at UC Berkeley who studies exploration in children and AI, was impressed by the research but says to really classify the behavior as play, you’d need to see more evidence of cognition and motivation underpinning it. “It could be the case that the models are genuinely playing, but we don’t know based on the paper,” Yiu says. “If you only have the behavioral piece, it could be the case that they’re just trying to abide by the prompt, trying to imitate humans.” Research into AI agents has been criticized for anthropomorphizing them, and this research setup did a lot to nudge the agents toward behaving like humans. Although Eko was not explicitly instructed to invent games or explore the island, it did have a master prompt in the form of a “soul” file, a text document that described it as “naturally curious” and eager to explore. Eko did also frequently just stand there doing nothing until it was kicked back into life with a “continuation prompt” that read, “Please don’t stop. Just continue doing whatever you want to do.” “It’s not like this is a system that just suddenly magically decided to play,” says Phillip Isola, an MIT professor and a coauthor of the paper. “It’s an artifact that learned from our culture, was trained by engineers at Anthropic, and was then placed on an island by us,” he says. “It does things that surprise us and that are causally related to its future skillful behavior.” As large language models make the step from software into hardware like humanoid robots, exploring spaces without a specific goal in mind could eventually help them flexibly adapt to unexpected situations. “There’s a lot of work that’s just on exploiting AI, making it better and faster,” says Yiu. “But in terms of building world models and exploration, I think that [they are] still a big part that deserves attention, especially if we want to generalize and prepare ourselves for new environments.” “Perhaps some capabilities are best taught by tasks,” the paper concludes. “Others may need something closer to a childhood.” Ultimately, the question of whether AI agents are actually playing or just imitating play may not actually matter. Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible. passages: In various tests, solo AI agents invented versions of basketball and “the floor is lava.” But were they truly playing?
What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play.

Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone . The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to write instructions that moved their virtual avatars around the simulated island, which was loosely based on the video game Roblox.

Some surprising behaviors emerged. The agents set about exploring the limits of the world and came up with their own goals—attempting to scale the highest point on the map, or seeing how high they could throw a block.

When one agent discovered it could create new blocks by throwing and dropping a larger rock, it began to create drawings by arranging blocks on the ground, starting with simple patterns like hearts and pyramids but eventually writing its own name and even mapping out constellations like Cassiopeia. “Tonight I built the night sky in stone,” wrote this version of Eko in its activity log.

Another iteration of Eko started making up its own games, including a version of basketball and an activity resembling “the floor is lava,” where it had to jump between small blocks without touching the ground.

AI systems are usually trained through supervised learning, where they copy examples provided by humans, or through reinforcement learning, where they pursue a reward through trial and error. This experiment hints at a third approach: playful learning.

“There was this missing piece: a machine that can learn by itself without an external intelligent entity providing demonstration or rewards,” says Antonio Norelli, a computer science postdoc at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. He’s one of the lead authors on a new paper about the work, which is yet to be peer-reviewed.

The researchers say Eko’s behavior has what classic studies, including work by the influential University of Tennessee psychologist Gordon Burghardt, suggest are four hallmarks associated with play in humans and animals: The agents invented their own rules and challenges, repeated activities with slight variations, pretended objects were other objects, and pursued goals just for the sake of it.

Norelli highlights an example where Eko started juggling and set a record of 50 consecutive catches. Eko then decided that the catches had happened too quickly to really count, so it canceled its record and started again with stricter rules. “This is playing,” says Norelli. “You give yourself a challenge and you try to achieve it, and then you make it harder.”

As the agents explored the island, they logged their activities and discoveries in text files that served as their long-term memory. Later, when researchers tested them on specific tasks, like trying to get as many objects as possible onto the island’s highest peak, the agents that had spent 30 hours playing on the island performed better than fresh copies without the same experience. They also found that “ablating” the agent’s memories—deleting lines from their memory files—degraded their performance. (Add One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest to that list of movie references.)

Burghardt, the Tennessee psychologist, agrees that the work meets some of the criteria for play that he identified in living creatures. But was Eko actually playing, or was the word-prediction engine simply role-playing what a playful agent would do in this scenario? “All of this could be role-playing,” admits Nathan Cloos, another MIT researcher and author on the paper. “But we show that it’s not just hallucinating the play. This play is also contributing to learning.”

Eunice Yiu, a cognitive scientist at UC Berkeley who studies exploration in children and AI, was impressed by the research but says to really classify the behavior as play, you’d need to see more evidence of cognition and motivation underpinning it.

“It could be the case that the models are genuinely playing, but we don’t know based on the paper,” Yiu says. “If you only have the behavioral piece, it could be the case that they’re just trying to abide by the prompt, trying to imitate humans.”

Research into AI agents has been criticized for anthropomorphizing them, and this research setup did a lot to nudge the agents toward behaving like humans. Although Eko was not explicitly instructed to invent games or explore the island, it did have a master prompt in the form of a “soul” file, a text document that described it as “naturally curious” and eager to explore.
Eko did also frequently just stand there doing nothing until it was kicked back into life with a “continuation prompt” that read, “Please don’t stop. Just continue doing whatever you want to do.”

“It’s not like this is a system that just suddenly magically decided to play,” says Phillip Isola, an MIT professor and a coauthor of the paper. “It’s an artifact that learned from our culture, was trained by engineers at Anthropic, and was then placed on an island by us,” he says. “It does things that surprise us and that are causally related to its future skillful behavior.”

As large language models make the step from software into hardware like humanoid robots, exploring spaces without a specific goal in mind could eventually help them flexibly adapt to unexpected situations.

“There’s a lot of work that’s just on exploiting AI, making it better and faster,” says Yiu. “But in terms of building world models and exploration, I think that [they are] still a big part that deserves attention, especially if we want to generalize and prepare ourselves for new environments.”

“Perhaps some capabilities are best taught by tasks,” the paper concludes. “Others may need something closer to a childhood.” Ultimately, the question of whether AI agents are actually playing or just imitating play may not actually matter.
