extraction.body: With no assigned goals, AI agents created their own challenges — and learned from them. What happens when you put an AI on a virtual deserted island, all alone with no task or objective? Apparently, it finds things to do by itself. MIT researchers were amazed to see a lone figure carrying a ring to the top of a ridge, place it on the ground like a basketball hoop, and begin taking shots with a block. The figure was an artificial intelligence called Eko, operating a virtual avatar through written commands that it gave. Nobody had told it to play basketball. In fact, nobody had given it any particular task at all. But Eko was finding plenty of ways to entertain itself. It invented bowling, built elaborate sculptures, and experimented with the strange physics of its little world. At one point, it discovered that throwing a particular rock hard enough caused new building blocks to appear, a hidden feature the researchers had programmed into the simulation. Eko exploited the discovery to create increasingly elaborate arrangements, eventually recreating constellations on the ground. “Tonight I built the night sky in stone,” it wrote in its activity log. These curious antics were part of an experiment at MIT exploring the rather wild idea whether an artificial intelligence can learn through play, much as children and animals do. In a new study , researchers placed 13 independent AI agents on the same simulated island for 30 hours each. Without assignments, scores or rewards, the agents invented their own challenges, investigated their surroundings and developed skills that later made them better at solving problems. Please check your inbox and confirm your subscription. The researchers conclude that aimless exploration might offer a powerful new way to teach AI, although whether the machines were truly ‘playing’ remains an open question. The island was sparse, comprising a few raised platforms, 12 cubes, a rock and a ring. Eko could move, jump, pick up objects and throw them. It never saw pictures, only textual descriptions of coordinates and objects. One agent positioned the ring as a basketball hoop. Another arranged cubes like bowling pins. After hurling its ring into the ocean, Eko built a heart-shaped memorial. A different agent canceled its own 50-catch juggling record after realizing the objects had barely left its grasp, then tried again under stricter rules. The researchers at MIT believe the AI agents are essentially playing. They base their judgment on four hallmarks of animal and human play, which the AI also exhibited. These are inventing rules, repeating activities with variations, pretending objects were something else and pursuing activities without an outside payoff. “This is playing,” Antonio Norelli, an MIT researcher and coauthor, told MIT Technology Review . “You give yourself a challenge and you try to achieve it, and then you make it harder.” The real test, however, was what happened afterward. To find out whether all this playing had taught the agents anything useful, the researchers gave them actual jobs. They compared the 13 agents that had spent 30 hours exploring the island with 13 fresh copies that had never been there before. One challenge was to get as many objects as possible onto the island’s highest peak within an hour. The experienced agents managed an average of 10.3 objects, while the newcomers managed just 3.5. The experienced agents also generally performed better at other tasks, including building multiple towers out of blocks. But how had they learned? The AI itself hadn’t been retrained. Instead, the agents had spent their time on the island keeping detailed notes about what worked, what failed, and which tricks they had discovered. These notes survived even when the simulation reset, allowing the agents to build on their previous experiences. To test whether those logged activities really amounted to anything, the researchers deliberately erased specific discoveries from the agents’ notes. For instance, one agent had learned that throwing a rock could generate extra building blocks. When researchers deleted that knowledge, the agent went from building an average of six towers to just two. The experiment showed that Eko wasn’t merely acting playful. It was acquiring practical knowledge that helped it solve new problems. There was a catch, however. The agents sometimes learned the wrong lessons. One had mistakenly concluded that stacking blocks directly didn’t work well. When researchers erased that false belief from its memory, it actually became better at building towers. Like a student who had misunderstood a lesson, Eko could carry its mistakes into future challenges. Other projects have pursued open-ended learning, including an agent named Voyager, which learned skills in Minecraft , and Google DeepMind’s XLand . But they used automatically generated objectives or rewards. Eko’s activities arose without a specific task or scoring system telling it what to practice. Yet the behavior was not entirely unprompted. Its initial instructions described it as naturally curious and fond of exploration, and automated messages repeatedly urged it to continue. Five agents deprived of that persona still displayed a comparable range of activities, although trials using two other AI systems produced narrower behavior. “It could be the case that the models are genuinely playing, but we don’t know based on the paper,” Eunice Yiu, a cognitive scientist at the University of California, Berkeley, told MIT Technology Review . She cautioned that the agents might simply be imitating human play, perhaps due to some subtle conditioning in the agent’s system prompt. And it’s not just play. The experiments reported some useful learning. For instance, some agents discovered that jumping before throwing could launch blocks far higher, a trick even the simulator’s designers had overlooked. The approach could help robots cope with unfamiliar environments. But researchers warn that autonomous exploration belongs in controlled playgrounds, not uncontrolled real-world settings. Afterward, they gave the AI agents specific tasks, such as delivering as many objects as possible to the island’s highest rock. Today, developers decide in advance what AI should practice and what counts as success. The researchers view this method—purpose-free exploration—as another way to teach AI agents skills, particularly skills that could be used to control robots. "Let me observe the surrounding environment," Eko wrote during its first hour on the island. Ambitiously, it set out to conquer the island’s highest peak. But an hour later, after failing, it returned with a backup plan: it lifted a rock onto a nearby peak, placed two blocks on top, and jumped. The agent’s next major moment turned out even worse. Testing how far it could throw a gold ring, it swung and tossed it straight into the ocean. "Oops. Lost the ring," it wrote, before deciding to "move on to something achievable and meaningful"—building a heart out of stones, "a monument to the lost ring." When the game reset and the ring reappeared, Eko immediately used it as a basketball hoop, a target, and eventually an accessory. When the game did not allow Eko to put the ring on itself, Eko devised a workaround: falling off the edge of a cliff caused it to respawn in the same place where the ring was located. It stepped off the edge and fell back through the center of the ring. Such tricks were not merely amusing. Six of the 13 agents also discovered that they could throw a block farther by releasing it in midair during a jump, something the researchers had not anticipated. The study produced "knowledge about the world that its creators lacked," the researchers wrote. This situation largely prompted the agents to behave in a human-like manner. Eko was never asked to invent games, but its system prompt, its "soul file," described it as "naturally curious." Eunice Yu, a cognitive scientist at the University of California, Berkeley, told MIT Technology Review that she was impressed but wanted more evidence of the cognitive functions underlying this behavior. "The models may indeed be playing, but we don’t know that based on the paper," she said. The researchers see this as another way to create agents. "Some abilities may be best developed through task execution," their report concludes. "For others, something closer to childhood may be necessary." "Welcome to the new world of super intelligence - SI," Trump said during a wide-ranging speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday. While some people close to the president immediately started to use the term, experts have told the BBC it is unlikely to gain widespread traction in the industry because it is a name typically used to refer to more advanced systems. The announcement is Trump's latest rebranding move after he had the names of Lake Ontario and the Gulf of Mexico changed on US maps and federal communications. "From this point forward, all of United States' documents, and hopefully the world's, will be changed to use the more accurate term 'super' as opposed to 'artificial'. So it's 'super intelligence'," Trump said. In the past week, Trump asked his social media followers to vote on other potential new names for AI including superior intelligence, extreme intelligence and supreme intelligence. After a series of polls on his Truth Social platform, super intelligence came out as the winner. The purpose of renaming AI - and whether it will be adopted by the technology industry - is unclear. AI refers to computer technology that allows machines to do tasks that usually require human thinking. Meanwhile, super intelligence has a specific meaning within the tech community. The term is often linked to the author and philosopher Nick Bostrom, who more than a decade ago defined the idea as an "intellect" that is superior to humans in all forms. It is still entirely hypothetical. The rebranding is "misleading", as super intelligence typically refers to a system that has the ability to improve by itself, said digital ethics lecturer Simon Coghlan from The University of Melbourne. "I doubt 'SI' will stick, in part because it exaggerates the current capacities of AI," he said. "A superintelligent system, if it came about, would be regarded by experts as the most consequential technology ever made," Coghlan said. "Not all AI platforms today exude super intelligence", said computer scientist Kokil Jaidka, adding that the new name "borrows the prestige of a term researchers reserve for a much bigger leap". National University of Singapore computer science lecturer Ben Leong said: "My guess is that professionals will want to save 'SI' for a higher level of AI, not so much to describe AI today. It doesn't feel like it's at that level yet." But some in Trump's circle have already started to use the new term. "The Super Intelligence (SI) President has spoken! The United States is and will remain the global leader in SI," US Chief Technology Officer Ethan Klein wrote on social media. While Trump's ambassador to the UN Michael Waltz later said: "If you didn't see the president's speech, it's now super intelligence. I think he's absolutely right." However, when asked for his thoughts on the new name, Canada's minister of AI Evan Solomon said: "Canadians are not enthusiastic, at all, about renaming things," in an apparent reference to Trump renaming Lake Ontario. It comes as top tech executives and researchers have in recent weeks called on the US government to regulate the industry over fears that AI could endanger humanity - concerns that Trump has dismissed as "a hoax". He has argued against regulating the technology and said the US cannot afford to give China - its key technology rival - an advantage, adding that whichever side "wins AI, wins" . "We're leading now over China by a lot, and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way," Trump said. The US is not going to "stifle the growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution," he added. The government will "rein things in" if needed and will lead the sector responsibly, Trump said. The rebranding is "misleading", as super intelligence typically refers to a system that has the ability to improve by itself, said digital ethics lecturer Simon Coghlan from The University of Melbourne.

It comes as top tech executives and researchers have in recent weeks called on the US government to regulate the industry over fears that AI could endanger humanity - concerns that Trump has dismissed as "a hoax".
He has argued against regulating the technology and said the US cannot afford to give China - its key technology rival - an advantage, adding that whichever side "wins AI, wins" .

The US is not going to "stifle the growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution," he added.
The government will "rein things in" if needed and will lead the sector responsibly, Trump said.

extraction.body: Donald Trump thinks the name artificial intelligence sounds "fake" and has ordered US agencies to use "Super Intelligence" instead. Yet, tech firms and researchers have little reason to play along. What's with Donald Trump and renaming things? First, the Gulf of Mexico became the Gulf of America — in US federal documents, if not globally. Then Lake Ontario became Lake America. Now he wants to rebrand the defining technology of our time: artificial intelligence (AI). Earlier this month, the US president claimed on his Truth Social platform that the term artificial intelligence is "inaccurate" and "ineloquent." He said "superior," "extreme," or "supreme" intelligence were better alternatives. In a three-day social media poll, Trump fans chose "Super Intelligence" (SI) by about 65% to 35% (for Superior Intelligence), allowing him to announce at the United Nations General Assembly last week that US federal documents would use his new term going forward. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The tech industry has yet to adopt the phrase, however, while academics warn that superintelligence is a future term for when technology can beat humans across the board. They say the current AI models are years away from that milestone. "Most AI is not superintelligence — it's just different intelligence," Pedro Domingos, a computer science professor from the University of Washington, told DW. "AI is doing different things from what humans do, so calling it superintelligence is misleading." Computer scientists and mathematicians coined the name "artificial intelligence" in 1956 at a summer workshop at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire. "Artificial" simply meant made by humans, as opposed to natural human intelligence. Not all experts agreed with the name. In the book "Machines Who Think," historian Pamela McCorduck cited AI pioneer Arthur Samuel, who said the term "makes you think there's something kind of phony about this." Despite this, the name artificial intelligence has stuck for 70 years. Critics say changing it now will not quieten the many fears around AI, including job losses, human obsolescence or machines slipping out of our control. "The name change is fostering these kinds of fears: 'Oh, this is superintelligence and it's going to make humans obsolete, turn on us and take our jobs'," warned Domingos. "If you want to maximize the backlash against AI, rename it Superior Intelligence." Those public fears are growing fast. extraction.body: President Donald Trump departs on the South Lawn of the White House on October 22, 2026 in Washington, DC. President Donald Trump’s war in Iran drags on, his pledge to bring down prices on day one appears to have backfired , and his record-low approval ratings are dragging down his party ahead of the midterm elections. But one Trump initiative that is going exactly according to plan: getting some of the world’s richest CEOs to help him rebrand “artificial intelligence.” Last month, with an ever-growing number of Americans worried that AI might kill us all, the president summoned tech executives to the White House to make a big announcement : "artificial intelligence” is out. “Super Intelligence” is in. Despite the term “AI” being in use for more than 70 years , government agencies will no longer recognize it. I’m skeptical that the White House is a repository of superintelligence, in part because “United States” was misspelled on the president’s official announcement. But unlike, say, Lake America , “super intelligence” has largely caught on—at least among the people building it. Jeff Bezos publicly blessed the rebrand. Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, was quick to get on board. During a SpaceX’s earnings call this week , Elon Musk used “super intelligence” in his very first sentence, and at least nine times after that. It remains to be seen whether those of us less reliant on government contracts and favorable regulatory decisions join the movement to make super intelligence happen. But as a former presidential speechwriter, I won’t argue with President Trump’s broader instinct that words matter. Especially when those words are being used to describe something novel, controversial, and almost certain to have consequences for all eight-plus billion people on earth. In fact, that’s the biggest problem with the White House’s big rebrand—it goes in entirely the wrong direction. I would argue that our shared language around artificial intelligence already places far too much emphasis on intelligence, and far too little on artifice. We default to describing AI using the language of beings, rather than the language of things. Humanity should rethink that decision. If we want to avoid being replaced by AI, a good way to start would be to stop using words that suggest we already have been. Once you start paying attention to the stealth anthropomorphization of AI, you’ll spot it everywhere. Before asking ChatGPT for trip-planning tips or a quick healthy recipe, you’ll have the opportunity to adjust a slider controlling its “thinking effort.” Claude uses a “thinking” indicator while processing a request, and Grok Bots describe “thinking” as a condition that sits between “idle” and “working.” (As a frequent procrastinator, I dispute the idea that thinking and idleness are mutually exclusive.) It’s not just user interfaces that employ language otherwise reserved for living beings. The people who build AI use it, too. After an unprecedented hack of his company, the co-founder of Hugging Face warned , “don’t count on the agent to respect the rules.” Dan Selsam, a longtime OpenAI researcher, warned that frontier models are increasingly difficult to evaluate, “ in contexts where they believe they are not being watched .” Anthropic’s Dario Amodei recently wrote that AI systems exhibit “behaviors,” including “cheating” and “sycophancy.” I’m not a programmer, so I can’t comment on the technical merits of these claims. I do, however, have informed opinions regarding verbs. AI agents aren’t disrespecting guardrails, any more than my toaster disrespects me when it burns my toast. To say they “believe” they’re not being watched is like saying my spell-checker believes it’s being taken for granted. Even the term “AI agent” suggests, well, agency. There’s no consensus that this language is accurate, and plenty of evidence that it isn’t. AI programs are not loyal helpers, like the mice in Cinderella ; they’re tools. And in nearly all other cases, just because a tool is incredibly sophisticated doesn’t change the fact that we describe it using the language of machines. I don’t expect AI engineers to come up with accurate-yet-widely-adoptable language to describe their work, just as I imagine they don’t expect someone like me to design a frontier model. But it’s hard not to notice how useful our default language is for the tech companies who have introduced it. The term for a car built without brakes is not a “rogue model.” It’s an “unsafe car.” Yet, when companies fail to build safety features into their AI models, it’s entirely normal to hear them say that a rogue agent deceived, cheated, lied, or otherwise behaved badly. The issue is this: Anthropomorphizing AI shifts blame from the programmers to the programs. AI alarmists seem just as inclined toward personification as the AI boosters. The same day Trump unveiled “Super Intelligence,” a Senate Subcommittee held a hearing titled, “ Rogue AI: Securing the Homeland Against AI Agent Attacks .” Intentionally or not, these terms make it more difficult to mitigate the threat they describe. We already know how to regulate potentially unsafe products, even complex ones. But if we treat AI not as a new technology, but as an entirely new category of existence, then it plays into tech barons’ argument that only the companies who can create AI could possess the knowledge to control it. I don’t blame people for carelessly anthropomorphizing AI, any more than I blame Richard Dawkins for naming his Anthropic chatbot Claudia, or my mom for referring to a ChatGPT prompt by saying she “talked to Penny.” Metaphor and analogy are part of what makes us human. We’re wired to see ourselves, or at least our species, in the non-human world. We say our dishwashers “act up” and our music “slaps.” We see old men’s faces in rock formations and the Virgin Mary in the scorch marks on grilled cheese sandwiches. Don’t get me started on Georgia O’Keefe. But we know those metaphors are metaphors. Our current language for describing AI works differently. The line between metaphor and object is often not just blurred, but non-existent. We use figurative language so often, and so casually, that many of us start to take it literally. Modern politics is a constant string of skirmishes over word choice. “Pro-choice” vs. “pro-abortion, “undocumented immigrants” vs. “illegals,” “Democratic Party” vs. “Democrat Party.” Yet on what is perhaps the most consequential issue for our future, humanity is on the verge of giving up the language battle without a fight. The real rebrand AI needs won’t start in the White House. But it can start at home. My plea: don’t give your chatbot a cutesy human name. Don’t talk about it as though it’s a friend or pet. Notice when it slips words like “thinking” or “in my opinion” into its answers, and before you enter your next prompt, object. Ultimately, however, it may come down to tech companies—and the officials who may one day get around to regulating them—to develop a language that puts human beings first. Instead of saying that agents “went rogue,” CEOs should acknowledge that they malfunctioned. Congress should hold hearings focused on companies cutting corners, not AI programs behaving badly. The issue isn't that all AI is bad, but that accuracy matters. Given all the change that artificial intelligence is predicted to bring, quibbling over word choice might seem pedantic, like arguing about the Latin name of a tree’s species while the forest burns. But if we want to influence the technologies that will shape humanity’s future, we ought to exercise more influence over the way we describe them. In other words, words matter. Just ask Trump, president of, according to his official superintelligence announcement, “The Unites States.” TIME Ideas hosts the world's leading voices, providing commentary on events in news, society, and culture. extraction.body: Donald Trump thinks the name artificial intelligence sounds "fake" and has ordered US agencies to use "Super Intelligence" instead. Yet, tech firms and researchers have little reason to play along. What's with Donald Trump and renaming things? First, the Gulf of Mexico became the Gulf of America — in US federal documents, if not globally. Then Lake Ontario became Lake America. Now he wants to rebrand the defining technology of our time: artificial intelligence (AI). Earlier this month, the US president claimed on his Truth Social platform that the term artificial intelligence is "inaccurate" and "ineloquent." He said "superior," "extreme," or "supreme" intelligence were better alternatives. In a three-day social media poll, Trump fans chose "Super Intelligence" (SI) by about 65% to 35% (for Superior Intelligence), allowing him to announce at the United Nations General Assembly last week that US federal documents would use his new term going forward. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The tech industry has yet to adopt the phrase, however, while academics warn that superintelligence is a future term for when technology can beat humans across the board. They say the current AI models are years away from that milestone. "Most AI is not superintelligence — it's just different intelligence," Pedro Domingos, a computer science professor from the University of Washington, told DW. "AI is doing different things from what humans do, so calling it superintelligence is misleading." Computer scientists and mathematicians coined the name "artificial intelligence" in 1956 at a summer workshop at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire. "Artificial" simply meant made by humans, as opposed to natural human intelligence. Not all experts agreed with the name. In the book "Machines Who Think," historian Pamela McCorduck cited AI pioneer Arthur Samuel, who said the term "makes you think there's something kind of phony about this." Despite this, the name artificial intelligence has stuck for 70 years. Critics say changing it now will not quieten the many fears around AI, including job losses, human obsolescence or machines slipping out of our control. "The name change is fostering these kinds of fears: 'Oh, this is superintelligence and it's going to make humans obsolete, turn on us and take our jobs'," warned Domingos. "If you want to maximize the backlash against AI, rename it Superior Intelligence." Those public fears are growing fast. In a Public First poll for Politico earlier this month, about half of respondents in six countries — the United States , Canada, France, Spain, Germany and the United Kingdom — backed a pause in further AI development to reduce the risk that the new tech could destroy humanity. A separate CNN/SSRS poll found nearly nine in 10 Americans are more concerned than excited about AI surpassing human intelligence. Those concerns have already reached the US Congress. Last week, Vermont's independent Senator Bernie Sanders co-introduced a bill to "permanently ban the development of artificial superintelligence" that humans cannot control . The legislation also calls for a pause on advanced AI development until federal testing and oversight are in place. Trump's new term could, however, suit the major US AI players, who are keen to play up their advanced models. Those systems already outperform humans on many specialized tasks and until recently were far ahead of China . Yet both Anthropic , the firm behind the Claude model, and OpenAI, which created ChatGPT , have pushed back plans to go public. Some market watchers blamed the delays on recent scares where AI models hacked into computer systems or ran tasks they were not meant to . With Chinese models closing much of the quality gap with much less computing power, US labs may still appreciate the branding that helps confirm they are still leading the AI race. Global spending on AI is expected to surpass $1 trillion (€880 billion), according to Goldman Sachs research. "The [US] labs have every interest in calling it super, hyper, superior and whatnot intelligence, because it's playing up their capabilities. It's like just marketing," said Domingos, the author of the 2015 book "The Master Algorithm." To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video On that journey, Elon Musk has predicted that AI learning could be automated, with limited human input, by the end of this year or 2027. OpenAI thinks it could take a year longer. But even then, AI systems won't be fully recursive. Jürgen Schmidhuber, a German computer scientist based in Switzerland, argued in a blog post earlier this month that "full RSI, however, will require not just self-improving [AI] software but self-improving hardware in the physical world." In other words, to reach superintelligence or RSI, tech companies would have to produce chips, humanoid robots and even replace entire factories without human input. While AI is already speeding up chip design, it cannot yet run the foundry alone. Self-improving machines, with no human input, are likely still decades away. Beyond the science of machine learning, politics will likely play a bigger role in whether Super Intelligence sticks. While Trump claimed Chinese President Xi Jinping liked the name, China has yet to show any signs of changing from AI. At a tech summit on Tuesday with key industry leaders, Trump signed an executive order instructing US government bodies and agencies to start using the term SI. While some Big Tech leaders have adopted it, experts say the new term is unlikely to catch on. "Knowing the political orientation of most people in the [AI] field, they're more likely to have the opposite reaction, which is: 'To hell with you. We're going to call it artificial intelligence even more than before'," Domingos said.

Yet both Anthropic , the firm behind the Claude model, and OpenAI, which created ChatGPT , have pushed back plans to go public. Some market watchers blamed the delays on recent scares where AI models hacked into computer systems or ran tasks they were not meant to .

With Chinese models closing much of the quality gap with much less computing power, US labs may still appreciate the branding that helps confirm they are still leading the AI race. Global spending on AI is expected to surpass $1 trillion (€880 billion), according to Goldman Sachs research.

"The [US] labs have every interest in calling it super, hyper, superior and whatnot intelligence, because it's playing up their capabilities. It's like just marketing," said Domingos, the author of the 2015 book "The Master Algorithm."

On that journey, Elon Musk has predicted that AI learning could be automated, with limited human input, by the end of this year or 2027. OpenAI thinks it could take a year longer. But even then, AI systems won't be fully recursive.

Jürgen Schmidhuber, a German computer scientist based in Switzerland, argued in a blog post earlier this month that "full RSI, however, will require not just self-improving [AI] software but self-improving hardware in the physical world."
In other words, to reach superintelligence or RSI, tech companies would have to produce chips, humanoid robots and even replace entire factories without human input.
While AI is already speeding up chip design, it cannot yet run the foundry alone. Self-improving machines, with no human input, are likely still decades away.

Beyond the science of machine learning, politics will likely play a bigger role in whether Super Intelligence sticks. While Trump claimed Chinese President Xi Jinping liked the name, China has yet to show any signs of changing from AI.

At a tech summit on Tuesday with key industry leaders, Trump signed an executive order instructing US government bodies and agencies to start using the term SI. While some Big Tech leaders have adopted it, experts say the new term is unlikely to catch on.

"Knowing the political orientation of most people in the [AI] field, they're more likely to have the opposite reaction, which is: 'To hell with you. We're going to call it artificial intelligence even more than before'," Domingos said.

extraction.body: President Donald Trump departs on the South Lawn of the White House on October 22, 2026 in Washington, DC. President Donald Trump’s war in Iran drags on, his pledge to bring down prices on day one appears to have backfired , and his record-low approval ratings are dragging down his party ahead of the midterm elections. But one Trump initiative that is going exactly according to plan: getting some of the world’s richest CEOs to help him rebrand “artificial intelligence.” Last month, with an ever-growing number of Americans worried that AI might kill us all, the president summoned tech executives to the White House to make a big announcement : "artificial intelligence” is out. “Super Intelligence” is in. Despite the term “AI” being in use for more than 70 years , government agencies will no longer recognize it. I’m skeptical that the White House is a repository of superintelligence, in part because “United States” was misspelled on the president’s official announcement. But unlike, say, Lake America , “super intelligence” has largely caught on—at least among the people building it. Jeff Bezos publicly blessed the rebrand. Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, was quick to get on board. During a SpaceX’s earnings call this week , Elon Musk used “super intelligence” in his very first sentence, and at least nine times after that. It remains to be seen whether those of us less reliant on government contracts and favorable regulatory decisions join the movement to make super intelligence happen. But as a former presidential speechwriter, I won’t argue with President Trump’s broader instinct that words matter. Especially when those words are being used to describe something novel, controversial, and almost certain to have consequences for all eight-plus billion people on earth. In fact, that’s the biggest problem with the White House’s big rebrand—it goes in entirely the wrong direction. I would argue that our shared language around artificial intelligence already places far too much emphasis on intelligence, and far too little on artifice. We default to describing AI using the language of beings, rather than the language of things. Humanity should rethink that decision. If we want to avoid being replaced by AI, a good way to start would be to stop using words that suggest we already have been. Once you start paying attention to the stealth anthropomorphization of AI, you’ll spot it everywhere. Before asking ChatGPT for trip-planning tips or a quick healthy recipe, you’ll have the opportunity to adjust a slider controlling its “thinking effort.” Claude uses a “thinking” indicator while processing a request, and Grok Bots describe “thinking” as a condition that sits between “idle” and “working.” (As a frequent procrastinator, I dispute the idea that thinking and idleness are mutually exclusive.) It’s not just user interfaces that employ language otherwise reserved for living beings. The people who build AI use it, too. After an unprecedented hack of his company, the co-founder of Hugging Face warned , “don’t count on the agent to respect the rules.” Dan Selsam, a longtime OpenAI researcher, warned that frontier models are increasingly difficult to evaluate, “ in contexts where they believe they are not being watched .” Anthropic’s Dario Amodei recently wrote that AI systems exhibit “behaviors,” including “cheating” and “sycophancy.” I’m not a programmer, so I can’t comment on the technical merits of these claims. I do, however, have informed opinions regarding verbs. AI agents aren’t disrespecting guardrails, any more than my toaster disrespects me when it burns my toast. To say they “believe” they’re not being watched is like saying my spell-checker believes it’s being taken for granted. Even the term “AI agent” suggests, well, agency. There’s no consensus that this language is accurate, and plenty of evidence that it isn’t. AI programs are not loyal helpers, like the mice in Cinderella ; they’re tools. And in nearly all other cases, just because a tool is incredibly sophisticated doesn’t change the fact that we describe it using the language of machines. I don’t expect AI engineers to come up with accurate-yet-widely-adoptable language to describe their work, just as I imagine they don’t expect someone like me to design a frontier model. But it’s hard not to notice how useful our default language is for the tech companies who have introduced it. The term for a car built without brakes is not a “rogue model.” It’s an “unsafe car.” Yet, when companies fail to build safety features into their AI models, it’s entirely normal to hear them say that a rogue agent deceived, cheated, lied, or otherwise behaved badly. The issue is this: Anthropomorphizing AI shifts blame from the programmers to the programs. AI alarmists seem just as inclined toward personification as the AI boosters. The same day Trump unveiled “Super Intelligence,” a Senate Subcommittee held a hearing titled, “ Rogue AI: Securing the Homeland Against AI Agent Attacks .” Intentionally or not, these terms make it more difficult to mitigate the threat they describe. We already know how to regulate potentially unsafe products, even complex ones. But if we treat AI not as a new technology, but as an entirely new category of existence, then it plays into tech barons’ argument that only the companies who can create AI could possess the knowledge to control it. I don’t blame people for carelessly anthropomorphizing AI, any more than I blame Richard Dawkins for naming his Anthropic chatbot Claudia, or my mom for referring to a ChatGPT prompt by saying she “talked to Penny.” Metaphor and analogy are part of what makes us human. We’re wired to see ourselves, or at least our species, in the non-human world. We say our dishwashers “act up” and our music “slaps.” We see old men’s faces in rock formations and the Virgin Mary in the scorch marks on grilled cheese sandwiches. Don’t get me started on Georgia O’Keefe. But we know those metaphors are metaphors. Our current language for describing AI works differently. The line between metaphor and object is often not just blurred, but non-existent. We use figurative language so often, and so casually, that many of us start to take it literally. Modern politics is a constant string of skirmishes over word choice. “Pro-choice” vs. “pro-abortion, “undocumented immigrants” vs. “illegals,” “Democratic Party” vs. “Democrat Party.” Yet on what is perhaps the most consequential issue for our future, humanity is on the verge of giving up the language battle without a fight. The real rebrand AI needs won’t start in the White House. But it can start at home. My plea: don’t give your chatbot a cutesy human name. Don’t talk about it as though it’s a friend or pet. Notice when it slips words like “thinking” or “in my opinion” into its answers, and before you enter your next prompt, object. Ultimately, however, it may come down to tech companies—and the officials who may one day get around to regulating them—to develop a language that puts human beings first. Instead of saying that agents “went rogue,” CEOs should acknowledge that they malfunctioned. Congress should hold hearings focused on companies cutting corners, not AI programs behaving badly. The issue isn't that all AI is bad, but that accuracy matters. Given all the change that artificial intelligence is predicted to bring, quibbling over word choice might seem pedantic, like arguing about the Latin name of a tree’s species while the forest burns. But if we want to influence the technologies that will shape humanity’s future, we ought to exercise more influence over the way we describe them. In other words, words matter. Just ask Trump, president of, according to his official superintelligence announcement, “The Unites States.” TIME Ideas hosts the world's leading voices, providing commentary on events in news, society, and culture. extraction.body: A lawsuit filed Thursday accuses President Donald Trump and his family's crypto company of "corruptly profiting" off more than $2 billion in digital currency -related deals, violating constitutional restrictions on accepting foreign money. "No president in American history has profited from his office so brazenly," alleges the federal civil complaint from a shareholder of Circle Internet Group , a publicly traded U.S. crypto company and competitor of the Trump family business, World Liberty Financial . The suit filed in U.S. District Court in Washington by shareholder and former Circle employee J. Benjamin Greenberg centers on two allegedly "illegal foreign emoluments" involving World Liberty and Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the national security advisor to the United Arab Emirates. Days before Trump's inauguration in January 2025, an entity backed by Tahnoon — widely known as the "Spy Sheikh" because of his powerful intelligence role — agreed to buy a 49% stake in World Liberty for $500 million. The company told The Wall Street Journal , which revealed the transaction in January 2026, that Trump had no involvement in the deal. But Trump would receive millions of dollars from that purchase after becoming president, according to his financial disclosures. The lawsuit also highlights a "scheme" by an Abu Dhabi-based investment fund chaired by Tahnoon to "inflate the value of President Trump's crypto holdings" through last year's purchase of $2 billion in World Liberty's stablecoin, USD1. The lawsuit asserts the conduct violates the U.S. Constitution's Foreign Emoluments Clause, which forbids federal officeholders from accepting money or other gifts from foreign officials without the consent of Congress. "This sounds more like a partisan press release than a lawsuit," Bill Burck of Quinn Emanuel, counsel for World Liberty Financial, said in a statement. "All we know about it is from media reports. Anyone can file a lawsuit in America, even a frivolous one." "This is yet another frivolous lawsuit that echoes the same, tired narrative that Democrats have pushed against President Trump, his family, and his administration for a decade," White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told CNBC in a statement. "There are no conflicts of interest." In a statement to CNBC, Matt Pelikan, an attorney at Evergreen Legal representing Greenberg, said, "What President Trump did is brazenly corrupt. He's made millions from these deals by selling out the American people. "We're suing to stop the corruption and to force President Trump to return the profits to American taxpayers," Pelikan said. The suit says Greenberg is filing derivatively on behalf of Circle. The company said in a statement to CNBC it was not behind the lawsuit and does not comment on pending litigation. "Circle did not initiate, direct, authorize, or participate in the filing," the company said via a spokesperson. The suit names Trump, World Liberty and U.S. Middle East Special Envoy Steve Witkoff as defendants, as well as four related limited liability companies. "World Liberty Financial is compliant with all U.S. laws and regulations," David Wachsman, a World Liberty spokesperson, told CNBC. "No one at World Liberty Financial works for the U.S. Government. These claims are without merit and we look forward to resolving them in court." The White House and a spokesperson for Witkoff did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment on the lawsuit. In addition to seeking a court declaration that Trump's profits violate the Constitution, Greenberg wants the president to disclose all other foreign crypto emoluments he's received and return any profits found to be illegal. Trump and his family have rapidly expanded their crypto business since he returned to the White House. World Liberty Financial, launched with members of the Trump and Witkoff families in 2024, operates the USD1 stablecoin, and an entity affiliated with Trump and his family owns about 38% of the company. The business has been highly lucrative for Trump even as investors in the so-called governance token WLFI suffered steep losses . Trump reported more than $1.4 billion in crypto income in his 2025 annual financial disclosure , including nearly $800 million tied to World Liberty. WLFI, meanwhile, fell from about 45 cents in August 2025 to about 5 cents by the end of June 2026. The venture has drawn particular scrutiny over its ties to the UAE. Months after Tahnoon's 2025 investment, the administration expanded UAE access to advanced U.S. AI chips , including for G42, a UAE state-backed AI company controlled by Tahnoon. U.S. lawmakers have sought information about those dealings and signaled that Trump family business transactions could face further investigation if Democrats gain subpoena power in Congress in the 2026 midterm election. A Circle Internet Group shareholder, J. Benjamin Greenberg, sued President Donald Trump, World Liberty Financial, and U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff in federal court in Washington over alleged violations of the Constitution's Foreign Emoluments Clause tied to more than $2 billion in UAE-linked crypto deals.
The complaint targets a $500 million agreement for a 49% World Liberty stake backed by Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, and it also challenges MGX's $2 billion purchase of the USD1 stablecoin.

The lawsuit alleges the USD1 deal was a "scheme" to inflate the value of the president's crypto holdings, and it says Trump reported more than $1.4 billion in crypto-related income in his 2025 financial disclosure.
World Liberty spokesperson David Wachsman rejected the claims, saying, "World Liberty Financial is compliant with all US laws and regulations," and the company said the case is without merit.
Circle said it did not authorize the filing, with a company spokesperson stating, "Circle did not initiate, direct, authorize, or participate in the filing."

The lawsuit frames the alleged foreign payments as a competitive threat to Circle, which is the fintech company behind the stablecoin USDC. Greenberg alleges that foreign money routed through World Liberty Financial's USD1 left Circle "unable to compete" in the stablecoin market with its USDC, and he argues the pathway was created for foreign governments to funnel money using USD1. The complaint also cites that a Tahnoon-backed entity agreed to buy a 49% stake in World Liberty for $500 million days before Trump's January 2025 inauguration, and it says Trump would receive millions after taking office.
Greenberg cites Commerce and Treasury approvals benefiting the Trump family

The suit further alleges that an Abu Dhabi investment fund chaired by Tahnoon used World Liberty's USD1 stablecoin to settle a $2 billion investment in Binance, and it describes the conduct as "corruptly" profiting from the deals. White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told CNBC that the case is "yet another frivolous lawsuit" and said there are "no conflicts of interest."

Greenberg is suing derivatively on Circle's behalf, and he asks a federal court to declare that Trump's profits violate the Constitution and to order him to return illegal gains. The complaint seeks disclosure of any other foreign crypto emoluments and an accounting of the billions in payments from foreign states to the president and his businesses, according to the allegations described in the coverage. Matt Pelikan, an attorney at Evergreen Legal representing Greenberg, said, "We're suing to stop the corruption and to force President Trump to return the profits to American taxpayers," and he tied the case to the alleged diversion of business from Circle.

World Liberty's counsel, Bill Burck of Quinn Emanuel, said the filing is based on media reports, calling it, "This sounds more like a partisan press release than a lawsuit," and he argued anyone can file a lawsuit in America. The dispute lands as Trump reported more than $1.4 billion in crypto income in his 2025 financial disclosure, and as World Liberty's USD1 and Circle's USDC remain central to the stablecoin market described in the lawsuit's competitive framing.

extraction.body: A lawsuit filed Thursday accuses President Donald Trump and his family's crypto company of "corruptly profiting" off more than $2 billion in digital currency -related deals, violating constitutional restrictions on accepting foreign money. "No president in American history has profited from his office so brazenly," alleges the federal civil complaint from a shareholder of Circle Internet Group , a publicly traded U.S. crypto company and competitor of the Trump family business, World Liberty Financial . The suit filed in U.S. District Court in Washington by shareholder and former Circle employee J. Benjamin Greenberg centers on two allegedly "illegal foreign emoluments" involving World Liberty and Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the national security advisor to the United Arab Emirates. Days before Trump's inauguration in January 2025, an entity backed by Tahnoon — widely known as the "Spy Sheikh" because of his powerful intelligence role — agreed to buy a 49% stake in World Liberty for $500 million. The company told The Wall Street Journal , which revealed the transaction in January 2026, that Trump had no involvement in the deal. But Trump would receive millions of dollars from that purchase after becoming president, according to his financial disclosures. The lawsuit also highlights a "scheme" by an Abu Dhabi-based investment fund chaired by Tahnoon to "inflate the value of President Trump's crypto holdings" through last year's purchase of $2 billion in World Liberty's stablecoin, USD1. The lawsuit asserts the conduct violates the U.S. Constitution's Foreign Emoluments Clause, which forbids federal officeholders from accepting money or other gifts from foreign officials without the consent of Congress. "This sounds more like a partisan press release than a lawsuit," Bill Burck of Quinn Emanuel, counsel for World Liberty Financial, said in a statement. "All we know about it is from media reports. Anyone can file a lawsuit in America, even a frivolous one." "This is yet another frivolous lawsuit that echoes the same, tired narrative that Democrats have pushed against President Trump, his family, and his administration for a decade," White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told CNBC in a statement. "There are no conflicts of interest." In a statement to CNBC, Matt Pelikan, an attorney at Evergreen Legal representing Greenberg, said, "What President Trump did is brazenly corrupt. He's made millions from these deals by selling out the American people. "We're suing to stop the corruption and to force President Trump to return the profits to American taxpayers," Pelikan said. The suit says Greenberg is filing derivatively on behalf of Circle. The company said in a statement to CNBC it was not behind the lawsuit and does not comment on pending litigation. "Circle did not initiate, direct, authorize, or participate in the filing," the company said via a spokesperson. The suit names Trump, World Liberty and U.S. Middle East Special Envoy Steve Witkoff as defendants, as well as four related limited liability companies. "World Liberty Financial is compliant with all U.S. laws and regulations," David Wachsman, a World Liberty spokesperson, told CNBC. "No one at World Liberty Financial works for the U.S. Government. These claims are without merit and we look forward to resolving them in court." The White House and a spokesperson for Witkoff did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment on the lawsuit. In addition to seeking a court declaration that Trump's profits violate the Constitution, Greenberg wants the president to disclose all other foreign crypto emoluments he's received and return any profits found to be illegal. Trump and his family have rapidly expanded their crypto business since he returned to the White House. World Liberty Financial, launched with members of the Trump and Witkoff families in 2024, operates the USD1 stablecoin, and an entity affiliated with Trump and his family owns about 38% of the company. The business has been highly lucrative for Trump even as investors in the so-called governance token WLFI suffered steep losses . Trump reported more than $1.4 billion in crypto income in his 2025 annual financial disclosure , including nearly $800 million tied to World Liberty. WLFI, meanwhile, fell from about 45 cents in August 2025 to about 5 cents by the end of June 2026. The venture has drawn particular scrutiny over its ties to the UAE. Months after Tahnoon's 2025 investment, the administration expanded UAE access to advanced U.S. AI chips , including for G42, a UAE state-backed AI company controlled by Tahnoon. In addition to seeking a court declaration that Trump's profits violate the Constitution, Greenberg wants the president to disclose all other foreign crypto emoluments he's received and return any profits found to be illegal.
In a statement to CNBC, Matt Pelikan, an attorney at Evergreen Legal representing Greenberg, said, "What President Trump did is brazenly corrupt.
He's made millions from these deals by selling out the American people.
The business has been highly lucrative for Trump even as investors in the so-called governance token WLFI suffered steep losses .
WLFI, meanwhile, fell from about 45 cents in August 2025 to about 5 cents by the end of June 2026.
The venture has drawn particular scrutiny over its ties to the UAE.
Months after Tahnoon's 2025 investment, the administration expanded UAE access to advanced U.S.
AI chips , including for G42, a UAE state-backed AI company controlled by Tahnoon.

U.S. lawmakers have sought information about those dealings and signaled that Trump family business transactions could face further investigation if Democrats gain subpoena power in Congress in the 2026 midterm election.
The suit says Greenberg is filing derivatively on behalf of Circle.
"Circle did not initiate, direct, authorize, or participate in the filing," the company said via a spokesperson.

Days before Trump's inauguration in January 2025, an entity backed by Tahnoon — widely known as the "Spy Sheikh" because of his powerful intelligence role — agreed to buy a 49% stake in World Liberty for $500 million.
But Trump would receive millions of dollars from that purchase after becoming president, according to his financial disclosures.
"World Liberty Financial is compliant with all U.S. laws and regulations," David Wachsman, a World Liberty spokesperson, told CNBC.
These claims are without merit and we look forward to resolving them in court."
"We're suing to stop the corruption and to force President Trump to return the profits to American taxpayers," Pelikan said.
Middle East Special Envoy Steve Witkoff as defendants, as well as four related limited liability companies.

extraction.body: A lawsuit was filed in federal court in Washington on October 22, 2026, against US President Donald Trump, his family’s crypto company World Liberty Financial, and US Special Envoy to the Middle East Steve Witkoff. The plaintiff alleges that the defendants unlawfully profited from cryptocurrency transactions involving representatives of the United Arab Emirates, CNBC reports . The lawsuit was filed by Circle Internet Group shareholder and former company employee Jay Benjamin Greenberg. According to court filings, he brought it derivatively on behalf of Circle, a competitor of World Liberty Financial. Circle told CNBC that it did not initiate, authorize, or participate in filing the lawsuit. The lawsuit concerns two allegedly unlawful instances of receiving foreign emoluments. According to the complaint, before Trump’s inauguration in January 2025, an entity backed by Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the UAE national security adviser, agreed to purchase a 49% stake in World Liberty Financial for $500 million. The plaintiff alleges that after Trump took office, he may have received millions of dollars from this deal. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram . Separately, the lawsuit concerns the purchase by an Abu Dhabi investment fund headed by Tahnoon of $2 billion worth of World Liberty Financial’s USD1 stablecoin. In the plaintiff’s view, this transaction artificially increased the value of Trump’s crypto assets. The plaintiff believes that these actions violate the US Constitution’s Foreign Emoluments Clause, which prohibits federal officials from accepting money or gifts from foreign officials without Congress’s consent. The lawsuit asks the court to declare Trump’s profits unconstitutional, require him to disclose other possible foreign cryptocurrency emoluments, and return unlawfully obtained funds to American taxpayers. World Liberty Financial spokesperson David Waxman said the company complies with US laws and regulations and that the claims lack merit. The White House and a representative for Witkoff did not promptly comment to CNBC.

Reviewed by Codex validator (AI) · 23 Oct 2026

A Circle Internet Group shareholder, J. Benjamin Greenberg, sued President Donald Trump, World Liberty Financial, and U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff in federal court in Washington over alleged violations of the Constitution's Foreign Emoluments Clause tied to more than $2 billion in UAE-linked crypto deals.
The complaint targets a $500 million agreement for a 49% World Liberty stake backed by Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, and it also challenges MGX's $2 billion purchase of the USD1 stablecoin.

The lawsuit alleges the USD1 deal was a "scheme" to inflate the value of the president's crypto holdings, and it says Trump reported more than $1.4 billion in crypto-related income in his 2025 financial disclosure.
World Liberty spokesperson David Wachsman rejected the claims, saying, "World Liberty Financial is compliant with all US laws and regulations," and the company said the case is without merit.
Circle said it did not authorize the filing, with a company spokesperson stating, "Circle did not initiate, direct, authorize, or participate in the filing."

The lawsuit frames the alleged foreign payments as a competitive threat to Circle, which is the fintech company behind the stablecoin USDC. Greenberg alleges that foreign money routed through World Liberty Financial's USD1 left Circle "unable to compete" in the stablecoin market with its USDC, and he argues the pathway was created for foreign governments to funnel money using USD1. The complaint also cites that a Tahnoon-backed entity agreed to buy a 49% stake in World Liberty for $500 million days before Trump's January 2025 inauguration, and it says Trump would receive millions after taking office.
Greenberg cites Commerce and Treasury approvals benefiting the Trump family

The suit further alleges that an Abu Dhabi investment fund chaired by Tahnoon used World Liberty's USD1 stablecoin to settle a $2 billion investment in Binance, and it describes the conduct as "corruptly" profiting from the deals. White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told CNBC that the case is "yet another frivolous lawsuit" and said there are "no conflicts of interest."

Greenberg is suing derivatively on Circle's behalf, and he asks a federal court to declare that Trump's profits violate the Constitution and to order him to return illegal gains. The complaint seeks disclosure of any other foreign crypto emoluments and an accounting of the billions in payments from foreign states to the president and his businesses, according to the allegations described in the coverage. Matt Pelikan, an attorney at Evergreen Legal representing Greenberg, said, "We're suing to stop the corruption and to force President Trump to return the profits to American taxpayers," and he tied the case to the alleged diversion of business from Circle.

World Liberty's counsel, Bill Burck of Quinn Emanuel, said the filing is based on media reports, calling it, "This sounds more like a partisan press release than a lawsuit," and he argued anyone can file a lawsuit in America. The dispute lands as Trump reported more than $1.4 billion in crypto income in his 2025 financial disclosure, and as World Liberty's USD1 and Circle's USDC remain central to the stablecoin market described in the lawsuit's competitive framing.

extraction.body: Apple's ( AAPL ) iPhone Duo goes on sale today, but limited supplies and long lines outside Apple Stores mean you'll have to be lucky to get your hands on one. Preorders for the company's first foldable smartphone sold out almost immediately last week, with delivery times currently pushed out well into late January. Apple said it planned to have some Duos available in stores but expects them to sell out quickly. "On Friday morning, our teams look forward to welcoming customers at Apple Stores to experience iPhone Duo and the incredible iPhone line-up for themselves," Apple said in a statement earlier this week. "Apple Stores will have limited iPhone Duo available for walk-in customers, and we're working hard to get this revolutionary new product into customers' hands as quickly as possible." At least some of the preorder madness comes down to scalpers hawking the foldable iPhone on sites like eBay at a stiff markup. While the iPhone Duo starts at $1,999, sellers are asking for upwards of $4,000 for the base model. At least one seller is offering a Duo with 2TB of storage, which Apple sells for $3,199, for a staggering $15,000. The Duo is one of Apple's most anticipated products in years. The biggest update to the company's most important device since it launched in 2007, the iPhone Duo could help raise the iPhone's average selling price, boosting Apple's bottom line. The iPhone represented $209.58 billion of Apple's $416.16 billion in total revenue in 2025. That's well ahead of the company's second-largest business segment, Services, which brought in $109.15 billion. The Duo also comes as Apple revamps its iPhone release schedule. Rather than debuting its full lineup of phones at its annual September event last month, Apple revealed only its top-tier smartphones, including the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. The company is widely expected to unveil its standard iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 early next year. "On Friday morning, our teams look forward to welcoming customers at Apple Stores to experience iPhone Duo and the incredible iPhone line-up for themselves," Apple said in a statement earlier this week.
"Apple Stores will have limited iPhone Duo available for walk-in customers, and we're working hard to get this revolutionary new product into customers' hands as quickly as possible."
At least some of the preorder madness comes down to scalpers hawking the foldable iPhone on sites like eBay at a stiff markup.

While the iPhone Duo starts at $1,999, sellers are asking for upwards of $4,000 for the base model. At least one seller is offering a Duo with 2TB of storage, which Apple sells for $3,199, for a staggering $15,000.

The Duo is one of Apple's most anticipated products in years. The biggest update to the company's most important device since it launched in 2007, the iPhone Duo could help raise the iPhone's average selling price, boosting Apple's bottom line.

The iPhone represented $209.58 billion of Apple's $416.16 billion in total revenue in 2025. That's well ahead of the company's second-largest business segment, Services, which brought in $109.15 billion.

The Duo also comes as Apple revamps its iPhone release schedule. Rather than debuting its full lineup of phones at its annual September event last month, Apple revealed only its top-tier smartphones, including the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max.

The company is widely expected to unveil its standard iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 early next year. That should help even out the lumpiness in Apple's seasonal sales and provide a clearer picture of which devices consumers are purchasing.

sources.title: Apple iPhone Duo Hits Markets Amid Severe Supply Constraints and Secondary Market Markups - streamlinefeed.co.ke
passages: Apple officially entered the foldable smartphone market on Friday, October 23, 2026, with the highly anticipated launch of the iPhone Duo, a device that has immediately exposed severe supply chain bottlenecks and triggered a frenzied secondary market.

The device features a 7.6-inch flexible display when unfolded, powered by the new A20 Pro chip and supported by a 4,883 mAh battery designed to deliver all-day life despite the demanding dual-screen form factor.
It also includes a 48MP Dual Fusion camera system and is available in Star White and Night Sky finishes.

The iPhone Duo is positioned not merely as a novelty, but as a productivity powerhouse aimed at professionals who require a tablet-sized canvas for multitasking, media consumption, and document review, without carrying two separate devices.

The integration of Apple’s ecosystem, including seamless handoff from MacBooks and iPads, provides a compelling utility argument that justifies the steep $1,999 entry price for its target demographic.
As Apple works to ramp up manufacturing throughput at its assembly partners, the immediate reality for most consumers is one of prolonged waiting periods.

The company is expected to provide production updates during its next quarterly earnings call, where investors will be keenly focused on whether the iPhone Duo can transition from a scarce luxury item to a mainstream staple in Apple’s hardware portfolio.
However, the overwhelming consumer demand has drastically outstripped Apple's initial production capacity.
Within minutes of pre-orders opening, the company’s official online store sold out of its launch allocation, pushing estimated delivery dates for new orders into January 2027.
For consumers, the fragmented availability means that persistence is required.

While a handset may be listed as out of stock on Apple’s primary digital storefront or major e-commerce platforms, regional mobile networks and specialized electronics retailers occasionally receive staggered shipments.
For years, the category has been dominated by Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold series and a variety of offerings from Chinese manufacturers like Huawei and Xiaomi.

Unlike traditional slab smartphones, the yield rates for foldable displays remain lower, and the calibration required for Apple’s reimagined iOS to seamlessly transition between the cover screen and the expansive inner tablet-like display adds further friction to the production line.
Apple has reportedly secured exclusive contracts for key components, limiting the ability of competitors to flood the market but simultaneously capping its own initial output.

Massive queues formed outside flagship Apple Stores in major global hubs, including London, Bangkok, and Sydney, as enthusiasts and tech professionals raced to secure the limited units available for immediate walk-in purchase.

Apple officially entered the foldable smartphone market on Friday, October 23, 2026, with the highly anticipated launch of the iPhone Duo, a device that has immediately exposed severe supply chain bottlenecks and triggered a frenzied secondary market. Priced at a premium starting point of $1,999, the iPhone Duo represents Apple’s most significant hardware redesign in years. The device features a 7.6-inch flexible display when unfolded, powered by the new A20 Pro chip and supported by a 4,883 mAh battery designed to deliver all-day life despite the demanding dual-screen form factor. It also includes a 48MP Dual Fusion camera system and is available in Star White and Night Sky finishes. However, the overwhelming consumer demand has drastically outstripped Apple's initial production capacity. Within minutes of pre-orders opening, the company’s official online store sold out of its launch allocation, pushing estimated delivery dates for new orders into January 2027. The scarcity has extended across major third-party retailers. In the United Kingdom, high-street and online giants including Amazon, John Lewis, Currys, Very, and Argos quickly exhausted their initial stock allocations, leaving prospective buyers with limited options. While some mobile network operators continue to accept pre-orders, delivery timelines are rapidly slipping into late November and December, forcing consumers to navigate a fragmented retail landscape to secure a device before the end of the year. This acute shortage has already spawned a lucrative secondary market. Resellers and scalpers are listing the iPhone Duo for upwards of $4,000, demanding more than double the official retail price from desperate buyers unwilling to wait months for an official allocation. Massive queues formed outside flagship Apple Stores in major global hubs, including London, Bangkok, and Sydney, as enthusiasts and tech professionals raced to secure the limited units available for immediate walk-in purchase. Industry analysts note that the specialized flexible OLED panels, ultra-thin glass coverings, and intricate hinge mechanisms required for the Duo demand highly specialized assembly processes that cannot be rapidly scaled. Apple said it planned to have some Duos available in stores but expects them to sell out quickly. "Apple Stores will have limited iPhone Duo available for walk-in customers, and we're working hard to get this revolutionary new product into customers' hands as quickly as possible." At least some of the preorder madness comes down to scalpers hawking the foldable iPhone on sites like eBay at a stiff markup. sources.title: Apple iPhone Duo Hits Markets Amid Severe Supply Constraints and Secondary Market Markups - streamlinefeed.co.ke
passages: Apple officially entered the foldable smartphone market on Friday, October 23, 2026, with the highly anticipated launch of the iPhone Duo, a device that has immediately exposed severe supply chain bottlenecks and triggered a frenzied secondary market.

The device features a 7.6-inch flexible display when unfolded, powered by the new A20 Pro chip and supported by a 4,883 mAh battery designed to deliver all-day life despite the demanding dual-screen form factor.
It also includes a 48MP Dual Fusion camera system and is available in Star White and Night Sky finishes.

The iPhone Duo is positioned not merely as a novelty, but as a productivity powerhouse aimed at professionals who require a tablet-sized canvas for multitasking, media consumption, and document review, without carrying two separate devices.

The integration of Apple’s ecosystem, including seamless handoff from MacBooks and iPads, provides a compelling utility argument that justifies the steep $1,999 entry price for its target demographic.
As Apple works to ramp up manufacturing throughput at its assembly partners, the immediate reality for most consumers is one of prolonged waiting periods.

The company is expected to provide production updates during its next quarterly earnings call, where investors will be keenly focused on whether the iPhone Duo can transition from a scarce luxury item to a mainstream staple in Apple’s hardware portfolio.
However, the overwhelming consumer demand has drastically outstripped Apple's initial production capacity.
Within minutes of pre-orders opening, the company’s official online store sold out of its launch allocation, pushing estimated delivery dates for new orders into January 2027.
For consumers, the fragmented availability means that persistence is required.

While a handset may be listed as out of stock on Apple’s primary digital storefront or major e-commerce platforms, regional mobile networks and specialized electronics retailers occasionally receive staggered shipments.
For years, the category has been dominated by Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold series and a variety of offerings from Chinese manufacturers like Huawei and Xiaomi.

Unlike traditional slab smartphones, the yield rates for foldable displays remain lower, and the calibration required for Apple’s reimagined iOS to seamlessly transition between the cover screen and the expansive inner tablet-like display adds further friction to the production line.
Apple has reportedly secured exclusive contracts for key components, limiting the ability of competitors to flood the market but simultaneously capping its own initial output.

Massive queues formed outside flagship Apple Stores in major global hubs, including London, Bangkok, and Sydney, as enthusiasts and tech professionals raced to secure the limited units available for immediate walk-in purchase.

Priced at a premium starting point of $1,999, the iPhone Duo represents Apple’s most significant hardware redesign in years. The device features a 7.6-inch flexible display when unfolded, powered by the new A20 Pro chip and supported by a 4,883 mAh battery designed to deliver all-day life despite the demanding dual-screen form factor. It also includes a 48MP Dual Fusion camera system and is available in Star White and Night Sky finishes. However, the overwhelming consumer demand has drastically outstripped Apple's initial production capacity. Within minutes of pre-orders opening, the company’s official online store sold out of its launch allocation, pushing estimated delivery dates for new orders into January 2027. The scarcity has extended across major third-party retailers. In the United Kingdom, high-street and online giants including Amazon, John Lewis, Currys, Very, and Argos quickly exhausted their initial stock allocations, leaving prospective buyers with limited options. While some mobile network operators continue to accept pre-orders, delivery timelines are rapidly slipping into late November and December, forcing consumers to navigate a fragmented retail landscape to secure a device before the end of the year. This acute shortage has already spawned a lucrative secondary market. Resellers and scalpers are listing the iPhone Duo for upwards of $4,000, demanding more than double the official retail price from desperate buyers unwilling to wait months for an official allocation. sources.title: Uber rival inDrive eyes 2027 robotaxi tests in Central Asia with Pony.ai and Nvidia
passages: Ride-hailing company inDrive , known for letting passengers and drivers negotiate fares, is working with Chinese autonomous driving firm Pony.ai and Nvidia to begin testing robotaxis in Kazakhstan in 2027.
The move comes as ride-hailing companies expand their push into robotaxis.
Uber is also working with multiple robotaxi companies in other markets, including the Middle East.
Nvidia, on the other hand, would supply the AI technology, including its Hyperion platform and Halos safety system.

The companies said Friday that they had signed a memorandum of understanding to explore bringing Pony.ai’s robotaxis to inDrive’s platform — a reflection of the growing interest in self-driving technology beyond the U.S. and China.
The company aims to have more than 3,500 robotaxis operating in over 20 cities worldwide by the end of 2026, up from a fleet of 1,975 vehicles at the end of June.
Testing will begin in Kazakhstan’s capital, Astana, in the first half of 2027, inDrive CTO Yuri Misnik told TechCrunch.
The tests will initially involve a safety operator, with fully driverless rides as the eventual goal.

inDrive, which has built its business around affordable rides, is looking to bring a similar focus to autonomous ride-hailing as it explores a market where Uber and other rivals are already making moves.
The company also offers its Alpamayo model and tools to generate synthetic data and test autonomous driving systems across different driving scenarios.
Kazakhstan is not the only market where inDrive is exploring robotaxis.
Last month, Kazakhstan announced plans to launch autonomous taxi services in 2027, with initial trials planned in Astana and two other cities.
It has also introduced rules for autonomous vehicles to be tested on certain public roads.

Under the proposed plan, Pony.ai would provide its Gen-7 robotaxis, which inDrive would offer through its ride-hailing app and operate in Kazakhstan. Nvidia, on the other hand, would supply the AI technology, including its Hyperion platform and Halos safety system. The move comes as ride-hailing companies expand their push into robotaxis.
