extraction.body: Ride-hailing company inDrive , known for letting passengers and drivers negotiate fares, is working with Chinese autonomous driving firm Pony.ai and Nvidia to begin testing robotaxis in Kazakhstan in 2027. The companies said Friday that they had signed a memorandum of understanding to explore bringing Pony.ai’s robotaxis to inDrive’s platform — a reflection of the growing interest in self-driving technology beyond the U.S. and China. Testing will begin in Kazakhstan’s capital, Astana, in the first half of 2027, inDrive CTO Yuri Misnik told TechCrunch. The tests will initially involve a safety operator, with fully driverless rides as the eventual goal. Under the proposed plan, Pony.ai would provide its Gen-7 robotaxis, which inDrive would offer through its ride-hailing app and operate in Kazakhstan. Nvidia, on the other hand, would supply the AI technology, including its Hyperion platform and Halos safety system. The move comes as ride-hailing companies expand their push into robotaxis. Earlier this month, Uber announced plans to test Pony.ai’s robotaxis in London , where it has also started offering supervised autonomous rides with British startup Wayve, an investor-backed partner . Uber is also working with multiple robotaxi companies in other markets, including the Middle East. inDrive, which has built its business around affordable rides, is looking to bring a similar focus to autonomous ride-hailing as it explores a market where Uber and other rivals are already making moves. “Our approach is capital-light by design,” said Misnik. “We work with a range of partners in different markets, combining their expertise with ours to deliver a better customer experience.” Nvidia says its Hyperion platform could lower the cost of developing robotaxis by giving companies a ready-made foundation of sensors and computing technology, rather than requiring them to build and integrate everything themselves. The company also offers its Alpamayo model and tools to generate synthetic data and test autonomous driving systems across different driving scenarios. “Those savings are particularly relevant in emerging markets, where ride-hailing is already relatively affordable and autonomous services need to compete on cost,” Ali Kani, Nvidia’s vice president of automotive, told TechCrunch. The announcement coincides with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s first visit to Kazakhstan on Friday. The Kazakhstan proposal would also add to Pony.ai’s ongoing push beyond China. The company aims to have more than 3,500 robotaxis operating in over 20 cities worldwide by the end of 2026, up from a fleet of 1,975 vehicles at the end of June. Last month, Kazakhstan announced plans to launch autonomous taxi services in 2027, with initial trials planned in Astana and two other cities. It has also introduced rules for autonomous vehicles to be tested on certain public roads. Astana’s harsh winters could make it a useful testing ground for robotaxis. The city, with a population of around 1.7 million, faces months of snow and ice, posing challenges for autonomous driving systems. “Launching here will provide an important opportunity to evaluate autonomous driving technology in challenging winter conditions,” inDrive founder and CEO Arsen Tomsky said. “Success in Astana could offer valuable insights for expanding autonomous mobility to other locations facing similar challenges.” Kazakhstan is not the only market where inDrive is exploring robotaxis. In December, the company signed a separate agreement with Saudi Arabia’s AI Driver to explore deploying autonomous vehicles powered by Chinese self-driving firm WeRide, starting with Riyadh. The companies had targeted a pilot in the first half of 2026, though it remains unclear whether testing has begun. “We are also looking at a number of other markets for future deployments,” said Misnik. “One of the main requisites for successful launch in our view is a favorable and collaborative regulatory environment to facilitate safe and sustainable testing on the roads.” inDrive operates in more than 1,200 cities across 47 countries. The company has also expanded beyond ride-hailing into delivery, intercity transportation, and financial services. passages: Ride-hailing company inDrive , known for letting passengers and drivers negotiate fares, is working with Chinese autonomous driving firm Pony.ai and Nvidia to begin testing robotaxis in Kazakhstan in 2027.

The companies said Friday that they had signed a memorandum of understanding to explore bringing Pony.ai’s robotaxis to inDrive’s platform — a reflection of the growing interest in self-driving technology beyond the U.S. and China.

Testing will begin in Kazakhstan’s capital, Astana, in the first half of 2027, inDrive CTO Yuri Misnik told TechCrunch. The tests will initially involve a safety operator, with fully driverless rides as the eventual goal.

Under the proposed plan, Pony.ai would provide its Gen-7 robotaxis, which inDrive would offer through its ride-hailing app and operate in Kazakhstan. Nvidia, on the other hand, would supply the AI technology, including its Hyperion platform and Halos safety system.

The move comes as ride-hailing companies expand their push into robotaxis. Earlier this month, Uber announced plans to test Pony.ai’s robotaxis in London , where it has also started offering supervised autonomous rides with British startup Wayve, an investor-backed partner . Uber is also working with multiple robotaxi companies in other markets, including the Middle East.

inDrive, which has built its business around affordable rides, is looking to bring a similar focus to autonomous ride-hailing as it explores a market where Uber and other rivals are already making moves.
“Our approach is capital-light by design,” said Misnik. “We work with a range of partners in different markets, combining their expertise with ours to deliver a better customer experience.”

Nvidia says its Hyperion platform could lower the cost of developing robotaxis by giving companies a ready-made foundation of sensors and computing technology, rather than requiring them to build and integrate everything themselves. The company also offers its Alpamayo model and tools to generate synthetic data and test autonomous driving systems across different driving scenarios.

“Those savings are particularly relevant in emerging markets, where ride-hailing is already relatively affordable and autonomous services need to compete on cost,” Ali Kani, Nvidia’s vice president of automotive, told TechCrunch.
The announcement coincides with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s first visit to Kazakhstan on Friday.

The Kazakhstan proposal would also add to Pony.ai’s ongoing push beyond China. The company aims to have more than 3,500 robotaxis operating in over 20 cities worldwide by the end of 2026, up from a fleet of 1,975 vehicles at the end of June.

Last month, Kazakhstan announced plans to launch autonomous taxi services in 2027, with initial trials planned in Astana and two other cities. It has also introduced rules for autonomous vehicles to be tested on certain public roads.

Astana’s harsh winters could make it a useful testing ground for robotaxis. The city, with a population of around 1.7 million, faces months of snow and ice, posing challenges for autonomous driving systems.

“Launching here will provide an important opportunity to evaluate autonomous driving technology in challenging winter conditions,” inDrive founder and CEO Arsen Tomsky said. “Success in Astana could offer valuable insights for expanding autonomous mobility to other locations facing similar challenges.”

Kazakhstan is not the only market where inDrive is exploring robotaxis. In December, the company signed a separate agreement with Saudi Arabia’s AI Driver to explore deploying autonomous vehicles powered by Chinese self-driving firm WeRide, starting with Riyadh. The companies had targeted a pilot in the first half of 2026, though it remains unclear whether testing has begun.

“We are also looking at a number of other markets for future deployments,” said Misnik. “One of the main requisites for successful launch in our view is a favorable and collaborative regulatory environment to facilitate safe and sustainable testing on the roads.”
inDrive operates in more than 1,200 cities across 47 countries. The company has also expanded beyond ride-hailing into delivery, intercity transportation, and financial services.

In 2027, there is one type of altcoin that I'm expecting to perform particularly well: beaten-down cryptocurrencies that have pretty much been left for dead in 2026. With that in mind, there's one name that I've already circled for a potential major rebound next year: Cardano (CRYPTO: ADA). Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Just five years ago, Cardano ranked as the fourth-largest cryptocurrency on the planet, trailing only Bitcoin, Ethereum, and BNB . At the time, Cardano had a market cap of $70 billion, and appeared to have a path to toppling Ethereum as the world's premier Layer-1 blockchain network. But that never happened. Down another 40% in 2026, Cardano now trades for a bargain-basement price of just $0.21. Its market cap has slid to less than $8 billion. In fact, Cardano's fall has been so precipitous that it has already dropped out of the list of the top 10 cryptocurrencies (as measured by market cap). But a few factors are working in Cardano's favor right now. One of these is a renewed emphasis on decentralized finance (DeFi). At the beginning of the year, the Cardano developer community released a far-reaching strategy document ("Cardano 2030 Strategic Framework") with details on how they planned to turn things around in DeFi. And they gave very specific goals for user growth, transaction activity, and market share gains. That might sound like pie-in-the-sky thinking, except for one fact: Cardano co-founder Charles Hoskinson is also one of the co-founders of Ethereum and knows a thing or two about putting together a world-class blockchain network. Hoskinson is currently working on a new programming language for the Cardano blockchain platform, and that could mean big things ahead if it opens up new opportunities in fast-growing areas such as artificial intelligence. If Cardano can turn things around next year, a good template could be Solana (CRYPTO: SOL), which saw a monster turnaround after losing 94% of its value in 2022. The following year, Solana soared by 924% as investors realized that it had been oversold amid broader fears of a full-fledged crypto meltdown. Like Solana, Cardano is a Layer-1 smart contract platform. And, similar to Solana several years ago, Cardano is currently trading at a massive discount to its all-time high. This is not to say that Cardano will 10x in 2027. But I wouldn't be surprised at all if it climbs back past the $1 mark. As recently as January 2025, Cardano traded for $1. That's nearly a 5x return, and much higher than Bitcoin or Ethereum is projected to return. It's a risky bet, of course, but at a price of just $0.21, Cardano is just too cheap to ignore. passages: Wall Street's biggest settlement firm just named Stellar as a future partner, sending XLM back onto traders' watchlists.
But before you chase the catalyst, the comparison with Ethereum reveals some uncomfortable truths about timing, tokenization dominance, and price reality.
Sam Daodu is a crypto analyst who's spent nearly a decade making blockchain understandable—no easy task when most whitepapers read like fever dreams.
He writes for 24/7 Wall St., covering Bitcoin, altcoins, and crypto market analysis for investors.
Before crypto, he was a tech writer (back when explaining "the cloud" was peak innovation).
Since 2018, he's written for CoinTelegraph, Yahoo Finance, The Block, Cryptonews, Zypto, Rain, and more—basically anywhere people want crypto news without the headache.
Sam runs MacLabs Marketing, a content agency for crypto brands tired of sounding like AI wrote their website.
He also publishes free crypto education on his site for Web3 enthusiasts who think "gas fees" is a typo.

When he's not writing or staring at charts, Sam's either: - Watching anime (currently convinced One Piece has better tokenomics than most altcoins) - At the gym sculpting himself into a Greek god - Listening to the music your mum warned you only bad boys listen to Connect: LinkedIn | Email | MacLabs Marketing
Technically, XLM must first recover to $0.20, roughly 12% above its current price and a level it held on October 10.
If DTCC postpones Stellar’s launch, XLM may lose its latest catalyst and keep trailing Ethereum as it has over the past 90 days.
Conversely, if DTCC announces a 2027 launch date for Stellar and XLM closes above $0.20, it could create a significant opportunity for XLM to make up ground.
In the XLM vs Ethereum comparison, Ethereum stands as the more reliable choice for investors interested in tokenization.
Investors considering XLM face significant risk from a potential DTCC catalyst that is still a year away and could change.

The Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC), a major player in settling U.S. stock trades, expects Stellar ( CRYPTO:XLM ) to join its upcoming Tokenization Service in 2027, according to its roadmap.
Tokenization converts stocks and bonds into digital tokens that can be traded on a blockchain.
Stellar will not be part of the October launch, and DTCC has not confirmed a specific date for its entry.
Ethereum significantly outpaces Stellar in tokenized assets, with $17 billion in tokenized RWAs and $147.1 billion in stablecoins.
However, Ethereum has already attracted substantial institutional investment that Stellar still needs to secure.
XLM is trading at approximately $0.18, down 0.6% in the last 24 hours.

The Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC), a major player in settling U.S. stock trades, expects Stellar ( CRYPTO:XLM ) to join its upcoming Tokenization Service in 2027, according to its roadmap. Tokenization converts stocks and bonds into digital tokens that can be traded on a blockchain. With this news, XLM is back on buyers’ radar, especially after a 15.3% decline over the past two weeks. XLM is trading at approximately $0.18, down 0.6% in the last 24 hours. By comparison, Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ) trades around $2,417 and plays a major role in the tokenized asset market, though its connection to DTCC’s upcoming service is less direct. So, in the XLM vs Ethereum debate, which cryptocurrency stands as the better investment to capitalize on the tokenization trend? The initial rollout will cover 25 stocks, ETFs, and U.S. Treasuries, with each token fully backed by a corresponding security held at the Depository Trust Company (DTC), a DTCC subsidiary. Token holders will have the flexibility to transfer their tokens at any time between registered wallets. DTCC estimates it will have around $30 trillion in assets available for tokenization. Before the official launch, DTCC conducted a successful test on July 15, turning DTC-held securities into tokens for live trades on both Besu and Canton, involving more than 30 participating firms. DTCC has described this initiative as part of a “multi-chain strategy” to ensure resiliency, scalability, and choice for users. While DTCC’s roadmap indicates a potential inclusion for Stellar and the Arc network in 2027, this plan is subject to change. Stellar will not be part of the October launch, and DTCC has not confirmed a specific date for its entry. Stellar has already made strides in this space, managing $3.6 billion in tokenized real-world assets (excluding stablecoins), ranking fourth among all networks, according to rwa.xyz data from October 17. These real-world assets (RWAs) include tokenized Treasury funds and private credit. However, despite its accomplishments, XLM’s price does not reflect this progress well. XLM trades 79.6% below its January 2018 peak of $0.88 and has fallen 41.4% over the past year. XLM’s supply also puts pressure on its price. Approximately 35.2 billion of 50 billion XLM tokens are in circulation, giving a fully diluted valuation (the value if all tokens were in circulation) of about $8.9 billion, compared with a market cap of around $6.3 billion. This indicates that more tokens could be released into the market, potentially absorbing new demand. The connection between Ethereum and DTCC comes through Besu, an Ethereum client, meaning DTCC’s private network uses Ethereum technology but operates separately from the public Ethereum blockchain. Ethereum significantly outpaces Stellar in tokenized assets, with $17 billion in tokenized RWAs and $147.1 billion in stablecoins. In contrast, Stellar holds only $535 million in stablecoins, according to the same data source. Price performance has also favored Ethereum. ETH trades 51.1% below its record high of $4,946 from August 2025 and is up 29.3% over the past 90 days, while XLM has dropped 3.8%. Over the last two weeks, ETH fell 9.3% , while XLM fell more sharply, down 15.3%. One advantage XLM has is its smaller market cap, with Ethereum’s $295.2 billion about 47 times larger. Smaller cryptocurrencies can often react more sharply to news from large partners. However, Ethereum has already attracted substantial institutional investment that Stellar still needs to secure. In the XLM vs Ethereum comparison, Ethereum stands as the more reliable choice for investors interested in tokenization. DTCC’s 2027 roadmap doesn’t change that. Investors considering XLM face significant risk from a potential DTCC catalyst that is still a year away and could change. For XLM to narrow the gap, DTCC’s October launch needs to progress smoothly, Stellar’s rollout date must be confirmed, and its tokenized asset base should keep growing. Technically, XLM must first recover to $0.20, roughly 12% above its current price and a level it held on October 10. If DTCC postpones Stellar’s launch, XLM may lose its latest catalyst and keep trailing Ethereum as it has over the past 90 days. Conversely, if DTCC announces a 2027 launch date for Stellar and XLM closes above $0.20, it could create a significant opportunity for XLM to make up ground. Stellar just cracked the top three blockchains for tokenized real-world assets, and XLM's price jumped the same week. But the connection between those two facts is far more complicated than it looks. XRP (CRYPTO: XRP) and Stellar (CRYPTO: XLM) were both built to solve the same remittance problem. International payments are slow, expensive, and routed through a chain of correspondent banks that each add delays and… XRP (CRYPTO:XRP) and Stellar have always been chasing the same prize, which is moving money and assets across borders without the old banking rails. XRP is far the bigger of the two, worth tens… Stellar just landed partnerships with a major US bank, the DTCC, and two federal regulators in a single month, yet XLM still trades far below a key resistance level that has blocked every rally… Stellar just crossed a technical threshold that XRP is still struggling to reach, but a surge in ETF inflows could flip the script heading into Q4. These two payments coins are telling very different… Stellar hosts more tokenized real-world assets than the XRP Ledger, yet XLM trades at a fraction of XRP's price. The reason comes down to a structural flaw in how Stellar's tokenization boom actually works. This move showcases the growing trend of tokenization, which has found increasing popularity as a new way to represent the ownership rights of real-world assets as digital tokens on a blockchain. XRP and Ethereum both sit far below their 2025 peaks, and the path back looks very different for each coin. ETF flows, banking partnerships, and upcoming upgrades will determine which one gets there first. extraction.body: If you're looking for a big winner in 2027, you'll likely need to widen your search beyond Bitcoin and Ethereum . In bull market cycles, these two cryptocurrencies perform well, of course, but nowhere near as well as more speculative altcoins with much smaller market caps. In 2027, there is one type of altcoin that I'm expecting to perform particularly well: beaten-down cryptocurrencies that have pretty much been left for dead in 2026. With that in mind, there's one name that I've already circled for a potential major rebound next year: Cardano (CRYPTO: ADA). Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Just five years ago, Cardano ranked as the fourth-largest cryptocurrency on the planet, trailing only Bitcoin, Ethereum, and BNB . At the time, Cardano had a market cap of $70 billion, and appeared to have a path to toppling Ethereum as the world's premier Layer-1 blockchain network. But that never happened. Down another 40% in 2026, Cardano now trades for a bargain-basement price of just $0.21. Its market cap has slid to less than $8 billion. In fact, Cardano's fall has been so precipitous that it has already dropped out of the list of the top 10 cryptocurrencies (as measured by market cap). But a few factors are working in Cardano's favor right now. One of these is a renewed emphasis on decentralized finance (DeFi). At the beginning of the year, the Cardano developer community released a far-reaching strategy document ("Cardano 2030 Strategic Framework") with details on how they planned to turn things around in DeFi. And they gave very specific goals for user growth, transaction activity, and market share gains. That might sound like pie-in-the-sky thinking, except for one fact: Cardano co-founder Charles Hoskinson is also one of the co-founders of Ethereum and knows a thing or two about putting together a world-class blockchain network. Hoskinson is currently working on a new programming language for the Cardano blockchain platform, and that could mean big things ahead if it opens up new opportunities in fast-growing areas such as artificial intelligence. If Cardano can turn things around next year, a good template could be Solana (CRYPTO: SOL), which saw a monster turnaround after losing 94% of its value in 2022. sources.title: Wall Street's Biggest Settlement Firm Is Lining Up Stellar for 2027. Is XLM a Better Buy Than Ethereum? - 24/7 Wall St.
passages: Wall Street's biggest settlement firm just named Stellar as a future partner, sending XLM back onto traders' watchlists.
But before you chase the catalyst, the comparison with Ethereum reveals some uncomfortable truths about timing, tokenization dominance, and price reality.
Sam Daodu is a crypto analyst who's spent nearly a decade making blockchain understandable—no easy task when most whitepapers read like fever dreams.
He writes for 24/7 Wall St., covering Bitcoin, altcoins, and crypto market analysis for investors.
Before crypto, he was a tech writer (back when explaining "the cloud" was peak innovation).
Since 2018, he's written for CoinTelegraph, Yahoo Finance, The Block, Cryptonews, Zypto, Rain, and more—basically anywhere people want crypto news without the headache.
Sam runs MacLabs Marketing, a content agency for crypto brands tired of sounding like AI wrote their website.
He also publishes free crypto education on his site for Web3 enthusiasts who think "gas fees" is a typo.

When he's not writing or staring at charts, Sam's either: - Watching anime (currently convinced One Piece has better tokenomics than most altcoins) - At the gym sculpting himself into a Greek god - Listening to the music your mum warned you only bad boys listen to Connect: LinkedIn | Email | MacLabs Marketing
Technically, XLM must first recover to $0.20, roughly 12% above its current price and a level it held on October 10.
If DTCC postpones Stellar’s launch, XLM may lose its latest catalyst and keep trailing Ethereum as it has over the past 90 days.
Conversely, if DTCC announces a 2027 launch date for Stellar and XLM closes above $0.20, it could create a significant opportunity for XLM to make up ground.
In the XLM vs Ethereum comparison, Ethereum stands as the more reliable choice for investors interested in tokenization.
Investors considering XLM face significant risk from a potential DTCC catalyst that is still a year away and could change.

The Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC), a major player in settling U.S. stock trades, expects Stellar ( CRYPTO:XLM ) to join its upcoming Tokenization Service in 2027, according to its roadmap.
Tokenization converts stocks and bonds into digital tokens that can be traded on a blockchain.
Stellar will not be part of the October launch, and DTCC has not confirmed a specific date for its entry.
Ethereum significantly outpaces Stellar in tokenized assets, with $17 billion in tokenized RWAs and $147.1 billion in stablecoins.
However, Ethereum has already attracted substantial institutional investment that Stellar still needs to secure.
XLM is trading at approximately $0.18, down 0.6% in the last 24 hours.

The Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC), a major player in settling U.S. stock trades, expects Stellar ( CRYPTO:XLM ) to join its upcoming Tokenization Service in 2027, according to its roadmap. Tokenization converts stocks and bonds into digital tokens that can be traded on a blockchain. With this news, XLM is back on buyers’ radar, especially after a 15.3% decline over the past two weeks. XLM is trading at approximately $0.18, down 0.6% in the last 24 hours. By comparison, Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ) trades around $2,417 and plays a major role in the tokenized asset market, though its connection to DTCC’s upcoming service is less direct. So, in the XLM vs Ethereum debate, which cryptocurrency stands as the better investment to capitalize on the tokenization trend? The initial rollout will cover 25 stocks, ETFs, and U.S. Treasuries, with each token fully backed by a corresponding security held at the Depository Trust Company (DTC), a DTCC subsidiary. Token holders will have the flexibility to transfer their tokens at any time between registered wallets. DTCC estimates it will have around $30 trillion in assets available for tokenization. Before the official launch, DTCC conducted a successful test on July 15, turning DTC-held securities into tokens for live trades on both Besu and Canton, involving more than 30 participating firms. DTCC has described this initiative as part of a “multi-chain strategy” to ensure resiliency, scalability, and choice for users. While DTCC’s roadmap indicates a potential inclusion for Stellar and the Arc network in 2027, this plan is subject to change. Stellar will not be part of the October launch, and DTCC has not confirmed a specific date for its entry. Stellar has already made strides in this space, managing $3.6 billion in tokenized real-world assets (excluding stablecoins), ranking fourth among all networks, according to rwa.xyz data from October 17. These real-world assets (RWAs) include tokenized Treasury funds and private credit. However, despite its accomplishments, XLM’s price does not reflect this progress well. XLM trades 79.6% below its January 2018 peak of $0.88 and has fallen 41.4% over the past year. XLM’s supply also puts pressure on its price. Approximately 35.2 billion of 50 billion XLM tokens are in circulation, giving a fully diluted valuation (the value if all tokens were in circulation) of about $8.9 billion, compared with a market cap of around $6.3 billion. This indicates that more tokens could be released into the market, potentially absorbing new demand. The connection between Ethereum and DTCC comes through Besu, an Ethereum client, meaning DTCC’s private network uses Ethereum technology but operates separately from the public Ethereum blockchain. Ethereum significantly outpaces Stellar in tokenized assets, with $17 billion in tokenized RWAs and $147.1 billion in stablecoins. In contrast, Stellar holds only $535 million in stablecoins, according to the same data source. Price performance has also favored Ethereum. ETH trades 51.1% below its record high of $4,946 from August 2025 and is up 29.3% over the past 90 days, while XLM has dropped 3.8%. Over the last two weeks, ETH fell 9.3% , while XLM fell more sharply, down 15.3%. One advantage XLM has is its smaller market cap, with Ethereum’s $295.2 billion about 47 times larger. Smaller cryptocurrencies can often react more sharply to news from large partners. However, Ethereum has already attracted substantial institutional investment that Stellar still needs to secure. In the XLM vs Ethereum comparison, Ethereum stands as the more reliable choice for investors interested in tokenization. DTCC’s 2027 roadmap doesn’t change that. Investors considering XLM face significant risk from a potential DTCC catalyst that is still a year away and could change. For XLM to narrow the gap, DTCC’s October launch needs to progress smoothly, Stellar’s rollout date must be confirmed, and its tokenized asset base should keep growing. Technically, XLM must first recover to $0.20, roughly 12% above its current price and a level it held on October 10. If DTCC postpones Stellar’s launch, XLM may lose its latest catalyst and keep trailing Ethereum as it has over the past 90 days. Conversely, if DTCC announces a 2027 launch date for Stellar and XLM closes above $0.20, it could create a significant opportunity for XLM to make up ground. Stellar just cracked the top three blockchains for tokenized real-world assets, and XLM's price jumped the same week. But the connection between those two facts is far more complicated than it looks. XRP (CRYPTO: XRP) and Stellar (CRYPTO: XLM) were both built to solve the same remittance problem. International payments are slow, expensive, and routed through a chain of correspondent banks that each add delays and… XRP (CRYPTO:XRP) and Stellar have always been chasing the same prize, which is moving money and assets across borders without the old banking rails. XRP is far the bigger of the two, worth tens… Stellar just landed partnerships with a major US bank, the DTCC, and two federal regulators in a single month, yet XLM still trades far below a key resistance level that has blocked every rally… Stellar just crossed a technical threshold that XRP is still struggling to reach, but a surge in ETF inflows could flip the script heading into Q4. These two payments coins are telling very different… Stellar hosts more tokenized real-world assets than the XRP Ledger, yet XLM trades at a fraction of XRP's price. The reason comes down to a structural flaw in how Stellar's tokenization boom actually works. This move showcases the growing trend of tokenization, which has found increasing popularity as a new way to represent the ownership rights of real-world assets as digital tokens on a blockchain. XRP and Ethereum both sit far below their 2025 peaks, and the path back looks very different for each coin. ETF flows, banking partnerships, and upcoming upgrades will determine which one gets there first. passages: Brick, the company behind the $59 gadget that blocks you from using apps on your phone, has launched a new device that’s designed to help you cut back on doomscrolling in bed.

extraction.body: Brick, the company behind the $59 gadget that blocks you from using apps on your phone, has launched a new device that’s designed to help you cut back on doomscrolling in bed. The $129 Brick Night introduces a location-based element: instead of requiring you to tap your phone against the device, like the OG Brick, this version uses Bluetooth to automatically kick in when you enter your bedroom (or any other room you put it in). The Brick Night uses two CR2477 batteries, and you can set a location zone of up to 25 feet x 25 feet. Still, the Brick Night is more than twice the price, and because it doesn’t include NFC capabilities, it can’t be used for both location-based and tap-based blocking — which would allow it to replace the original Brick.

sources.title: 8 Phone Blocking Apps You Should Try Instead Of Brick - BGR
passages: If you're an iPhone user looking for an alternative to Brick that doesn't require paying for an expensive physical device, Foqos is a good place to start.
Foqos is completely free and open source, and offers similar phone blocking features as Brick.
Foqos integrates directly into the native iPhone blocking experience using the Screen Time API.
But instead of using a $60 device, you use free tools and a combination of software features to make sure that the distracting elements of your phone are locked away.
The apps listed here all offer ways to block distracting apps for a certain time, helping you focus.
App store ratings, user feedback, and expert reviews underlined the quality and utility of the apps we've recommended as worthy alternatives to try, instead of Brick.
Unlike the Brick, it comes in the form of a metal card that's discreet and easy to store.
You tap the Bloom card on your smartphone to lock the device, and then tap it again to unlock the restrictions.
Once it's locked, hide the card, give it to your spouse, or leave it in a different room.
Sure, you can set up screen time limits on your iPhone or Android smartphone, but they can be easily ignored or extended.
However, if you make the addictive apps harder to access, you might actually find that your smartphone usage goes down.
This method was popularized by the Brick app, which comes with a physical device that you must scan to unblock apps.
It offers native integration for blocking apps and websites, and you can even block addicting features inside social media apps (like Reels in Instagram or Shorts in YouTube).
If deep breathing isn't working for you, you can try a 4-7-8 breathing exercise, box breathing, mood journaling, or even a math problem.
If blocking and hiding apps feels like a bit too much, you could try a gentler approach with One Sec – available on iPhone, iPad, Android, and major browsers.
The app also offers a timer based option, where the apps will stay blocked until the time is up.
You can't just uninstall these apps to get around the block either.
In Foqos you can create custom profiles based on which apps or websites you want to block, creating a routine for different parts of your life.
Unlike Brick, which is a total block, Bloom offers breaks.

extraction.body: It is too easy to lose a couple of hours each evening to doomscrolling. You open a social media app to check on your friends, and minutes later, you're already lost in a marathon scrolling session. And these aren't highbrow art movies, or even a Marvel film. It's mostly content you won't even remember tomorrow. Sure, you can set up screen time limits on your iPhone or Android smartphone, but they can be easily ignored or extended. However, if you make the addictive apps harder to access, you might actually find that your smartphone usage goes down. This method was popularized by the Brick app, which comes with a physical device that you must scan to unblock apps. The concept is great, but it costs $59. Don't want to spend that much? There are other ways to get there, with apps that have strict modes to make unblocking impossible until the focus time runs out. You can't just uninstall these apps to get around the block either. If you're an iPhone user looking for an alternative to Brick that doesn't require paying for an expensive physical device, Foqos is a good place to start. Foqos is completely free and open source, and offers similar phone blocking features as Brick. Foqos integrates directly into the native iPhone blocking experience using the Screen Time API. But instead of using a $60 device, you use free tools and a combination of software features to make sure that the distracting elements of your phone are locked away. Foqos uses NFC tags and QR codes as the physical replacement for a separate device. NFC tags are quite cheap to buy online, and QR codes can be printed for free. In Foqos you can create custom profiles based on which apps or websites you want to block, creating a routine for different parts of your life. For example, you can block Instagram and TikTok when you're working, and Gmail and Slack when it's evening time. Once the profile is enabled, make sure that the QR code or the NFC tag is away from your reach. When you're done focusing, scan the QR code or the NFC tag using the Foqos app to unlock app access. The app also offers a timer based option, where the apps will stay blocked until the time is up. Switchly is a free and open-source phone blocker app designed for Android. It offers native integration for blocking apps and websites, and you can even block addicting features inside social media apps (like Reels in Instagram or Shorts in YouTube). Similar to Foqos, you can set it up so that the only way to unblock apps is using NFC tags, QR codes, or a barcode. The app also takes advantage of Android's background processing to help you create custom blocking routines using schedules, Wi-Fi networks, Bluetooth, and location tracking. You start off by creating a profile, adding apps and websites you want to block, and then setting up a blocking method. This can be a simple schedule, or a mixed approach, including NFC tags and QR codes for unblocking content early. You can even automate this process, so that profiles (and blocking) are enabled based on the Wi-Fi network you connect to. If you want dedicated hardware for blocking apps, but don't want to spend $60, Bloom is a good alternative. Unlike the Brick, it comes in the form of a metal card that's discreet and easy to store. The concept is similar to Brick. You tap the Bloom card on your smartphone to lock the device, and then tap it again to unlock the restrictions. Once it's locked, hide the card, give it to your spouse, or leave it in a different room. The Bloom card and the Bloom app work on both iPhone and Android, and the app itself is free, with no subscriptions or in-app purchases. The card costs $39. While deleting the Bloom app from your smartphone can unblock apps, Bloom offers a strict mode that stops you from deleting any app from your smartphone until the time is up, or it's unlocked using the card. Unlike Brick, which is a total block, Bloom offers breaks. You can take up to three five minute breaks, directly on your smartphone without touching the Bloom card. For emergencies, or for quickly checking in, this can be useful, although it may prove to be a slippery slope for some. Jomo is a feature-rich screen time app designed for iPhone. The free app offers a single blocking session, and it might be enough for most users. The $29.99/year subscription unlocks up to 10 sessions, a strict mode, and Apple Health integration. Jomo offers multiple modes and options for blocking apps. It works on iPhones, iPads, and Macs, and uses the Screen Time API for a native integration. What sets it apart, though, is its customizable barrier. Jomo adds an extra step before you can unlock an app. You might have to scan a QR code, enter a password, or a long string of text, solve a puzzle, and more. There's also an AI feature that asks for a selfie before it will unlock the app. When it comes to app and website blocking, Jomo offers many different options. Using the Rules feature, you can block an app for a particular amount of time — such as one hour, or set limits — like only three opens in a day, or set a cut-off time — perhaps to exit the app after 15 minutes of use. The app is highly customizable, and you can easily mix and match rules and unlocking features to create the perfect setup that works for you. If you're on the hunt for a truly free screen-time utility that works across major platforms like iPhone, Android, Mac, Windows, and iPad, take a look at ScreenZen . There are no premium tiers here, though you can donate to show your support for the developer. ScreenZen is not technically an app-blocking utility, but it will annoy you into submission. ScreenZen offers a delay-based system. When you first open an app, it will show a countdown before you can actually open the app. This serves as a bit of a pause, and is itself customizable. The pause can be a couple of seconds, or can be extended to minutes. The clever bit is that you can set it up so that the delay time increases each time you open the app. First time you open Instagram? Wait for 10 seconds. The sixth time? Wait for a minute. You can push it further with Interventions, which makes you solve math problems or complete a task before you can unlock the app. ScreenZen also offers a Lock mode to prevent you from uninstalling it. If blocking and hiding apps feels like a bit too much, you could try a gentler approach with One Sec – available on iPhone, iPad, Android, and major browsers. One Sec takes a science-backed approach and according to research conducted in association with the Max Planck Institute and Heidelberg University, users reduce app usage by around 57% on average. Much like ScreenZen, it works by interrupting the opening of a distracting app. However, when One Sec takes over the screen it's with a slow-breathing exercise, before a confirmation of whether you do indeed wish to open the app in question. If so, you can go ahead and open it, no guilt necessary. Of course, the idea is that as you use the app more and more, that answer shifts to a no instead. The interruptions are customizable. If deep breathing isn't working for you, you can try a 4-7-8 breathing exercise, box breathing, mood journaling, or even a math problem. Additionally, you can ask One Sec to interrupt you while you're already using the distracting app, such as five minutes after opening Instagram, or even at every five minute mark of use — this way you can annoy yourself into quitting a doomscrolling habit. One Sec is completely free to use with one app or website, but to block more apps and to unlock customization options, you'll have to upgrade to One Sec Pro for $19.99 per year. When it comes to design and features, Opal is quite a polished and mature app, for iOS, Android, and Mac. It's also the most expensive service on this list, with a subscription costing $99.99 per year. Though, to reap the benefits, you don't necessarily need to pay up. For free, Opal will let you run what it calls a single rule for blocking apps and websites — such as a scheduled session, a time limit, or an open limit. On top of this, you get access to basic timers and soundscapes, and the day's Opal score. To unlock all limits on rules, and introduce harder unblocking steps, you'll have to spring for the Opal Pro upgrade. Similar to the Whoop app , Opal combines three key metrics — sleep, focus, and rest — to give you an overall score for your digital well-being. You can set a custom focus timer when you really want to focus on work, but it's the automation rules that sync between devices that are the main draw. For example, you can set a week day mode to block all social media apps, or a weekend mode for all your work apps. As Opal's rules are quite customizable, you can add in a set number of unblocks for apps like Instagram and TikTok, if you so wish. Session's aim is to get you to a focused life, but it does that via the Pomodoro route. It's an Apple based app and website blocker, but only when you're in a Pomodoro session. Pomodoro is one of those tech habits that can make you more productive, and help you save time, with a 25 minute session where you focus on the task at hand and then a five minute break. When you're focused on work, you can't access YouTube, or scroll through the news websites. And a Pomodoro session is customizable, so you can initiate a 40 minute session, with a 20 minute break, if you please. If you're all in on the Apple ecosystem, Session syncs your timers, sessions, and blocklist across your iPhone, iPad, and Mac. This means that you won't be tempted by Instagram on your iPhone when you're trying to work on your Mac. However this, and other features are only available on the paid Pro version of the Session app. It comes with a seven day free trial and then costs $4.99 per month, or $39.99 per year. It's also available as a part of the Setapp Mac app subscription. The apps listed here all offer ways to block distracting apps for a certain time, helping you focus. You can set a custom focus timer when you really want to focus on work, but it's the automation rules that sync between devices that are the main draw. For example, you can set a week day mode to block all social media apps, or a weekend mode for all your work apps. extraction.body: Robinhood is seeing growing demand for prediction markets tied to bitcoin, gold and oil, as traders increasingly look beyond sports and elections to bet on moves in financial markets. Price volatility contracts tied to those assets are among the fastest-growing products in prediction markets, according to JB Mackenzie, VP and GM for futures and prediction markets at Robinhood. Sports is the largest product the platform offers, said Mackenzie at the NEXTPredict conference in New York on Thursday. However, he said there is a shift in how people use the platform. "We've now started to see price volatility contracts, such as bitcoin, crude oil, gold, start to dominate the marketplace, and they're the fastest growing products that are out there," Mackenzie said. Prediction markets allow traders to buy contracts based on whether an event will happen, with prices reflecting the market's implied probability of an outcome. A contract might ask whether bitcoin will trade above a certain price at a set time, giving traders a way to take a position without buying the cryptocurrency itself. The market has grown from its roots in elections into sports, economic data and short-term price bets. Robinhood entered the business through a partnership with Kalshi, a federally regulated prediction market exchange, and has since made event contracts a growing part of its trading platform. extraction.body: The Ohio State University will break ground Tuesday morning on the Timashev Technology Tower, a planned multi-story innovation and research facility. Ohio State University President Ravi Bellamkonda joined Morning Edition Host Stu Osborne to discuss the new facility. sources.title: IBM, Baringa, and MegaCorp Logistics detail the shift from reactive to predictive supply chain AI - MarketScale
passages: Experts from IBM, Baringa, and MegaCorp Logistics discuss the transition from reactive to predictive AI in supply chains.
This change aims to enhance operational efficiency amidst global challenges such as geopolitical and climate disruptions.
Their collective message to supply chain directors: the window for running reactive logistics is closing, and the cost of staying in that posture is rising.
Supply chain modelling used to run on one or two variables.
Today, according to Danny Lin, Partner of Procurement and Supply Chain at Baringa, that framework is obsolete.

Speaking in a Supply Chain Digital webinar published July 7, 2026, Lin described a fundamental shift toward multivariate, AI-driven models that treat volatility as a design condition rather than an exception to manage around.
Clark Campos, Director of Mexico Logistics and Operations at MegaCorp Logistics, framed the tariff problem in operational terms.
Cross-border operators today need to know not just where freight is, but whether current inventory positioning still makes sense if a new tariff takes effect.
That kind of forward-looking question, he noted, is exactly what predictive AI tools are being built to answer, shifting the question from 'what happened' to 'are we positioned correctly right now.'
Pushpinder Singh, Partner and Global Practice Leader for Supply Chain Transformation at IBM , added a workforce dimension that operations leaders are already feeling.

Role lifecycles across supply chain functions have compressed from five to seven years down to roughly two to four years, he said, as responsibilities shift faster than traditional onboarding can accommodate.

AI is helping close that gap by shortening the time it takes new personnel to reach operational competency, a practical benefit that sits alongside the more-discussed forecasting and visibility use cases.
Predictive AI is being implemented to replace traditional reactive logistics models.
The panel converged on a clear warning for organizations mid-deployment: attempting to roll AI out across every supply chain function simultaneously is a reliable path to failed initiatives.

Today, according to Danny Lin, Partner of Procurement and Supply Chain at Baringa, that framework is obsolete. Speaking in a Supply Chain Digital webinar published July 7, 2026, Lin described a fundamental shift toward multivariate, AI-driven models that treat volatility as a design condition rather than an exception to manage around. The webinar, hosted in association with Amazon Business, brought together senior practitioners from IBM, Baringa, Aveya, and MegaCorp Logistics . Their collective message to supply chain directors: the window for running reactive logistics is closing, and the cost of staying in that posture is rising. Geopolitical fragmentation, shifting trade policies, and climate-related disruption have combined to make historical baselines unreliable planning inputs. The panel pointed to maritime choke points and sudden tariff changes as examples of shocks that, under traditional models, force executives into firefighting mode. AI-enabled monitoring changes that calculus by running continuous scans across supplier networks and flagging emerging risks in real time, before delays propagate downstream. Clark Campos, Director of Mexico Logistics and Operations at MegaCorp Logistics, framed the tariff problem in operational terms. Cross-border operators today need to know not just where freight is, but whether current inventory positioning still makes sense if a new tariff takes effect. That kind of forward-looking question, he noted, is exactly what predictive AI tools are being built to answer, shifting the question from 'what happened' to 'are we positioned correctly right now.' Lin noted during the session that the shift is less about reacting faster and more about embracing a dynamic supply chain architecture, one designed to absorb change rather than resist it. That mindset shift, in his view, is where durable competitive advantages are built. Abhijit Supekar, Senior Director of Global Supply Chain at Aveya, zeroed in on a gap that limits many existing deployments: the tendency to feed AI models only internal ERP data. He argued that genuine predictive power requires external signals, including supplier location risk, financial health indicators, and other inputs that sit entirely outside a company's own systems. Procurement teams that build those connections, he said, are positioned to make sourcing decisions before a supplier stress event surfaces on an invoice. That framing positions AI not as a reporting layer on top of existing logistics software but as a strategic sourcing instrument. The implication for procurement directors is concrete: the data architecture decisions made now, specifically which external feeds get integrated and how, will determine the quality of AI recommendations for years ahead. Pushpinder Singh, Partner and Global Practice Leader for Supply Chain Transformation at IBM , added a workforce dimension that operations leaders are already feeling. Role lifecycles across supply chain functions have compressed from five to seven years down to roughly two to four years, he said, as responsibilities shift faster than traditional onboarding can accommodate. AI is helping close that gap by shortening the time it takes new personnel to reach operational competency, a practical benefit that sits alongside the more-discussed forecasting and visibility use cases. The panel converged on a clear warning for organizations mid-deployment: attempting to roll AI out across every supply chain function simultaneously is a reliable path to failed initiatives. Singh pointed to governance structure and decision ownership as the real differentiators between organizations that scale AI and those that stall. A simple, clear governance model matters more than the sophistication of the underlying algorithm. Start at the critical pinch points. You know where those are. That answer's going to be different for everyone. But I would start there, and then scale from there. , Danny Lin, Partner of Procurement and Supply Chain, Baringa, via Supply Chain Digital Lin's recommended timeline for supply chain directors is a 12-to-18-month horizon: identify the two or three operational friction points generating the most reactive overhead, deploy predictive capabilities there first, prove the value in measurable terms, and then extend the model. That sequence avoids the organizational fatigue that comes with overbuilt initial deployments. extraction.body: Independent Intelligence for Logistics & Supply Chain Leaders Independent Intelligence for Logistics & Supply Chain Leaders A transportation management system supplier can have an excellent product, strong customer references, a capable sales organization, and an established position in the market. Yet a prospective customer searching for a solution may never encounter that supplier. Not because the company lacks the necessary capabilities, but because an AI-generated comparison has already presented a different set of alternatives. This matters to companies selling logistics and supply chain technology. For years, suppliers have used search optimization, industry research, webinars, customer stories, and digital marketing to reach buyers. Those investments still matter. But AI-generated responses may now shape a buyer’s understanding of the market before that person visits a supplier website or contacts sales. New research from Semrush , published October 21, illustrates the change in Google’s search results. Semrush tracked 400 U.S. desktop commercial keywords in banking, ecommerce, and software from September 2025 through August 2026. Google’s AI Overviews appeared for 88% of these keywords at the end of the study, up from 45.75%. Review searches reached nearly 90% coverage, while ‘best product for a particular use’ searches reached 96.12%. Weighted by estimated search volume, coverage was approximately 97% within the sample. The study measured whether Google displayed AI Overviews, not whether other AI assistants recommended particular suppliers. It did not examine logistics technology specifically or measure clicks or conversions. Even with those limits, it offers a useful signal: AI-generated summaries are becoming a prominent part of commercial software discovery. For suppliers of transportation management systems, warehouse management systems, supply chain planning software, visibility platforms, automation, robotics, and related technologies, the implications deserve attention. Consider a distribution executive evaluating warehouse management software. coreStoryFacts.text: Experts from IBM, Baringa, and MegaCorp Logistics discuss the transition from reactive to predictive AI in supply chains.
This change aims to enhance operational efficiency amidst global challenges such as geopolitical and climate disruptions.
Their collective message to supply chain directors: the window for running reactive logistics is closing, and the cost of staying in that posture is rising.
Supply chain modelling used to run on one or two variables.
Today, according to Danny Lin, Partner of Procurement and Supply Chain at Baringa, that framework is obsolete.

Speaking in a Supply Chain Digital webinar published July 7, 2026, Lin described a fundamental shift toward multivariate, AI-driven models that treat volatility as a design condition rather than an exception to manage around.
Clark Campos, Director of Mexico Logistics and Operations at MegaCorp Logistics, framed the tariff problem in operational terms.
Cross-border operators today need to know not just where freight is, but whether current inventory positioning still makes sense if a new tariff takes effect.
That kind of forward-looking question, he noted, is exactly what predictive AI tools are being built to answer, shifting the question from 'what happened' to 'are we positioned correctly right now.'
Pushpinder Singh, Partner and Global Practice Leader for Supply Chain Transformation at IBM , added a workforce dimension that operations leaders are already feeling.

Role lifecycles across supply chain functions have compressed from five to seven years down to roughly two to four years, he said, as responsibilities shift faster than traditional onboarding can accommodate.

AI is helping close that gap by shortening the time it takes new personnel to reach operational competency, a practical benefit that sits alongside the more-discussed forecasting and visibility use cases.
Predictive AI is being implemented to replace traditional reactive logistics models.
The panel converged on a clear warning for organizations mid-deployment: attempting to roll AI out across every supply chain function simultaneously is a reliable path to failed initiatives.

extraction.body: Independent Intelligence for Logistics & Supply Chain Leaders Independent Intelligence for Logistics & Supply Chain Leaders A transportation management system supplier can have an excellent product, strong customer references, a capable sales organization, and an established position in the market. Yet a prospective customer searching for a solution may never encounter that supplier. Not because the company lacks the necessary capabilities, but because an AI-generated comparison has already presented a different set of alternatives. This matters to companies selling logistics and supply chain technology. For years, suppliers have used search optimization, industry research, webinars, customer stories, and digital marketing to reach buyers. Those investments still matter. But AI-generated responses may now shape a buyer’s understanding of the market before that person visits a supplier website or contacts sales. New research from Semrush , published October 21, illustrates the change in Google’s search results. Semrush tracked 400 U.S. desktop commercial keywords in banking, ecommerce, and software from September 2025 through August 2026. Google’s AI Overviews appeared for 88% of these keywords at the end of the study, up from 45.75%. Review searches reached nearly 90% coverage, while ‘best product for a particular use’ searches reached 96.12%. Weighted by estimated search volume, coverage was approximately 97% within the sample. The study measured whether Google displayed AI Overviews, not whether other AI assistants recommended particular suppliers. It did not examine logistics technology specifically or measure clicks or conversions. Even with those limits, it offers a useful signal: AI-generated summaries are becoming a prominent part of commercial software discovery. For suppliers of transportation management systems, warehouse management systems, supply chain planning software, visibility platforms, automation, robotics, and related technologies, the implications deserve attention. Consider a distribution executive evaluating warehouse management software. The first question might concern the best WMS platforms for automated distribution centers, robotics integration, or complex omnichannel fulfillment. Google’s AI Overviews may summarize relevant options within search results; separately, AI assistants can generate their own supplier comparisons. Both can influence which names a buyer investigates, but the Semrush study measured only Google’s Overviews. Smaller suppliers are not necessarily disadvantaged. A specialist may appear when its capabilities closely match the buyer’s requirements, without the marketing budget of a major software company. That opportunity depends on accurate, accessible information. The distinction is important because logistics technology markets are not interchangeable collections of software products. A TMS focused on complex international transportation operates in a different environment from one designed for domestic freight procurement. Warehouse management solutions vary substantially in their ability to support robotics, labor optimization, high-volume fulfillment, and multitenant operations. Planning, visibility, and orchestration platforms may share similar marketing language while addressing very different operational decisions. If an AI system cannot recognize those differences, a supplier’s technical differentiation may disappear within a generalized market description. Much of the discussion about AI visibility focuses on search rankings, keyword strategies, and website optimization. Those considerations matter, but they do not fully address the problem facing enterprise technology suppliers. The deeper issue is whether the information describing your company is accurate, sufficiently detailed, consistent across sources, and useful for evaluating your technology against real operational requirements. Independent market intelligence can help suppliers understand how their capabilities fit within a complex competitive landscape. At ARC Advisory Group, we examine supply chain technology markets, supplier capabilities, adoption patterns, and changing buyer requirements. That work can help suppliers replace broad claims with a more precise market position. Our MarketMap research provides one example. Across categories including transportation management, warehouse management, supply chain planning, autonomous exception management, and decision intelligence, ARC examines supplier capabilities and strategic direction within a structured market framework. These assessments are designed to help technology buyers understand their alternatives while providing suppliers with insight into the markets in which they compete. MarketMap positioning is based on independent research, not purchased placement. ARC’s broader advisory work can help suppliers identify competitive opportunities, test buyer perceptions through voice-of-the-customer research, and assess market entry, product direction, and growth options. Effective communication starts with an accurate view of the market. Product capabilities, customer profiles, buyer priorities, and competitive boundaries should inform the descriptions suppliers use on websites, in technical materials, and in customer discussions. ARC does not determine how Google or another AI platform characterizes a supplier. What rigorous market intelligence can do is help suppliers develop a more defensible and consistent explanation of where their technology fits and why it matters. Logistics Viewpoints provides a complementary channel for market education, executive perspectives, and engagement with professionals evaluating logistics technology and operating strategies. Our coverage concentrates on transportation, warehousing, automation, fulfillment, visibility, logistics software, and the technologies connecting these functions. Suppliers can contribute more than product announcements. A substantive discussion of warehouse automation, for example, should examine facility requirements, WMS integration , labor constraints, throughput economics, deployment complexity, and measurable results. That helps buyers understand the technology, not merely recognize a vendor name. LV offers sponsored webinars, podcasts, executive discussions, and supplier spotlight programs for that kind of market education. When grounded in operating evidence, these formats can support informed buyer conversations and create material that remains useful beyond the initial event. Independent editorial coverage remains distinct from commercial sponsorship. Advertising relationships do not determine editorial conclusions or ARC research assessments, and commercial programs should be clearly identified. That distinction matters because credibility is central to the value of industry information, particularly when buyers and AI systems are attempting to distinguish meaningful technical evidence from promotional claims. Detailed articles, technical discussions, interviews, and presentations can make technology-market information accessible to buyers and potentially to AI systems. Publication, however, does not guarantee citation or inclusion in an AI-generated answer. ARC can help clarify a supplier’s market position and the evidence behind its value proposition. LV can provide industry-facing programs that explain operational problems, demonstrate relevant capabilities, and engage prospective buyers. Visibility is valuable, but visibility that does not lead to understanding or qualified engagement has limited commercial value. Google’s growing use of AI Overviews in commercial searches is one visible part of a broader shift in how buyers find suppliers and interpret markets. Other AI assistants may also influence discovery, although their behavior was not measured in the Semrush study. Supply chain technology purchases will continue to require rigorous assessment. Buyers still need demonstrations, reference checks, integration analysis, implementation planning, and financial justification. No credible AI-generated summary can replace that work. But the information encountered before those formal evaluations begin may increasingly influence which suppliers receive the opportunity to participate. For technology companies, this makes market understanding and communication more closely connected than ever. Competitive differentiation must be technically meaningful, supported by evidence, and explained consistently across the channels buyers use to research the market. ARC’s market research and LV’s industry engagement programs address related but distinct needs: credible competitive understanding and substantive communication with prospective buyers. The question for suppliers is no longer simply whether a prospective customer can find your company online. It is whether, when that customer asks AI which suppliers deserve consideration, your company is part of the answer, and whether the explanation is accurate enough to earn the next conversation. If you are a supply chain technology supplier considering how AI is changing your visibility, competitive positioning, or market engagement strategy, I would welcome a discussion about where ARC and LV can help. Jim Frazer Vice President, Supply Chain Services ARC Advisory Group jfrazer@arcweb.com ARC will put WMS, TMS, Supply Chain Planning, Decision Intelligence, and Autonomous Exception Management on one architectural canvas. See where the boundaries are moving — and what technology buyers should do about it. Independent ARC Advisory Group research and Logistics Viewpoints analysis. Securities and Exchange Commission that it learned of a cyberattack on Wednesday targeting one of its lab testing systems, Quanum, which allows doctor’s offices, hospitals, and healthcare practices to request lab tests for patients while also handling billing.

extraction.body: Medical lab testing giant Quest Diagnostics has confirmed a cyberattack and data breach affecting an as-yet unspecified amount of sensitive patient information stored in its systems, according to a legally required disclosure with U.S. regulators. Quest said in an 8-K filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission that it learned of a cyberattack on Wednesday targeting one of its lab testing systems, Quanum, which allows doctor’s offices, hospitals, and healthcare practices to request lab tests for patients while also handling billing. The platform stores a large amount of patient health and medical records, as well as associated diagnostic and billing data. The company said the unauthorized access included the accessing of “certain patient records.” Quest said it notified law enforcement and is investigating. The cyberattack on Quest is the latest major cyber incident to affect the healthcare industry this year. A series of cyberattacks and data breaches have sparked weeks of disruption and allowed the theft of millions of patient electronic health records and other medical information. Healthtech companies have become a major target for financially motivated cybercriminals, who aim to steal as much sensitive data as possible and threaten to publish it if they aren’t paid a ransom. In recent months, a cyberattack resulted in the mass-wiping of employee devices at medical tech maker Stryker in March, and a hack on medical implant manufacturer Boston Scientific in August forced the company’s network offline for weeks, sparking “global disruption” to its operations. Meanwhile, separate hacks throughout the year caused massive breaches of patient data at medical recordkeeping company CareCloud , Scotland-based healthtech provider Craneware , and U.S. pharmaceutical distribution giant McKesson . The lab-testing giant has not yet said how many healthcare customers, or patients, had information stolen during the attack on its Quanum systems. Quest’s website and materials say Quanum is used by about half a million clinicians in thousands of locations across North America. It’s unclear how many health records Quanum holds, but one 2026 case study on Quest’s website shows how a single health system with more than 6 million patients can hold hundreds of millions of related medical documents and charts. Quest did not say when the breach began or whether any hacking group has contacted the company with demands, such as payment in exchange to not release the stolen data. Amanda Rivera, a spokesperson for Quest, did not answer TechCrunch’s questions about the incident and referred to its security notice . In the notice , Quest said that some patients’ protected health information was taken, including “personal information and patient records,” but the company is still investigating what specific kinds of data were taken. (The website post currently contains “noindex” code , which tells search engines not to list the page in search results, making it far more difficult for people to find the page.) This is Quest’s second known major data breach in a decade, after losing 11.9 million patient records in a cyberattack on a third-party billing company in 2019. Quest said in an 8-K filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission that it learned of a cyberattack on Wednesday targeting one of its lab testing systems, Quanum, which allows doctor’s offices, hospitals, and healthcare practices to request lab tests for patients while also handling billing. sources.title: OpenAI makes its Jev competitor widely available as decision model competition heats up
passages: Public benchmarks like the AIM System One Index and the Artificial Analysis Decision Index tend to favor D1 Ultra, a new decision model that Liquid released last week, and Base Lab’s Elephant-1.
However, TypeSafe’s offerings are, for now, the most widely-queried on OpenRouter.

OpenAI made its Decisions API model widely available to users for the first time, entering the market for fast, cheap intelligence that recently made TypeSafe, a startup founded by a former researcher at the frontier lab, a $7.6 billion company .
In initial trials with customers like Box, Datadog, Ramp, and Speak, engineers used the API to replace OpenAI’s LLMs with higher throughput.
Andrew Hsu, the CTO at Speak, which builds AI language tutors, said the Decisions API allowed the company to cut the time between actions from 1.4 seconds to .13 seconds.

TypeSafe CEO Diogo Almeida distrusts benchmarks and urges people to trial the models in their own work, but even TypeSafe released its own rankings last week alongside the release of its latest Jev model, which includes new features including support for images and smart-if statements.
Felix Wunderlich, the chief growth officer at Opper AI, which built the benchmark, said the classic game “is an interesting test because of its nonstop stream of quick, high-stakes decisions.
At every junction the model must decide where to go in a few hundred milliseconds.”
As these offerings get faster and cheaper, we can expect them to live up to Jev’s namesake, an economist who explained how using a resource more efficiently makes it more ubiquitous.
Or, as Handa sees it, there will be an expanding “crazy set of use cases” that were hiding in plain sight until the decision models revealed them.
Software developers quickly found that these decision or System One models could replace LLMs in a variety of workflows, operating more quickly and a at dramatically lower cost.

extraction.body: OpenAI made its Decisions API model widely available to users for the first time, entering the market for fast, cheap intelligence that recently made TypeSafe, a startup founded by a former researcher at the frontier lab, a $7.6 billion company . TypeSafe’s Jev model created a category for deep learning models that act as super classifiers: Given a set of options, they can quickly make choices and offer a confidence rating in their decision. Software developers quickly found that these decision or System One models could replace LLMs in a variety of workflows, operating more quickly and a at dramatically lower cost. Nikunj Handa, the product lead for OpenAI’s APIs, told TechCrunch that his colleagues saw Jev and said “wow, we we have like a million use cases for this.” Handa’s team sprinted to offer their own version: Rather than building a specifically calibrated decision model, the team took ChatGPT Luna and reconfigured it to speed up the inference and lower the cost. “The big unlock with Decisions API has been the speed, shrinking things from one to three seconds to 100, 120, 180 milliseconds,” Handa said. “In the future, we may sort of like have specific training to make our models like even better in these ways. But right now, it’s just plain old Luna that gets the job done.” Announced at the company’s developer day on September 29, the Decisions API became available to all customers on Thursday. OpenAI added new voice and visual modalities to the public version, and worked to ensure lower latency in regions around the world by targeting its inference resources geographically. In initial trials with customers like Box, Datadog, Ramp, and Speak, engineers used the API to replace OpenAI’s LLMs with higher throughput. Andrew Hsu, the CTO at Speak, which builds AI language tutors, said the Decisions API allowed the company to cut the time between actions from 1.4 seconds to .13 seconds. OpenAI also used the product to improve their Dots voice assistant’s responsiveness. Still, it’s not clear exactly what makes a good decision model, other than “it works for you” — optimization across intelligence, cost, calibration, and speed seems to differ by workload. TypeSafe CEO Diogo Almeida distrusts benchmarks and urges people to trial the models in their own work, but even TypeSafe released its own rankings last week alongside the release of its latest Jev model, which includes new features including support for images and smart-if statements. Public benchmarks like the AIM System One Index and the Artificial Analysis Decision Index tend to favor D1 Ultra, a new decision model that Liquid released last week, and Base Lab’s Elephant-1. The latest Jev model remains competitive on both indices, in seventh and third, with OpenAI’s Decision Model falling eighth and fourteenth, respectively. However, TypeSafe’s offerings are, for now, the most widely-queried on OpenRouter. The most fun Jev benchmark, however, is JevMan , a benchmark where decision models play PacMan; the latest Jev model tops that ranking. Felix Wunderlich, the chief growth officer at Opper AI, which built the benchmark, said the classic game “is an interesting test because of its nonstop stream of quick, high-stakes decisions. At every junction the model must decide where to go in a few hundred milliseconds.” Where OpenAI’s arguably more capable model may have an advantage is in multi-modality—for image classification, “Luna is extremely powerful and has been showing better calibrations,” Handa told TechCrunch, adding that OpenAI customers want the Decisions API to be more flexible about using images as outputs as well. Handa also saw further increases in speed enabling new use cases: “Can we get this to something like you know 60 milliseconds, and then you could imagine like an API like call like for every single frame in like a video?” As these offerings get faster and cheaper, we can expect them to live up to Jev’s namesake, an economist who explained how using a resource more efficiently makes it more ubiquitous. Or, as Handa sees it, there will be an expanding “crazy set of use cases” that were hiding in plain sight until the decision models revealed them.
