sources.title: Is a job guarantee the solution to mass AI unemployment? - The Guardian
passages: Whether a crisis of mass AI-related job loss turns out to be actual or perceived, one policy idea that is attracting growing attention and support could directly mitigate this problem: a job guarantee.
sources.body: Whether a crisis of mass AI-related job loss turns out to be actual or perceived, one policy idea that is attracting growing attention and support could directly mitigate this problem: a job guarantee.

extraction.body: In a preface to his book Capitalism and Freedom, the American economist Milton Friedman famously observed that a crisis can propel once-fringe ideas into the political mainstream. “Only a crisis – actual or perceived – produces real change. When that crisis occurs, the actions that are taken depend on the ideas that are lying around,” he wrote. The job of intellectuals, thinktanks and economists, he argued, is to refine the quality of these ambient ideas, so that good ones are ready when disaster strikes. A chorus of influential voices is now predicting that AI may trigger crises of vast magnitude. Bill Gates has declared that AI will advance so rapidly that within a decade, humans will not be needed “for most things”. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has warned that the technology could cause widespread unemployment within one to five years, eliminating many positions in law, tech, finance and other white-collar professions. Even if these predictions are wrong, investors who bet heavily on the technology may conclude that AI is a bubble, and this in itself could cause a recession and widespread job loss. Whether a crisis of mass AI-related job loss turns out to be actual or perceived, one policy idea that is attracting growing attention and support could directly mitigate this problem: a job guarantee. In its most ambitious form, such a program would ensure that anyone who wants work is guaranteed a meaningful, decently paid job. By creating a public option for employment, its supporters argue, a job guarantee could protect millions of people from the financial and psychological damage of joblessness and mobilize a vast labor force to tackle urgent societal problems, from infrastructure and climate adaptation to elder care and childcare. The concept of a job guarantee has a long history, both as an ideal and an actual policy. Article 23 of the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights states: “Everyone has the right to work, to free choice of employment, to just and favourable conditions of work and to protection against unemployment.” During the Great Depression in the 1930s, Franklin D Roosevelt established the Works Progress Administration (WPA), which employed millions of Americans in ambitious public works projects that constructed roads, bridges, sewers, playing fields and much more. More recently, France , India and Argentina are among the countries that have launched versions of a job guarantee. Though a job guarantee and universal basic income (UBI) are often grouped together, a recent global survey found greater support for job guarantees than UBIs. Polling of Americans by the Democratic strategist David Shor also shows the same pattern , with greater support for the creation of well-paid jobs than for direct income support. This makes sense, the venture capitalist and civic activist Nick Hanauer said, because “jobs represent so much more than income in human societies. They represent connection and dignity and enfranchisement and participation.” Algernon Austin, director for race and economic justice at the Center for Economic and Policy Research, agreed: “A job guarantee is significantly preferable to UBI because work is more than just income. When you have a job, you gain work experience and you gain skills and you gain a network.” Calculating the cost of a job guarantee depends on a holistic assessment of its impacts. During a US Senate hearing on affordability in June, John Kennedy, a Republican senator for Louisiana, suggested that a job guarantee would cost trillions of dollars and was impossible. When Dr Julie Margetta Morgan, president of the public policy thinktank the Century Foundation, told Kennedy that she supported a federal job guarantee, he replied : “Do you believe in the Easter bunny?” Economists who study job guarantees see the calculation of costs and benefits differently. Max Kasy, a professor of economics at Oxford who has studied a recent job guarantee experiment in Austria, said that while the wages a job guarantee pays participants comprise a cost, such programs also save money in multiple ways. “The cost saving comes from the fact that you don’t have to pay unemployment benefits, or maybe disability benefits or early retirement benefits. Then people who are working pay taxes and make social insurance contributions, so that’s additional revenue for the state. And then they hopefully do something that’s actually useful for society,” he said. Participants in the job guarantee experiment in Austria also experienced social and psychological benefits . While the monetary value of greater wellbeing may be hard to quantify, such intangibles are crucial, according to Pavlina Tcherneva, a professor of economics at Bard College. “Providing a good job to a person is absolutely transformative,” she said. Factoring in the costs of health problems that come from precarious unemployment and long-term unemployment, she added, makes the policy even more attractive, saying: “It’s not only affordable, it’s an investment.” In September, the US representative Ayanna Pressley, a Democrat from Massachusetts, reintroduced a congressional resolution calling for the creation of a federal job guarantee, something she first proposed in 2021. Her proposal would create a federally funded but locally administered job guarantee that pays participants at least $25 an hour, with regular adjustments to reflect the rising cost of living. The jobs would include a range of sectors, such as emergency preparedness, relief and recovery after natural disasters, care for children and seniors, and public art projects modelled on the WPA’s popular Federal Art Project. Another recent proposal would directly tax AI companies to fund a federal job guarantee. The plan, which is supported by Democratic US representatives Greg Casar of Texas, Valerie Foushee of North Carolina and Sara Jacobs of California, would tax large AI companies on whatever was higher: the value of their “tokens” – units of data used in AI models – or their revenue from AI products. If the unemployment rate rose, the tax rate would increase. “AI CEOs are openly predicting their technology could put millions of Americans out of work, and our government is doing nothing to save jobs and protect working people,” Casar said in a written statement. In Cleveland, Ohio, a non-profit called Universal Basic Employment (UBE) is launching a small pilot study with a cohort of five workers who drive vans at a transportation company. Rather than create new jobs from scratch, the program subsidizes the wages of existing private-sector jobs in a way that benefits both workers and employers, according to Devin Cotten, founder and CEO of UBE. Cotten and his team wanted workers to make what they call an autonomous wage – the pay level at which people are no longer eligible for most social safety net benefits. In Cleveland, that was just over $27 per hour. At a cost of almost half a million dollars for one year, UBE’s pilot will split that $27 figure with employers. The drivers currently make about $15 an hour, so the employer will save money, and the workers will get a sizable raise. The program is not meant to replace other forms of assistance such as housing vouchers, Cotten said. But workers receiving more money as wages, rather than as a siloed benefit, can build their credit, perhaps qualify for a mortgage and also keep dollars circulating in the local economy, helping to revitalize poor neighborhoods. Such a model may even attract a broader base of political support. “Work is a shared value across political lines,” Cotten said. “I think crafting a solution based on work allows us to be a bipartisan solution.”

Bill Gates has declared that AI will advance so rapidly that within a decade, humans will not be needed “for most things”. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has warned that the technology could cause widespread unemployment within one to five years, eliminating many positions in law, tech, finance and other white-collar professions. Even if these predictions are wrong, investors who bet heavily on the technology may conclude that AI is a bubble, and this in itself could cause a recession and widespread job loss.

Whether a crisis of mass AI-related job loss turns out to be actual or perceived, one policy idea that is attracting growing attention and support could directly mitigate this problem: a job guarantee.

In its most ambitious form, such a program would ensure that anyone who wants work is guaranteed a meaningful, decently paid job. By creating a public option for employment, its supporters argue, a job guarantee could protect millions of people from the financial and psychological damage of joblessness and mobilize a vast labor force to tackle urgent societal problems, from infrastructure and climate adaptation to elder care and childcare.

The concept of a job guarantee has a long history, both as an ideal and an actual policy. Article 23 of the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights states: “Everyone has the right to work, to free choice of employment, to just and favourable conditions of work and to protection against unemployment.” During the Great Depression in the 1930s, Franklin D Roosevelt established the Works Progress Administration (WPA), which employed millions of Americans in ambitious public works projects that constructed roads, bridges, sewers, playing fields and much more. More recently, France , India and Argentina are among the countries that have launched versions of a job guarantee.

Though a job guarantee and universal basic income (UBI) are often grouped together, a recent global survey found greater support for job guarantees than UBIs. Polling of Americans by the Democratic strategist David Shor also shows the same pattern , with greater support for the creation of well-paid jobs than for direct income support. This makes sense, the venture capitalist and civic activist Nick Hanauer said, because “jobs represent so much more than income in human societies. They represent connection and dignity and enfranchisement and participation.”

Algernon Austin, director for race and economic justice at the Center for Economic and Policy Research, agreed: “A job guarantee is significantly preferable to UBI because work is more than just income. When you have a job, you gain work experience and you gain skills and you gain a network.”

Calculating the cost of a job guarantee depends on a holistic assessment of its impacts. During a US Senate hearing on affordability in June, John Kennedy, a Republican senator for Louisiana, suggested that a job guarantee would cost trillions of dollars and was impossible. When Dr Julie Margetta Morgan, president of the public policy thinktank the Century Foundation, told Kennedy that she supported a federal job guarantee, he replied : “Do you believe in the Easter bunny?”

Economists who study job guarantees see the calculation of costs and benefits differently. Max Kasy, a professor of economics at Oxford who has studied a recent job guarantee experiment in Austria, said that while the wages a job guarantee pays participants comprise a cost, such programs also save money in multiple ways.

“The cost saving comes from the fact that you don’t have to pay unemployment benefits, or maybe disability benefits or early retirement benefits. Then people who are working pay taxes and make social insurance contributions, so that’s additional revenue for the state. And then they hopefully do something that’s actually useful for society,” he said.

Participants in the job guarantee experiment in Austria also experienced social and psychological benefits . While the monetary value of greater wellbeing may be hard to quantify, such intangibles are crucial, according to Pavlina Tcherneva, a professor of economics at Bard College.

“Providing a good job to a person is absolutely transformative,” she said. Factoring in the costs of health problems that come from precarious unemployment and long-term unemployment, she added, makes the policy even more attractive, saying: “It’s not only affordable, it’s an investment.”

In September, the US representative Ayanna Pressley, a Democrat from Massachusetts, reintroduced a congressional resolution calling for the creation of a federal job guarantee, something she first proposed in 2021. Her proposal would create a federally funded but locally administered job guarantee that pays participants at least $25 an hour, with regular adjustments to reflect the rising cost of living. The jobs would include a range of sectors, such as emergency preparedness, relief and recovery after natural disasters, care for children and seniors, and public art projects modelled on the WPA’s popular Federal Art Project.

Another recent proposal would directly tax AI companies to fund a federal job guarantee. The plan, which is supported by Democratic US representatives Greg Casar of Texas, Valerie Foushee of North Carolina and Sara Jacobs of California, would tax large AI companies on whatever was higher: the value of their “tokens” – units of data used in AI models – or their revenue from AI products.

If the unemployment rate rose, the tax rate would increase. “AI CEOs are openly predicting their technology could put millions of Americans out of work, and our government is doing nothing to save jobs and protect working people,” Casar said in a written statement.

In Cleveland, Ohio, a non-profit called Universal Basic Employment (UBE) is launching a small pilot study with a cohort of five workers who drive vans at a transportation company. Rather than create new jobs from scratch, the program subsidizes the wages of existing private-sector jobs in a way that benefits both workers and employers, according to Devin Cotten, founder and CEO of UBE.

Cotten and his team wanted workers to make what they call an autonomous wage – the pay level at which people are no longer eligible for most social safety net benefits. In Cleveland, that was just over $27 per hour. At a cost of almost half a million dollars for one year, UBE’s pilot will split that $27 figure with employers. The drivers currently make about $15 an hour, so the employer will save money, and the workers will get a sizable raise.

The program is not meant to replace other forms of assistance such as housing vouchers, Cotten said. But workers receiving more money as wages, rather than as a siloed benefit, can build their credit, perhaps qualify for a mortgage and also keep dollars circulating in the local economy, helping to revitalize poor neighborhoods.

Such a model may even attract a broader base of political support. “Work is a shared value across political lines,” Cotten said. “I think crafting a solution based on work allows us to be a bipartisan solution.”

sources.title: SpaceX’s mobile carrier push reportedly involves tapping into 80,000 cell sites
passages: SpaceX is planning to access at least 80,000 cell sites as part of efforts to compete directly with Verizon, T-Mobile, and AT&T, according to a report from Bloomberg.

Earlier this month, SpaceX acquired a portfolio of low-band spectrum licenses, while also receiving FCC approval to deploy 15,000 upgraded V2 Starlink Mobile satellites — moves the company says will “pave the way” for Starlink Mobile to become a “major” carrier in the US.

When asked about a potential partnership with SpaceX, Amazon, or other satellite services during an earnings call on Wednesday, Crown Castle CEO Chris Hillabrant said, “I don’t think I want to get into customer-specific detail, but you can assume that we’re talking to all parties.” SpaceX plans to pair a network of cell towers with its constellation of direct-to-cell satellites.
Sources tell the publication that SpaceX is in talks with Crown Castle Inc., one of the nation’s largest cell tower owners.

When asked about a potential partnership with SpaceX, Amazon, or other satellite services during an earnings call on Wednesday, Crown Castle CEO Chris Hillabrant said, “I don’t think I want to get into customer-specific detail, but you can assume that we’re talking to all parties.” SpaceX plans to pair a network of cell towers with its constellation of direct-to-cell satellites. Sources tell the publication that SpaceX is in talks with Crown Castle Inc., one of the nation’s largest cell tower owners.

extraction.body: “We believe Canada should be able to reach orbit on its own terms.” Welcome to Edition 9.16 of the Rocket Report! Lots of SpaceX-related news this week including a couple of Thursday shockers. In one story, the company told the US Space Force thanks, but no thanks after being offered three military launch contracts. Then, on the civil space side of things, SpaceX’s Starship may required up to 22 refuelings to support a lunar landing, a NASA safety panel said. As always, we welcome reader submissions , and if you don’t want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar. Miura 5 getting closer to launch . PLD Space says its Miura 5 rocket, due to undertake its inaugural launch next year, is nearing final integration, Aviation Week reports . The rocket is one of three Miura 5s the company has already manufactured, with the other two designed to qualify key system elements, CEO Raúl Torres said in an October 19 program update. PLD Space now targets a first flight of the small-lift vehicle before mid-2027. Fully integrated stage … “Manufacturing these three vehicles has allowed our teams to work continuously across different stages of production and integration, applying the lessons learned from each qualification campaign directly to the launch vehicle,” Torres said. One Miura 5 second stage is now fully integrated to kick off system-level testing under representative operating conditions. The second stage is at PLD’s Teruel test facility for its qualification campaign, including wet dress rehearsal and a static hot-fire test. Reaction Dynamics seeks to raise $350 million . One of three prominent Canadian launch startups, Reaction Dynamics, said it is seeking to raise $350 million to grow its staff from 68 to more than 350 people, spaceQ reports . The company is developing the small-lift Aurora rocket, which Reaction Dynamics hopes will reach orbit in 2028. Reaction Dynamics also announced plans to build a medium-lift rocket, Borealis, for a debut by 2031. You’ve got the aurora, and the borealis … With a lift capacity of 6 tons to low-Earth orbit, Borealis would carry a little under half of the advertised payload capacity of Rocket Lab’s Neutron vehicle. “We founded Reaction Dynamics because we believe Canada should be able to reach orbit on its own terms,” the company’s founder and chief executive, Bachar Elzein, said. “Aurora is how we get to orbit in 2028. Borealis is how we deliver sovereign access to orbit, at scale, by 2031.” Both of the dates appear to be highly aspirational, but we wish them luck. Rocket Lab sets next Electron launch date . After 97 launches of Electron, it is not exactly news that Rocket Lab is preparing for its 98th launch of the vehicle. The mission , launching three HAWK satellites for the constellation operator HawkEye 360, is due to launch as early as 07:00 UTC on Friday, October 23. So why are you writing about it ? … Two reasons. First of all, it’s worth noting that Rocket Lab continues to be only the second company to develop and frequently fly a purely commercial rocket. Secondly, we love the name of the mission, “We’re Not Hawking Around.” Kudos to the Rocket Lab team for keeping launch fun and fresh, even after moving through dozens of launches. SpaceX says no thanks to Space Force launches . The Space Force recently tried to book rides for three future satellite missions, but SpaceX declined to offer its services, Politico reports . No other rocket companies offered to take them either, the publication reported. A top Space Force official, Brig. Gen. Eric Zarybnisky, the acting portfolio acquisition executive, acknowledged growing pains for the government and space industry as demand for rockets increases. “Temporarily, there are some things we’ll need to work through, again, as we get new providers flying,” he said. SpaceX has been declining to sign new Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy launch contracts for all kinds of customers. No one else has capacity … The three Space Force missions that didn’t find a ride were listed through the National Security Space Launch initiative. Two of the missions were for the Space Development Agency. The agency is a branch of the Space Force that’s building a network of hundreds of military satellites in low-Earth orbit to provide expanded data services, and missile warning and tracking capabilities. Other potential launch providers, United Launch Alliance and Blue Origin, are both working through setbacks with their launch vehicles. Zarybnisky remained optimistic that Blue Origin and ULA will work through their technical problems and that new competitors will get up and running in time. Who will win the medium-lift launch race ? It has been 13 years since the debut of a new medium-lift rocket in the United States, the Antares vehicle developed by Orbital Sciences Corporation. Nearly a decade and a half later, there is a new generation of medium-lift vehicles coming online, and they are starkly different from Antares, which had not just Russian engines but a core stage manufactured in Ukraine. Which comes first … In a new article, Ars updates the status of four medium-lift rockets under development in the United States: Stoke Space’s Nova, Relativity Space’s Terran R, Rocket Lab’s Neutron, and the Eclipse vehicle being built by Firefly and Northrop Grumman. The publication also (somewhat hazardously) predicts the order in which the four rockets will make their debut. Japanese rocket launches historic Phobos mission . Japan launched a $578 million mission Monday on a five-year expedition to land on the largest moon of Mars and retrieve samples for return to Earth, Ars reports . The robotic Martian Moons eXploration mission, known as MMX, lifted off at 3:41 pm EDT Monday (4:41 am Japan Standard Time Tuesday) from Tanegashima Space Center in southern Japan. This has been tried before … The MMX spacecraft rode into orbit atop a 207-foot-tall (63-meter) H3 rocket, Japan’s flagship launch vehicle. The rocket assigned to MMX debuted a new souped-up configuration with four strap-on solid rocket boosters, full-throttle main engines, and an extended payload shroud to accommodate the demands of Japan’s heaviest and most ambitious interplanetary mission to date. MMX is not the first mission to attempt a sample return from Phobos. Russia’s Phobos-Grunt sample return mission failed soon after launch in 2011, before it could set off for Mars. (submitted by tsunam) Chinese rocket debris found in Midwest . In September, a Chinese rocket took off from a remote spaceport in the Gobi Desert, released 10 satellites into orbit, then reignited its engine and put itself on a trajectory to rain down debris over the American Midwest, Ars reports . The rocket’s flight on September 15 lasted between 75 and 80 minutes, and it came down without completing a full orbit of the Earth. Social media posts at the time showed streaks of fiery debris falling from the sky, heading north over Kansas toward Minnesota. The overnight spectacle was also visible on the western horizon from Wisconsin. A surprising find … The exact time, location, and direction of the debris allowed experts to connect it to the launch of a Zhuque-2E rocket, a medium-lift vehicle built by a Chinese company called LandSpace. The rocket had launched from Dongfeng, a commercial launch zone co-located with the military-run Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China, less than two hours before. The incident was largely forgotten until the last few days, when a farmer in rural Minnesota discovered a circular metal object about 11 feet in diameter lay amid the forest of corn stalks. Arianespace targets Nov. 23 return for Ariane 6 . Arianespace has announced that the next Ariane 6 launch will take place no earlier than November 23, marking the rocket’s return to flight after ground testing reportedly revealed an issue with one of its turbopumps, European Spaceflight reports . The flight will carry 36 Amazon Leo satellites aboard an Ariane 64, the rocket’s four-booster configuration. It will be the fifth Ariane 6 flight of 2026 and the tenth since the rocket’s inaugural flight in July 2024. Situation is on track … Arianespace’s new announcement follows a report from French newspaper La Tribune, published a day earlier, claiming ArianeGroup had resolved an anomaly affecting a liquid hydrogen turbopump that had disrupted the rocket’s launch schedule. According to the report, the anomaly was first detected during an engine acceptance test shortly before the start of summer. Asked by European Spaceflight to comment on the report, an ArianeGroup spokesperson declined to address it directly and instead pointed to the newly announced launch date. “The next launch has been announced today, so the situation is on track.” How many Starships will be required for a lunar landing ? On Thursday, the NASA Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel held its quarterly meeting, during which panel member Charlie Precourt (a former NASA astronaut) spoke about risks associated with the Artemis Program and landing humans on the Moon, Ars reports . One of these is the number of refuelings required to support a Starship lunar landing. Uncertainty remains … “With respect to Artemis IV, however, we’ve got a large number of firsts that reduce the likelihood of mission success,” Precourt said. “We need to keep our eyes on numerous required fuelings for the lander. I think the last estimate is around 22 flights.” In response to this, SpaceX founder Elon Musk replied that NASA’s safety panel estimate was not accurate. “That’s way too high,” Musk said. “Actual number will be more like 6 to 8.” SpaceX will attempt a rocket and upper stage catch . It has been a little more than three weeks since the 14th test flight of the massive Starship rocket, which largely went well despite some issues with the Raptor rocket engine. SpaceX has gleaned enough data from that test to attempt a catch of both the Super Heavy first stage of the rocket and the Starship upper stage on the next flight, Ars reports . SpaceX founder Elon Musk said he believes success is “more likely than not” for these attempts, but he added the company is hardware rich if there are failures. Working with the FAA … Both catches would happen at the company’s launch site in South Texas, Starbase. SpaceX is currently targeting November for this 15th test flight. One of the big hurdles is regulatory, as the Starship vehicle must return to the launch site over land, including northern Mexico. “We have had significant constructive engagement with the FAA, and we expect the license for our Flight 15 to include return to launch site and tower catch for both stages,” SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell said. Blue Origin goes bigger on New Glenn . Blue Origin announced a major expansion of its already considerable Florida launch facilities last Friday with the intent of eventually flying more than 100 rockets a year from there, Ars reports . The company said it would add two launch pads for the New Glenn rocket, in addition to two already under construction at Cape Canaveral. The company is also investing heavily in a new manufacturing facility that will produce up to 150 upper stages for a larger variant of the New Glenn rocket. More missions … The company also plans to procure two additional landing ships to catch and return the first stage of the New Glenn rocket (it currently has one, named Jacklyn). Finally, Blue Origin said it would add a new customer integration facility, built in conjunction with the US Space Force, that will feature four payload bays to process multiple missions at the same time. “These investments are centered on one goal: building the capacity to support more missions, more reliably, and more efficiently,” said Ian Richardson, senior vice president of operations at Blue Origin. October 23 : Electron | We’re Not Hawking Around | Māhia Peninsula, New Zealand | 07:00 UTC

extraction.body: “We believe Canada should be able to reach orbit on its own terms.” Welcome to Edition 9.16 of the Rocket Report! Lots of SpaceX-related news this week including a couple of Thursday shockers. In one story, the company told the US Space Force thanks, but no thanks after being offered three military launch contracts. Then, on the civil space side of things, SpaceX’s Starship may required up to 22 refuelings to support a lunar landing, a NASA safety panel said. As always, we welcome reader submissions , and if you don’t want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar. Miura 5 getting closer to launch . PLD Space says its Miura 5 rocket, due to undertake its inaugural launch next year, is nearing final integration, Aviation Week reports . The rocket is one of three Miura 5s the company has already manufactured, with the other two designed to qualify key system elements, CEO Raúl Torres said in an October 19 program update. PLD Space now targets a first flight of the small-lift vehicle before mid-2027. Fully integrated stage … “Manufacturing these three vehicles has allowed our teams to work continuously across different stages of production and integration, applying the lessons learned from each qualification campaign directly to the launch vehicle,” Torres said. One Miura 5 second stage is now fully integrated to kick off system-level testing under representative operating conditions. The second stage is at PLD’s Teruel test facility for its qualification campaign, including wet dress rehearsal and a static hot-fire test. Reaction Dynamics seeks to raise $350 million . One of three prominent Canadian launch startups, Reaction Dynamics, said it is seeking to raise $350 million to grow its staff from 68 to more than 350 people, spaceQ reports . The company is developing the small-lift Aurora rocket, which Reaction Dynamics hopes will reach orbit in 2028. Reaction Dynamics also announced plans to build a medium-lift rocket, Borealis, for a debut by 2031. You’ve got the aurora, and the borealis … With a lift capacity of 6 tons to low-Earth orbit, Borealis would carry a little under half of the advertised payload capacity of Rocket Lab’s Neutron vehicle. “We founded Reaction Dynamics because we believe Canada should be able to reach orbit on its own terms,” the company’s founder and chief executive, Bachar Elzein, said. “Aurora is how we get to orbit in 2028. Borealis is how we deliver sovereign access to orbit, at scale, by 2031.” Both of the dates appear to be highly aspirational, but we wish them luck. Rocket Lab sets next Electron launch date . After 97 launches of Electron, it is not exactly news that Rocket Lab is preparing for its 98th launch of the vehicle. The mission , launching three HAWK satellites for the constellation operator HawkEye 360, is due to launch as early as 07:00 UTC on Friday, October 23. So why are you writing about it ? … Two reasons. First of all, it’s worth noting that Rocket Lab continues to be only the second company to develop and frequently fly a purely commercial rocket. Secondly, we love the name of the mission, “We’re Not Hawking Around.” Kudos to the Rocket Lab team for keeping launch fun and fresh, even after moving through dozens of launches. SpaceX says no thanks to Space Force launches . The Space Force recently tried to book rides for three future satellite missions, but SpaceX declined to offer its services, Politico reports . No other rocket companies offered to take them either, the publication reported. A top Space Force official, Brig. Gen. Eric Zarybnisky, the acting portfolio acquisition executive, acknowledged growing pains for the government and space industry as demand for rockets increases. “Temporarily, there are some things we’ll need to work through, again, as we get new providers flying,” he said. SpaceX has been declining to sign new Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy launch contracts for all kinds of customers. No one else has capacity … The three Space Force missions that didn’t find a ride were listed through the National Security Space Launch initiative. Two of the missions were for the Space Development Agency. The agency is a branch of the Space Force that’s building a network of hundreds of military satellites in low-Earth orbit to provide expanded data services, and missile warning and tracking capabilities. Other potential launch providers, United Launch Alliance and Blue Origin, are both working through setbacks with their launch vehicles. Zarybnisky remained optimistic that Blue Origin and ULA will work through their technical problems and that new competitors will get up and running in time. Who will win the medium-lift launch race ? It has been 13 years since the debut of a new medium-lift rocket in the United States, the Antares vehicle developed by Orbital Sciences Corporation. Nearly a decade and a half later, there is a new generation of medium-lift vehicles coming online, and they are starkly different from Antares, which had not just Russian engines but a core stage manufactured in Ukraine. Which comes first … In a new article, Ars updates the status of four medium-lift rockets under development in the United States: Stoke Space’s Nova, Relativity Space’s Terran R, Rocket Lab’s Neutron, and the Eclipse vehicle being built by Firefly and Northrop Grumman. The publication also (somewhat hazardously) predicts the order in which the four rockets will make their debut. Japanese rocket launches historic Phobos mission . Japan launched a $578 million mission Monday on a five-year expedition to land on the largest moon of Mars and retrieve samples for return to Earth, Ars reports . The robotic Martian Moons eXploration mission, known as MMX, lifted off at 3:41 pm EDT Monday (4:41 am Japan Standard Time Tuesday) from Tanegashima Space Center in southern Japan. This has been tried before … The MMX spacecraft rode into orbit atop a 207-foot-tall (63-meter) H3 rocket, Japan’s flagship launch vehicle. The rocket assigned to MMX debuted a new souped-up configuration with four strap-on solid rocket boosters, full-throttle main engines, and an extended payload shroud to accommodate the demands of Japan’s heaviest and most ambitious interplanetary mission to date. MMX is not the first mission to attempt a sample return from Phobos. Russia’s Phobos-Grunt sample return mission failed soon after launch in 2011, before it could set off for Mars. (submitted by tsunam) Chinese rocket debris found in Midwest . In September, a Chinese rocket took off from a remote spaceport in the Gobi Desert, released 10 satellites into orbit, then reignited its engine and put itself on a trajectory to rain down debris over the American Midwest, Ars reports . The rocket’s flight on September 15 lasted between 75 and 80 minutes, and it came down without completing a full orbit of the Earth. Social media posts at the time showed streaks of fiery debris falling from the sky, heading north over Kansas toward Minnesota. The overnight spectacle was also visible on the western horizon from Wisconsin. A surprising find … The exact time, location, and direction of the debris allowed experts to connect it to the launch of a Zhuque-2E rocket, a medium-lift vehicle built by a Chinese company called LandSpace. The rocket had launched from Dongfeng, a commercial launch zone co-located with the military-run Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China, less than two hours before. The incident was largely forgotten until the last few days, when a farmer in rural Minnesota discovered a circular metal object about 11 feet in diameter lay amid the forest of corn stalks. Arianespace targets Nov. 23 return for Ariane 6 . Arianespace has announced that the next Ariane 6 launch will take place no earlier than November 23, marking the rocket’s return to flight after ground testing reportedly revealed an issue with one of its turbopumps, European Spaceflight reports . The flight will carry 36 Amazon Leo satellites aboard an Ariane 64, the rocket’s four-booster configuration. It will be the fifth Ariane 6 flight of 2026 and the tenth since the rocket’s inaugural flight in July 2024. Situation is on track … Arianespace’s new announcement follows a report from French newspaper La Tribune, published a day earlier, claiming ArianeGroup had resolved an anomaly affecting a liquid hydrogen turbopump that had disrupted the rocket’s launch schedule. According to the report, the anomaly was first detected during an engine acceptance test shortly before the start of summer. Asked by European Spaceflight to comment on the report, an ArianeGroup spokesperson declined to address it directly and instead pointed to the newly announced launch date. “The next launch has been announced today, so the situation is on track.” How many Starships will be required for a lunar landing ? On Thursday, the NASA Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel held its quarterly meeting, during which panel member Charlie Precourt (a former NASA astronaut) spoke about risks associated with the Artemis Program and landing humans on the Moon, Ars reports . One of these is the number of refuelings required to support a Starship lunar landing. Uncertainty remains … “With respect to Artemis IV, however, we’ve got a large number of firsts that reduce the likelihood of mission success,” Precourt said. “We need to keep our eyes on numerous required fuelings for the lander. I think the last estimate is around 22 flights.” In response to this, SpaceX founder Elon Musk replied that NASA’s safety panel estimate was not accurate. “That’s way too high,” Musk said. “Actual number will be more like 6 to 8.” SpaceX will attempt a rocket and upper stage catch . It has been a little more than three weeks since the 14th test flight of the massive Starship rocket, which largely went well despite some issues with the Raptor rocket engine. SpaceX has gleaned enough data from that test to attempt a catch of both the Super Heavy first stage of the rocket and the Starship upper stage on the next flight, Ars reports . SpaceX founder Elon Musk said he believes success is “more likely than not” for these attempts, but he added the company is hardware rich if there are failures. Working with the FAA … Both catches would happen at the company’s launch site in South Texas, Starbase. SpaceX is currently targeting November for this 15th test flight. One of the big hurdles is regulatory, as the Starship vehicle must return to the launch site over land, including northern Mexico. “We have had significant constructive engagement with the FAA, and we expect the license for our Flight 15 to include return to launch site and tower catch for both stages,” SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell said. Blue Origin goes bigger on New Glenn . Blue Origin announced a major expansion of its already considerable Florida launch facilities last Friday with the intent of eventually flying more than 100 rockets a year from there, Ars reports . The company said it would add two launch pads for the New Glenn rocket, in addition to two already under construction at Cape Canaveral. The company is also investing heavily in a new manufacturing facility that will produce up to 150 upper stages for a larger variant of the New Glenn rocket. More missions … The company also plans to procure two additional landing ships to catch and return the first stage of the New Glenn rocket (it currently has one, named Jacklyn). Finally, Blue Origin said it would add a new customer integration facility, built in conjunction with the US Space Force, that will feature four payload bays to process multiple missions at the same time. “These investments are centered on one goal: building the capacity to support more missions, more reliably, and more efficiently,” said Ian Richardson, senior vice president of operations at Blue Origin. October 23 : Electron | We’re Not Hawking Around | Māhia Peninsula, New Zealand | 07:00 UTC

In September, a Chinese rocket took off from a remote spaceport in the Gobi Desert, released 10 satellites into orbit, then reignited its engine and put itself on a trajectory to rain down debris over the American Midwest, Ars reports . The rocket’s flight on September 15 lasted between 75 and 80 minutes, and it came down without completing a full orbit of the Earth. Social media posts at the time showed streaks of fiery debris falling from the sky, heading north over Kansas toward Minnesota. The overnight spectacle was also visible on the western horizon from Wisconsin.

A surprising find … The exact time, location, and direction of the debris allowed experts to connect it to the launch of a Zhuque-2E rocket, a medium-lift vehicle built by a Chinese company called LandSpace. The rocket had launched from Dongfeng, a commercial launch zone co-located with the military-run Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China, less than two hours before. The incident was largely forgotten until the last few days, when a farmer in rural Minnesota discovered a circular metal object about 11 feet in diameter lay amid the forest of corn stalks.

Arianespace targets Nov. 23 return for Ariane 6 . Arianespace has announced that the next Ariane 6 launch will take place no earlier than November 23, marking the rocket’s return to flight after ground testing reportedly revealed an issue with one of its turbopumps, European Spaceflight reports . The flight will carry 36 Amazon Leo satellites aboard an Ariane 64, the rocket’s four-booster configuration. It will be the fifth Ariane 6 flight of 2026 and the tenth since the rocket’s inaugural flight in July 2024.

Situation is on track … Arianespace’s new announcement follows a report from French newspaper La Tribune, published a day earlier, claiming ArianeGroup had resolved an anomaly affecting a liquid hydrogen turbopump that had disrupted the rocket’s launch schedule. According to the report, the anomaly was first detected during an engine acceptance test shortly before the start of summer. Asked by European Spaceflight to comment on the report, an ArianeGroup spokesperson declined to address it directly and instead pointed to the newly announced launch date. “The next launch has been announced today, so the situation is on track.”

How many Starships will be required for a lunar landing ? On Thursday, the NASA Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel held its quarterly meeting, during which panel member Charlie Precourt (a former NASA astronaut) spoke about risks associated with the Artemis Program and landing humans on the Moon, Ars reports . One of these is the number of refuelings required to support a Starship lunar landing.

Uncertainty remains … “With respect to Artemis IV, however, we’ve got a large number of firsts that reduce the likelihood of mission success,” Precourt said. “We need to keep our eyes on numerous required fuelings for the lander. I think the last estimate is around 22 flights.” In response to this, SpaceX founder Elon Musk replied that NASA’s safety panel estimate was not accurate. “That’s way too high,” Musk said. “Actual number will be more like 6 to 8.”

SpaceX will attempt a rocket and upper stage catch . It has been a little more than three weeks since the 14th test flight of the massive Starship rocket, which largely went well despite some issues with the Raptor rocket engine. SpaceX has gleaned enough data from that test to attempt a catch of both the Super Heavy first stage of the rocket and the Starship upper stage on the next flight, Ars reports . SpaceX founder Elon Musk said he believes success is “more likely than not” for these attempts, but he added the company is hardware rich if there are failures.

Working with the FAA … Both catches would happen at the company’s launch site in South Texas, Starbase. SpaceX is currently targeting November for this 15th test flight. One of the big hurdles is regulatory, as the Starship vehicle must return to the launch site over land, including northern Mexico. “We have had significant constructive engagement with the FAA, and we expect the license for our Flight 15 to include return to launch site and tower catch for both stages,” SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell said.

Blue Origin goes bigger on New Glenn . Blue Origin announced a major expansion of its already considerable Florida launch facilities last Friday with the intent of eventually flying more than 100 rockets a year from there, Ars reports . The company said it would add two launch pads for the New Glenn rocket, in addition to two already under construction at Cape Canaveral. The company is also investing heavily in a new manufacturing facility that will produce up to 150 upper stages for a larger variant of the New Glenn rocket.

More missions … The company also plans to procure two additional landing ships to catch and return the first stage of the New Glenn rocket (it currently has one, named Jacklyn). Finally, Blue Origin said it would add a new customer integration facility, built in conjunction with the US Space Force, that will feature four payload bays to process multiple missions at the same time. “These investments are centered on one goal: building the capacity to support more missions, more reliably, and more efficiently,” said Ian Richardson, senior vice president of operations at Blue Origin.

sources.title: Etsy bans AI-generated recipes and patterns from its online marketplace - CNBC
passages: Etsy said Thursday it will no longer allow merchants to sell AI-generated recipes and patterns on its online marketplace, as part of a wider push to set firmer rules around the use of artificial intelligence on its platform.
Misleading, AI-generated products or images present a new challenge for Etsy and other online marketplaces.
The products are usually marketed as digital downloads, such as crochet or sewing patterns.
Users then "put in effort to achieve a finished product," the company said.
"Today, many active buyers say they can't tell which items involve AI-generated content," the company wrote.
"It's become a top-three barrier to shopping more often on Etsy.

And you, our seller community, have told us you're concerned about your work appearing alongside items that use AI in misleading ways, and that it's becoming harder for buyers to recognize your role in creating your items."
Sellers will also be required to include at least one unedited photo of the actual item they're selling.
Founded in 2005, Etsy is known for its mix of craft makers and artisan goods.

The company has been leaning more into that reputation as it has battled an influx of generic, mass-produced items from resellers and increasing competition from Amazon and Walmart , as well as newer e-commerce upstarts like TikTok, Temu and Shein.
Etsy said in a separate notice to sellers that it was making the changes as AI threatens to erode buyers' and sellers' trust in the platform.
Etsy has also partnered with OpenAI on shopping features, including launching a ChatGPT app for product discovery.

extraction.body: Etsy said Thursday it will no longer allow merchants to sell AI-generated recipes and patterns on its online marketplace, as part of a wider push to set firmer rules around the use of artificial intelligence on its platform. In a blog post , Etsy said it's banning the sale of "functional guides" that are created using AI, including patterns, cooking recipes and instructions. The products are usually marketed as digital downloads, such as crochet or sewing patterns. Users then "put in effort to achieve a finished product," the company said. Sellers will also be required to show an actual item made using the instructions, not an AI-generated or simulated result, "so buyers know what to expect," Etsy said. Etsy said in a separate notice to sellers that it was making the changes as AI threatens to erode buyers' and sellers' trust in the platform. "Today, many active buyers say they can't tell which items involve AI-generated content," the company wrote. "It's become a top-three barrier to shopping more often on Etsy. And you, our seller community, have told us you're concerned about your work appearing alongside items that use AI in misleading ways, and that it's becoming harder for buyers to recognize your role in creating your items." As part of the move, Etsy said it's barring sellers from creating bot-generated listings without any human involvement. Sellers will also be required to include at least one unedited photo of the actual item they're selling. Etsy told sellers it will continue to allow AI-generated art on its platform as long as merchants "play a clear role in what they create and are transparent about the process." "Sellers must still disclose when an item is created using AI and cannot misrepresent AI-generated work as handmade or entirely their own creation," the company added. Founded in 2005, Etsy is known for its mix of craft makers and artisan goods. The company has been leaning more into that reputation as it has battled an influx of generic, mass-produced items from resellers and increasing competition from Amazon and Walmart , as well as newer e-commerce upstarts like TikTok, Temu and Shein. Misleading, AI-generated products or images present a new challenge for Etsy and other online marketplaces. Etsy has in recent years struggled to curb the proliferation of AI-made crochet patterns and other AI "slop." Amazon recently required sellers to label photos or videos that feature AI-generated people in response to recent legislation mandating the disclosure. While Etsy has cracked down on the use of AI in listings, it's been infusing the technology throughout more of its website. The company has used AI to build more detailed profiles of shoppers and surface relevant products in search results. The standard defenses against cyberattacks are no longer sufficient: we need ways to prove that code is free of bugs. Formal software verification could provide this guarantee, but it has historically required years of expert effort, making it impractical for most real-world projects. In a collaboration with Theorem , however, we show this is no longer the case: LLMs can now produce formal proofs at large scale, enabling new software development workflows that include proven security guarantees. Using Claude, we proved security properties at the assembly code level (RISC-V) in over 100 real-world open-source software libraries. To our knowledge, this represents the first large-scale effort to use AI to apply formal verification to production software at the assembly code level. While writing the proofs, Claude also discovered bugs that had eluded detection for years, despite trillions of test runs . As model capabilities continue to improve, we expect formal verification to become an essential part of secure software development. Even mature, heavily tested software contains bugs, and LLMs are increasingly adept at finding them. The Linux kernel—one of the most well-tested pieces of software today, deployed on billions of devices worldwide—recently had over 1,000 vulnerabilities disclosed. With frontier models becoming more capable of chaining seemingly benign bugs into critical exploits, we need techniques that can detect and fix these bugs before they can be exploited in the wild. Ideally, such techniques could find and patch all bugs, and then provide some proof that there are no more to be found. Formal verification is one way to do this. In formal verification, developers translate their code into a mathematical model, then try to prove that it always follows some defined set of security rules. If they fail to prove this, that means there could be a bug in the code that would violate a rule, and the nature of the failure implies what the bug might be. Repeating this process (after eliminating the cause of failure each time) will ultimately yield proof that the code is devoid of any bug that would violate those rules. However, formal verification isn’t easy. Proofs can be many times larger than the original code, and writing them requires significant effort and a niche, highly specialized skill set. For instance, it took two person-years to implement the seL4 operating system kernel, but 20 person-years to formally verify it . Accordingly, formal verification has been practical only in truly mission-critical applications, such as Airbus’s avionics code . But LLMs are making it far easier. Frontier models can now produce correctness proofs for real-world software fully autonomously. To demonstrate this, we asked Claude to prove useful security properties across 123 open-source libraries, including showing that some of their executable artifacts can never crash under certain conditions. Specifically, Claude proved that these programs will always exit normally without triggering memory-safety errors or failing assertions, for every input less than 64 MB and every modeled Linux operating system (OS) response and memory layout, under certain assumptions (namely that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V 1 CPU using Linux OS). This is still far away from fixing all possible bugs, but it does get us much closer than before and provides a roadmap toward that end. We’re publishing a subset of these proofs so that anyone can verify and reuse them, along with the RISC-V and OS semantics . Theorem , our collaborator on this project, is also offering to run the same pipeline for other open-source projects , and is publishing a Claude skill to help developers get started with verifying their own code. Formal verification is a broad field with many methodologies. Below, we also describe our initial explorations using other formal verification methods to accelerate other security or software development tasks, such as assessing the security of the zlib compression algorithm, proving behavioral equivalence of a Python interpreter written in Rust, and rooting out long-standing bugs in critical software. The road ahead for formal verification is promising. The cost of writing proofs is falling as models become more intelligent. Moreover, as more code is formalized and methods of achieving security guarantees become more standardized, the ability to reuse or modify proofs across codebases will amortize the cost. We encourage all developers to explore formal verification with LLMs— especially those who previously tried it with less capable models and found it didn’t work. In the rest of this post, we cover our formal verification experiments in more detail. To prove that a piece of software is correct, we must first state what “correct” even means. Correctness is defined by the specification (spec). In some programs, there is a clear way to formally specify the program’s intended behavior. For example, a PNG decoder takes a sequence of bytes and (following RFC 2083 ) decodes these bytes into the corresponding image. But for most programs, things aren’t so straightforward. What would it mean for a text editor or a web browser to be “correct”? The difficulty of obtaining a comprehensive and unambiguous spec is a significant obstacle to verifying software at a larger scale. To address this for the code in the open-source libraries that we sought to prove, we take the approach of automatically converting their preexisting compilable test suites into a spec by encoding the rule “this test suite always passes,” using a general model of what it means to execute any RISC-V-compiled binary on Linux. Historically, proving such specs was intractable, given the inherent complexity of writing a proof that can encompass and make an argument over all possible behaviors and interactions of tens of thousands of assembly instructions over any input (and the fact that proofs tend to be extremely large as a result). This is where today’s LLMs come in: churning through millions of lines of code in pursuit of a well-defined goal is a task that LLMs are extremely well suited for. For this project, we started with fuzz tests . In these tests, developers write an entry point 2 into their code that takes inputs, such that any input that causes a crash is a bug the authors care about. Then the fuzzer, a testing engine, generates enormous numbers of semirandom and mutated inputs at the entry point to try to find a bug (visualized in Figure 1). The longer a fuzzer runs, the more bugs it can find. But this is inherently a brute-force process, with no guarantee of exercising every possible code path, regardless of how many inputs you try. This can also occur even when the properties are not directly specified by the developer. For example, in order for Claude to complete its OSS-Fuzz proof for cpp-httplib, it was necessary to rule out the possibility of a stack overflow due to too much recursion in the std::set destructor. This recursion depth is bounded by the maximum depth of a tree, so Claude had to prove (on machine code!) that libc++’s red-black tree rebalancing algorithm is correctly optimized to keep the tree’s depth logarithmically bounded. Formal verification is an expansive domain. The fuzz-test-to-proof example above is one instance of LLMs making formal verification more widely usable by directly applying proofs to machine code. We’ve also seen success using LLMs with formal verification in other ways. For example, we asked Claude to write a formal spec of RFC 1950 , the technical document that defines the zlib compression file format. Then, we had Claude prove that the zlib implementation in the Linux kernel correctly implements that spec. As with the examples above, Claude proved this property at the binary level, except instead of RISC-V, Claude directly proved the x86-compiled binary using Claude-generated (and heavily tested) formal semantics of the x86 ISA. 7 We then repeated this process for half a dozen other widely used libraries. Along the way, we found some minor (unexploitable) bugs in corner cases, which are in the process of being filed upstream. We draw two conclusions from this exercise: (1) these extremely well-tested codebases are already almost fully correct, and (2) it is possible to prove end-to-end correctness properties about real existing codebases. In another experiment, we asked Claude to develop an interpreter for a large subset of Python in Rust, and to prove (using Verus, a verification tool for Rust) that it adheres to the CPython semantics outlined in an academic paper. We then measured the adherence to CPython’s behavior empirically, running over 1.7 million randomly generated Python programs, finding identical behavior with CPython in 99.95% of tests, with remaining test differences as unsurprising known corner cases. We also found issues in several widely used and critical applications via formal verification attempts of simple security properties. In one of them, we discovered a previously unknown logic bug that had been latent for more than a decade. During an effort to verify a widely used PDF reader, we found as many security bugs in one week as are typically reported in a year. See the Appendix for more details on some of these efforts. One of the key limitations of LLM-assisted formal verification is that the proofs can take hundreds of millions of tokens to produce. Cost-efficiency is critical if our goal is to make these methods available to the entire software ecosystem. Fortunately, there are compelling reasons to expect efficiency to improve. We built 36 small verification tasks from real OSS-Fuzz code . Opus 5.5 proves half of them with about 40% fewer tokens than Opus 5. We expect this trend to continue as models are trained on long verification tasks. When agents work separately, they often end up duplicating a lot of effort. Proofs, like software, are recursively built from smaller proofs—and the smaller the proofs are, the more reusable they tend to be. To measure the impact of this, we let agents copy each other’s proofs as they worked on proving their own targets. When given access to this shared workspace, agents needed 17% fewer tokens than when they worked alone, and some agents even succeeded after previously failing in a solo attempt. We observed the same phenomenon occurring at scale during our OSS-Fuzz proof effort. Most of a proof concerns code that every program contains (particularly initialization of the C runtime and AddressSanitizer), so very different programs can end up with significantly overlapping proofs. Agent teams took advantage of this by copying another team’s finished proof and then adapting it to their own program (Figure 6). This reusability of proofs is how Mathlib , a shared library of formal mathematics in Lean, grew to nearly 300,000 theorems submitted by over 700 contributors: each new proof builds on the existing body of work. We accumulated a similar body of proofs in the course of our OSS-Fuzz effort, some of which we’re including in our release (we are not releasing proofs that may reveal an unpatched bug in the open-source software). As we graduate from these initial experiments, we need a strategy for verifying the enormous body of existing software, starting with the most critical dependencies. As we’ve shown, this can be achieved at scale by using generic specs and working at the binary level, sidestepping the need to rewrite entire codebases in another language. This approach also facilitates the reuse of proofs at package-level granularity, which means that each dependency only needs to be verified once. Dependencies follow a power law: proving even a small set of shared libraries makes a huge swath of software feasible to prove. For more details, see Theorem’s roadmap for verifying the entirety of the Nix ecosystem, which includes critical infrastructure like glibc, OpenSSL, and cURL. In practice, formal verification can sometimes prove less about the security of the code than we would like. “Formally verified” does not mean “bug-free.” Claude can write a proof showing that a compiled program’s behavior satisfies the requirements of a formal spec (which is verified by an external proof checker). However, a proof checker can’t tell you whether your spec matches reality. To match reality, the spec must correctly encompass and model everything about the real-world machine that the verified program runs on, including the CPU and operating system. When bugs show up in verified code, it’s because the spec, or the assumed semantics of the machine, differs from reality. Fortunately, this also means we know where to look for remaining bugs, and how to design a system where those still-possibly-buggy gaps are minimized. Below are the ways this applies to our proofs, and ideas for future work that would close those gaps. The real machine does something the model doesn’t describe. Our proofs are about single-threaded, static RISC-V binaries linked against musl libc. However, most people run these libraries on x86 or ARM and dynamically link them against glibc. To close this gap, we’d need system models that more closely resemble deployed systems. For example, a step toward this would be generating accurate semantics for x86. The trajectory is clear: formal verification, which was historically practical only for bespoke expert-crafted guarantees in the most safety-critical code, will soon be as practical as fuzzing is today for almost all production software. Just like static types, testing frameworks, and other correctness tooling, verification will mature from “bolted-on” to “built-in,” driven not only by LLMs but also by innovations in language design and development workflows. In today’s world—where LLMs automatically scan for and find increasingly more code vulnerabilities—we must use processes that can guarantee code security properties. LLM-scaled formal verification is a promising approach toward securing these guarantees at a scope and scale that were previously unattainable. We encourage others to experiment so we can collectively build a world in which robust software has proliferated very widely and software bugs are a well-understood and quickly addressable rarity. 07 We think that the ability of Claude to—entirely autonomously—generate the formal semantics of an ISA is a separate interesting lesson. While we can not be sure our semantics themselves are perfect, empirically we have found that single-stepping through our semantics can boot an Ubuntu userspace on top of a Linux kernel. Generating these semantics also identified hundreds of mistakes in the official reference documentation, along with a smaller number of bugs in the hardware itself. AI research and products that put safety at the frontier. AI will have a vast impact on the world. We built 36 small verification tasks from real OSS-Fuzz code . Opus 5.5 proves half of them with about 40% fewer tokens than Opus 5. We expect this trend to continue as models are trained on long verification tasks.

When agents work separately, they often end up duplicating a lot of effort. Proofs, like software, are recursively built from smaller proofs—and the smaller the proofs are, the more reusable they tend to be. To measure the impact of this, we let agents copy each other’s proofs as they worked on proving their own targets. When given access to this shared workspace, agents needed 17% fewer tokens than when they worked alone, and some agents even succeeded after previously failing in a solo attempt.

We observed the same phenomenon occurring at scale during our OSS-Fuzz proof effort. Most of a proof concerns code that every program contains (particularly initialization of the C runtime and AddressSanitizer), so very different programs can end up with significantly overlapping proofs. Agent teams took advantage of this by copying another team’s finished proof and then adapting it to their own program (Figure 6).

This reusability of proofs is how Mathlib , a shared library of formal mathematics in Lean, grew to nearly 300,000 theorems submitted by over 700 contributors: each new proof builds on the existing body of work. We accumulated a similar body of proofs in the course of our OSS-Fuzz effort, some of which we’re including in our release (we are not releasing proofs that may reveal an unpatched bug in the open-source software).

As we graduate from these initial experiments, we need a strategy for verifying the enormous body of existing software, starting with the most critical dependencies. As we’ve shown, this can be achieved at scale by using generic specs and working at the binary level, sidestepping the need to rewrite entire codebases in another language.

This approach also facilitates the reuse of proofs at package-level granularity, which means that each dependency only needs to be verified once. Dependencies follow a power law: proving even a small set of shared libraries makes a huge swath of software feasible to prove. For more details, see Theorem’s roadmap for verifying the entirety of the Nix ecosystem, which includes critical infrastructure like glibc, OpenSSL, and cURL.
In practice, formal verification can sometimes prove less about the security of the code than we would like.

“Formally verified” does not mean “bug-free.” Claude can write a proof showing that a compiled program’s behavior satisfies the requirements of a formal spec (which is verified by an external proof checker). However, a proof checker can’t tell you whether your spec matches reality. To match reality, the spec must correctly encompass and model everything about the real-world machine that the verified program runs on, including the CPU and operating system. When bugs show up in verified code, it’s because the spec, or the assumed semantics of the machine, differs from reality. Fortunately, this also means we know where to look for remaining bugs, and how to design a system where those still-possibly-buggy gaps are minimized. Below are the ways this applies to our proofs, and ideas for future work that would close those gaps.

The real machine does something the model doesn’t describe. Our proofs are about single-threaded, static RISC-V binaries linked against musl libc. However, most people run these libraries on x86 or ARM and dynamically link them against glibc. To close this gap, we’d need system models that more closely resemble deployed systems. For example, a step toward this would be generating accurate semantics for x86.

The trajectory is clear: formal verification, which was historically practical only for bespoke expert-crafted guarantees in the most safety-critical code, will soon be as practical as fuzzing is today for almost all production software. Just like static types, testing frameworks, and other correctness tooling, verification will mature from “bolted-on” to “built-in,” driven not only by LLMs but also by innovations in language design and development workflows.

In today’s world—where LLMs automatically scan for and find increasingly more code vulnerabilities—we must use processes that can guarantee code security properties. LLM-scaled formal verification is a promising approach toward securing these guarantees at a scope and scale that were previously unattainable. We encourage others to experiment so we can collectively build a world in which robust software has proliferated very widely and software bugs are a well-understood and quickly addressable rarity.

07 We think that the ability of Claude to—entirely autonomously—generate the formal semantics of an ISA is a separate interesting lesson. While we can not be sure our semantics themselves are perfect, empirically we have found that single-stepping through our semantics can boot an Ubuntu userspace on top of a Linux kernel. Generating these semantics also identified hundreds of mistakes in the official reference documentation, along with a smaller number of bugs in the hardware itself.

AI research and products that put safety at the frontier. AI will have a vast impact on the world. Anthropic is a public benefit corporation dedicated to securing its benefits and mitigating its risks.

This is where today’s LLMs come in: churning through millions of lines of code in pursuit of a well-defined goal is a task that LLMs are extremely well suited for. sources.title: Oura sues rival Ultrahuman again, threatening its U.S. smart ring comeback
passages: Smart ring maker Oura has sued Indian rival Ultrahuman again, seeking to block U.S. sales of its Ring Pro (pictured above) just months after the redesign helped the Bengaluru-based startup return to the American market following an import ban.
Ultrahuman is not the only rival facing legal pressure from Oura.
The company has also pursued patent infringement claims against smart-ring makers including Samsung , RingConn , Circular , and Zepp Health .

passages: Smart ring maker Oura has sued Indian rival Ultrahuman again, seeking to block U.S. sales of its Ring Pro (pictured above) just months after the redesign helped the Bengaluru-based startup return to the American market following an import ban. The case is the latest in a string of patent disputes Oura has brought against competing smart-ring makers, including Samsung and RingConn.

In a complaint filed Thursday in a federal court in Texas, Oura alleged that Ultrahuman’s Ring Pro infringes two of its patents covering the ring’s design and internal components, including its battery and sensors. Oura is seeking monetary damages and a permanent injunction that would stop Ultrahuman from selling the ring.

Ultrahuman’s redesigned Ring Pro, launched in February, received a favorable ruling from U.S. Customs and Border Protection in March, paving the way for the startup’s return to the U.S. market . The decision followed an import ban on Ultrahuman’s earlier Ring Air, which took effect after Oura secured a patent infringement ruling from the International Trade Commission in August last year.

“Ultrahuman has a history of copying Oura’s innovations, as demonstrated by the 2025 ITC ruling against the company,” an Oura spokesperson said in a statement to TechCrunch. “Ultrahuman introduced a redesigned ring but failed to address continued infringement of Oura’s patents, seeking instead to capitalize on our innovation and the market leadership we have built.”

Oura argues that the Customs ruling covered only the patent involved in the earlier dispute, not the two patents cited in its latest lawsuit: D804,471 and 12,769,363. “To protect its patent rights, Oura is now forced to file this complaint of patent infringement,” the company said in its filing.

One of those patents, 12,769,363, is also very new. It was issued to Oura on October 20, just two days before it filed the lawsuit. It covers a smart-ring design incorporating internal components such as a curved battery, circuit board, magnets, and sensors.

Oura has also named Texas-based electronics manufacturer SVTronics as a defendant in the lawsuit. The complaint says SVTronics manufactures the Ring Pro at a facility in Plano, Texas, allegedly under Ultrahuman’s direction and control. It also alleges that both companies infringe Oura’s patents through the manufacture, importation, and sale of the device in the U.S.
Ultrahuman co-founder and CEO Mohit Kumar told TechCrunch the startup was confident in the Ring Pro and would fight the new allegations.

“Oura has now chosen to assert different patents, including one that issued just two days before this lawsuit was filed,” Kumar said. “We will address these claims through the appropriate legal process and will defend our position vigorously. There is no court order affecting Ring Pro, and it remains available to customers in the U.S.”

Oura and Ultrahuman have been fighting over patents since 2023, when Oura sued the Indian startup over its Ring Air, which had helped Ultrahuman make a name for itself in the U.S. Oura brought a separate case before the U.S. International Trade Commission in 2024 that helped it secure a ruling last year, leading to the import ban on the Ring Air.

Ultrahuman is not the only rival facing legal pressure from Oura. The company has also pursued patent infringement claims against smart-ring makers including Samsung , RingConn , Circular , and Zepp Health . Some of those disputes have ended in licensing agreements, with RingConn and Circular agreeing to pay royalties to Oura to continue selling their products .

The dispute emerges as the smart-ring market continues to grow. Research firm IDC expects global shipments to rise 12.8% this year to 4.9 million units and reach about 6.3 million by 2030. While Oura remains a leading player in the category, Ultrahuman is among the growing competitors.

The lawsuit also comes just weeks after Oura shelved its $2.2 billion IPO , citing “uncertainty” in the market. The company has continued to add features to its smart rings, introducing new fitness metrics earlier this week that help users track how workouts affect their cardiovascular health.

In September, Ultrahuman raised $70 million from investors including Qualcomm Ventures and Labcorp, valuing the startup at about $365 million. The startup is also working with Qualcomm on a new smart ring that could run more software directly on the device, as it looks to expand beyond health and fitness tracking into areas such as AI interactions and gaming.
The article has been updated to include comments from Ultrahuman co-founder and CEO Mohit Kumar.

sources.title: Mark Zuckerberg’s creative plan to pay California’s proposed billionaire tax without losing control of Meta
passages: Now, however, the New York Times has reported there’s another reason for the new class: helping Zuckerberg pay for California’s proposed “billionaire tax,” if voters approve it.
Because the new shares carry no votes, he could sell some of them to cover the tax without giving up voting control.
The shares give the holder an ownership stake but no vote on company decisions.

Meta says it will use the stock for capital raising, employee pay, and acquisitions — including its expensive push into AI — while maintaining the current voting structure that favors its founder and CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, who controls around 60% of the vote.
“Looks like billionaires will stay and figure out a way to pay the tax,” Democratic U.S.
Representative Ro Khanna, a vocal proponent of the tax, wrote on X, after news of Meta’s strategy spread online. “If we pass Prop 40, poor California kids can have healthcare,” he added.

When reached for comment by TechCrunch, Meta referred us to a quote included in its recent earnings press release that reiterates that part of the motivation for the creation of the stock was to keep Zuckerberg onboard: “The Special Committee affirmed its belief that it was important for Mr.
Zuckerberg to continue to lead the Company from California, including because it was crucial that Mr.
Zuckerberg remains in close coordination with the Company’s management and in close proximity to Meta Superintelligence Labs.”
Google co-founder Sergey Brin has aggressively campaigned against the measure, even spending a small fortune in an effort to defeat it.

Proposition 40 , which was drafted by Berkeley tax law professors and is being sponsored by California’s largest healthcare union (SEIU United Healthcare Workers West), would level a one-time 5% wealth tax on the net worth of several hundred California billionaires who primarily live in the state.
The Times also reports that Zuckerberg pressed Meta’s board to come up with a plan to protect him from the tax.
According to the paper, he told board members in September that if they couldn’t reach an agreement, he’d list his Palo Alto property for sale, potentially kicking off a media firestorm.
Not long afterward, the stock plan materialized, the newspaper writes.
The filing also describes how the plan would work.
Meta is creating a new class of nonvoting shares, called Class C, and will give shareholders one of them for every Class A or Class B share they own.
The dividend “will not change the voting power of any shareholder,” Meta says.
The Times reporting is partially based on a recent SEC filing that Meta made, which documents the concern surrounding Proposition 40 and how it informed discussions that led to the new stock class.
The filing says that as far back as July, Zuckerberg was discussing the billionaire tax with board members.
